questions.question: Tokenizing "The children are selling the clothes to each other." by splitting on white space and punctuation gives how many tokens?
questions.explanation: The slide's own example: ["The", "children", "are", "selling", "the", "clothes", "to", "each", "other", "."]: the full stop is its own token.

questions.question: True or False: For many African languages tokenization is non-trivial because they are agglutinative: one written word can contain a subject marker, tense, object marker, verb root and more.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The slide splits "Abashana bayazithengiselana izimpahla" into many morphemes ("Aba-shana ba-ya-zi-theng-is-el-an-a"). Whitespace splitting leaves huge, rare words.

questions.question: Why does whitespace tokenization work worse for isiZulu than for English?
choices: Words are agglutinative, so each whitespace "word" packs several morphemes and most word forms are rare
isiZulu has no spaces between words
isiZulu has no punctuation
isiZulu words are always shorter than English words
questions.explanation: A whitespace token in isiZulu often corresponds to a whole English clause, so the vocabulary explodes and most words are seen rarely. This returns in L4 (BPE) and L9 (tokenizers for African languages).

questions.question: Which output is typical of stemming rather than lemmatization?
choices: "studies" → "studi"
"ran" → "run"
"better" → "good"
"mice" → "mouse"
questions.explanation: Stemming chops off endings with crude heuristics, so it can produce non-words. Mapping "ran" → "run" or "better" → "good" needs a vocabulary and morphological analysis: lemmatization.

questions.question: True or False: Lemmatization uses a vocabulary and morphological analysis, normally aiming to remove inflectional endings only and return the dictionary form (the lemma).
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The slide's definition: runs, running, ran → run.

questions.question: Which statements about stemming and lemmatization are true?
choices: Both aim to reduce inflectional (and sometimes derivationally related) forms to a common base form
Lemmatization returns a dictionary word (the lemma)
Stemming always returns a valid dictionary word
"car, cars, car's, cars'" → "car" is an example of this kind of reduction
questions.explanation: Stemming is a crude heuristic and can produce non-words.

questions.question: Which of these is a bound morpheme?
choices: "-ness" in "kindness"
"kind" in "kindness"
"cat"
"run"
questions.explanation: A bound morpheme does not occur on its own in the language; "-ness" only appears attached to a root or stem.

questions.question: True or False: An unbound (free) morpheme is one that can be found on its own in the language.
choices: True
False

questions.question: Which pair is an example of inflection rather than derivation?
choices: come + s → comes
kind + ness → kindness
teach + er → teacher
happy + ness → happiness
questions.explanation: Inflection usually keeps the word class and is required by grammar ("comes" is still a verb). Derivation forms a new word and usually changes the class (adjective → noun).

questions.question: Which statements about derivation and inflection are true?
choices: Derivation forms a new word or stem, usually changing the word class
Inflection changes meaning in a predictable way and is invoked by grammar (obligatory)
Inflection usually changes a noun into a verb
Both work by adding affixes

questions.question: What is a corpus?
choices: A computer-readable collection of text or speech
The vocabulary of a model
A single sentence used for testing
A table of word counts
questions.explanation: Plural: corpora (slide 15).

questions.question: True or False: The data a BPE tokenizer is trained on (its corpus) does not have to be the same data used to train the model.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: L4 slide 37: the tokenizer's input is "a corpus of text to train the tokenizer, not necessarily the same data we use to train our model".

questions.question: With a vocabulary of 50,000 words, what is the cosine similarity between the one-hot vectors of "cat" and "kitten"?
questions.explanation: Different one-hot vectors are orthogonal, so their dot product (and cosine) is 0 for every pair: one-hot vectors capture no similarity of meaning.

questions.question: Which are problems with one-hot word vectors?
choices: Their size equals the vocabulary size
They are sparse (almost all zeros)
Every pair of words is equally (dis)similar
They cannot be fed into a linear layer
questions.explanation: A one-hot vector times a weight matrix selects a row: that is exactly an embedding lookup (Quiz 1 Q19).

questions.question: The "Tej" example (A bottle of ___ is on the table; ___ makes you drunk; we make ___ out of honey) shows that:
choices: We can infer a word's meaning from the contexts it appears in
Rare words cannot be understood
Meaning comes from spelling
Words have no meaning outside a dictionary
questions.explanation: Tej is an alcoholic drink made from honey: you can work this out from its contexts alone. Rows of the context table that are similar (Tej and wine) belong to words with similar meaning.

questions.question: True or False: Count-based methods first build a word–context matrix and then reduce its dimensionality, because the raw matrix is huge and sparse.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slides 33–35: (1) construct the matrix, (2) reduce its dimensionality (e.g. truncated SVD), because of size and sparsity.

questions.question:
Use the corpus "I saw a cute grey cat. a loving, cute cat" with punctuation removed (so the tokens are: I saw a cute grey cat a loving cute cat). The context of a word is the words up to 2 positions to its left and right.
Give the co-occurrence counts (a) $N(cat, cute)$, (b) $N(cute, a)$, (c) $N(grey, saw)$, (d) $N(a, cute)$.
questions.solution:
Positions: 1 I, 2 saw, 3 a, 4 cute, 5 grey, 6 cat, 7 a, 8 loving, 9 cute, 10 cat.
(a) Both "cat"s have "cute" within 2 positions (position 4 for the cat at 6; position 9 for the cat at 10): 2.
(b) "cute" at 4 has "a" at 3; "cute" at 9 has "a" at 7: 2.
(c) "grey" at 5 sees positions 3–7; "saw" is at 2: 0.
(d) 2: the matrix is symmetric for a symmetric window.
questions.explanation: This is the slide's toy corpus; check your full table against the finished one on slide 42.

questions.question: True or False: In a co-occurrence matrix with a symmetric window, $N(w, c) = N(c, w)$.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Each time $c$ is within $L$ words of $w$, $w$ is within $L$ words of $c$.

questions.question:
A word–context count matrix has rows (words) w1, w2, w3 and columns (contexts) c1, c2, c3:
$$\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}$$
Using $\text{PMI}(w, c) = \log_2 \frac{P(w, c)}{P(w)P(c)}$ with probabilities from the counts, and $\text{PPMI} = \max(0, \text{PMI})$ (0 for zero counts), give (a) PPMI(w1, c1), (b) PPMI(w1, c2), (c) PPMI(w3, c3).
questions.explanation: PPMI is in Tutorial 1.4, not on the slides (L2 recommends a PMI reading). PMI compares how often $w$ and $c$ co-occur with how often they would by chance; negative values are unreliable with sparse counts, so they are clipped to 0.

questions.question: Why is PPMI often used instead of raw co-occurrence counts?
choices: Raw counts are dominated by frequent words such as "the"; PMI measures whether two words co-occur more than chance
PPMI makes the matrix smaller
Raw counts cannot be negative
PPMI turns the matrix into one-hot vectors
questions.explanation: Frequent function words co-occur with everything. PMI divides by what independence predicts, and PPMI clips unreliable negative values to 0.

questions.question: Label the Word2Vec skip-gram path and its two ways to train context predictions.

image.alt: A centre word flows through an embedding and context scores, then branches to two training choices, numbered 1–5.

questions.explanation: Skip-gram starts from a centre word and predicts surrounding words. A full softmax scores the whole vocabulary; negative sampling instead distinguishes the true pair from a few sampled non-pairs with sigmoid decisions. Both train the word vectors.

questions.question: True or False: Word2Vec learns word vectors by going over the text with a sliding window and, for each central word, adjusting the vectors to increase the probability of its context words.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 4: an iterative method, one window position at a time.

questions.question: What does Word2Vec minimise?
choices: The average negative log-likelihood of the context words given each central word: $-\frac{1}{T}\sum_t \sum_{-m \le j \le m, j \ne 0} \log P(w_{t+j} \mid w_t, \theta)$
The squared distance between every pair of word vectors
The number of co-occurrences in the word–context matrix
The negative log-likelihood of the central word given the whole document
questions.explanation: Slide 11: the likelihood is a product over positions and window offsets; the loss is its average negative log.

questions.question: True or False: Minimising the negative log-likelihood is the same as maximising the likelihood of the observed context words.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: $-\log$ is decreasing, so the minimum of $-\log L$ is the maximum of $L$.

questions.question: In Word2Vec, $P(o \mid c) = \frac{\exp(u_o^\top v_c)}{\sum_{w \in V} \exp(u_w^\top v_c)}$. Which statements are true?
choices: Each word has two vectors: $v_w$ when it is a central word and $u_w$ when it is a context word
The dot product measures similarity: a larger dot product gives a larger probability
The denominator normalises over the entire vocabulary
After training, both vector sets are always concatenated
questions.explanation: Once trained, the context vectors are usually thrown away and only the word (central) vectors are used (slide 12).

questions.question:
A toy Word2Vec model has vocabulary {cute, grey, the, cat}. The central vector of "cat" is $v_{cat} = (1,0.5)$ and the context vectors are $u_{cute} = (1,1)$, $u_{grey} = (0.5,0)$, $u_{the} = (0,-1)$, $u_{cat} = (2,1)$.
(a) $P(cute \mid cat)$  (b) $P(the \mid cat)$  (c) the loss term $J = -\log P(cute \mid cat)$ (natural log).
questions.solution:
Dot products $u_w^\top v_{cat}$: cute 1.5, grey 0.5, the -0.5, cat 2.5.
Softmax: cute 0.2369, grey 0.0871, the 0.0321, cat 0.6439.
(c) $-\ln 0.2369 = 1.4402$.
questions.explanation: Note that "cat" also has a context vector: a word can be in its own vocabulary of contexts, which is one reason Word2Vec keeps two vectors per word.

questions.question: One gradient step on $J_{t,j} = -\log P(cute \mid cat)$ with the full softmax does what?
choices: Increases the similarity of $v_{cat}$ and $u_{cute}$ and decreases the similarity of $v_{cat}$ with $u_w$ for all other words
Increases the similarity of $v_{cat}$ with every context vector
Updates only $u_{cute}$
Updates every central vector $v_w$
questions.explanation: Slides 22–23. Only $v_{cat}$ among the central vectors, and every $u_w$ among the context vectors, are updated at this step.

questions.question: True or False: Word2Vec pushes $v_{cat}$ away from the context vectors of "grey" and "playing" at a step about "cute", even though they are also valid contexts of "cat"; on average over all updates it still learns the right distribution.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 23: this sounds strange, but we make updates for every context word, so on average the vectors learn the distribution of possible contexts.

questions.concept: Why the full softmax is inefficient
questions.question: Why is training Word2Vec with the full softmax extremely inefficient?
choices: Every step needs dot products with, and updates to, the context vectors of all |V| words
The sliding window is too small
Gradients cannot be computed through a softmax
Each word needs a separate model
questions.explanation: The normalising sum has |V| terms (often hundreds of thousands), and all |V| context vectors change at each step.

questions.concept: Why the full softmax is inefficient
questions.question: A vocabulary has 100,000 words and negative sampling uses $K = 5$ negatives. How many vectors are updated at one step (a) with the full softmax, (b) with negative sampling?
questions.solution:
(a) $v_{cat}$ plus $u_w$ for every word: $|V| + 1 = 100001$.
(b) $v_{cat}$, $u_{cute}$ and the $K$ negatives: $K + 2 = 7$.

questions.question:
With negative sampling the loss for one (central, context) pair is $J = -\log \sigma(u_o^\top v_c) - \sum_{w \in \text{neg}} \log \sigma(-u_w^\top v_c)$. Take $v_c = (1,1)$, $u_o = (1,0.5)$ and three negatives (0.5,-1), (-1,0), (0,0.5).
(a) $\sigma(u_o^\top v_c)$  (b) the positive term $-\log\sigma(u_o^\top v_c)$  (c) the total loss (natural logs).
questions.explanation: A binary logistic classifier: the true pair should score high, the $K$ random pairs low. No sum over the vocabulary.

questions.question: True or False: In negative sampling the softmax over the whole vocabulary is replaced by sigmoids for the true context word and $K$ randomly chosen "negative" words.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 26; the sigmoid is $\sigma(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-x})$.

questions.question: True or False: Skip-gram predicts each context word from the central word (one at a time); CBOW predicts the central word from the sum of the context vectors.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 27.

questions.question: Where does GloVe get its information from?
choices: Global corpus co-occurrence statistics

questions.question: Which statements about evaluating word embeddings are true?
choices: Intrinsic evaluation (similarity, analogy) is usually fast but may not tell you what is better in practice
Extrinsic evaluation on a real task tells you directly what is better, but training several task models is expensive
Correlation with human similarity scores is an intrinsic benchmark
Using embeddings in a POS tagger and measuring accuracy is intrinsic
questions.explanation: A POS tagger is a downstream task, so that is extrinsic (Quiz 1 Q33).

questions.question:
Toy embeddings: king $(3,1,2)$, man $(2,0,1)$, woman $(2,2,1)$, queen $(3,3,2)$, prince $(3,0,2)$, girl $(1,2,0)$.
(a)–(c) Compute $v(king) - v(man) + v(woman)$.
(d) Its cosine similarity with $v(queen)$.
(e) Its cosine similarity with $v(prince)$.
questions.solution:
$(3,1,2) - (2,0,1) + (2,2,1) = (3,3,2)$.
Cosines: queen 1, girl 0.8581, prince 0.7687: the nearest (excluding the query words) is queen.
questions.explanation: Analogy benchmarks (intrinsic): find the word closest to $v(a^*) - v(a) + v(b)$ and check it is the expected one.

questions.question: True or False: The analogy $v(kings) - v(king) + v(queen) \approx v(queens)$ is an example of a syntactic relationship captured linearly in the embedding space.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 32 separates semantic (king/queen) and syntactic (singular/plural) analogies.

questions.question: What does Lecture 2 say about semantic spaces of different languages?
choices: They are (somewhat) linearly related: one space can be linearly mapped onto another so that translations match
They are unrelated, so translation needs parallel sentences
They are identical without any mapping
They only align for languages with the same alphabet
questions.explanation: Slides 37–38: "Word Translation Without Parallel Data".

questions.question: True or False: The cross-lingual mapping result suggests word translations can be learned with little or no parallel data.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The cited paper learns the mapping without parallel data; your notes add that a few seed translations help.

questions.question: Compute the cosine similarity of (a) $(1,2,2)$ and $(2,1,2)$, (b) $(1,2,2)$ and $(-1,-2,-2)$, (c) $(1,2,2)$ and $(2, 4, 4)$.
questions.solution: $\cos = \frac{a \cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}$. (a) $8/(3 \times 3) = 0.8889$. (b) $-9/9 = -1$ (opposite direction). (c) Same direction: 1, whatever the length.

questions.question: Let $W = [v_1\ v_2\ v_3\ v_4]$ (columns are word vectors) and $x = (0, 0, 1, 0)^\top$ be a one-hot input. What is $Wx$, and what does this say about an embedding layer?
choices: $v_3$: multiplying by a one-hot vector just selects a column, so an embedding layer (look up index 3) is functionally the same as a linear layer on one-hot input
$v_1 + v_2 + v_3 + v_4$: an embedding layer sums all word vectors
The zero vector, because most of $x$ is zero
$v_3^\top v_3$: an embedding layer computes a dot product
questions.explanation: Devon: "If you're in an exam, and I may ask this… draw the matrix as a vector of vectors and do the dot product." Storing the index instead of a giant one-hot vector is what makes the embedding layer efficient (L2).

questions.question: In Word2Vec's objective, why do we talk about the likelihood $L(\theta)$ rather than just a probability?
choices: The likelihood is a function of the parameters $\theta$ given the observed data, $L(\theta) = P(\text{data} \mid \theta)$; training searches for the $\theta$ that makes the observed context words most probable
Likelihood and probability are two names for the same function of the data
The likelihood is the probability of the parameters given the data
Likelihoods are always larger than probabilities
questions.explanation: Devon's Gaussian example: slide the mean until the data is most probable. He said he wants you to understand this distinction; then the negative (to minimise) and the log (products become sums, more stable).

choices: True
False
questions.question: True or False: Word2Vec's loss treats every context word in the window as independent of the others, which is why the probabilities of the context words are simply multiplied.
questions.explanation: True. Devon: "make clear notes of this… it all corresponds to a massive independence assumption." Unnatural, but doing a simple thing fast on a huge corpus works.

questions.question: In $P(o \mid c) = \dfrac{\exp(u_o^\top v_c)}{\sum_{w} \exp(u_w^\top v_c)}$, why is the dot product passed through $\exp$ before normalising?
choices: Dot products (propensities) can be negative, which would make the ratio ill-defined; exp maps them to positive values and keeps their order (it is monotonic)
To make training slower and more stable
Because the dot product is always larger than 1
To turn the dot product into a distance
questions.explanation: Devon's propensity argument: probability = propensity ÷ sum of propensities only works for positive propensities. A "definitely not a cat" score of −2 would give a 'probability' above 1.

questions.question: Which statements about the move from the full softmax to negative sampling in Word2Vec are true?
choices: The full softmax sums over the whole vocabulary at every update, which is too slow
Only $K$ random negative words (not the true context word) are pushed down per update
The multiclass softmax becomes several binary (sigmoid / logistic) decisions
It works because negative sampling makes the vectors orthogonal
Negative sampling uses the true context word as one of the negatives
questions.explanation: Devon: "As long as you understand how Word2Vec goes from the softmax classification to the sigmoid, I am happy." With two classes, fixing one propensity at 0 turns softmax into a sigmoid, and exp being monotonic keeps the ordering.

questions.question: What weakness of CBOW did Devon point out compared with skip-gram?
choices: The context vectors are summed, so one well-trained context word can dominate the sum and carry the prediction while the others stay poor (an attribution / credit-assignment problem)
CBOW can't be trained with gradient descent
CBOW predicts the context words, so it is slower than skip-gram
CBOW needs labelled data
questions.explanation: Skip-gram forces a good representation for each context word separately (four separate data points), which Devon prefers; CBOW's sum also loses order.

choices: True
False
questions.question: True or False: Word2Vec spaces trained separately on English and Spanish can be mapped onto each other with a single linear map learned from a few word pairs, and translations of words not in those pairs then come out "for free".
questions.explanation: True (L2). This suggests semantic spaces across languages are roughly linear transformations of each other.

questions.question: Explain how skip-gram Word2Vec learns word embeddings. Include the training objective (why a negative log-likelihood), the independence assumption, how $P(o \mid c)$ is computed, and how and why negative sampling changes it. (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
By the distributional hypothesis, a word's meaning comes from its context, so the parameters (each word's focal vector $v$ and context vector $u$) are trained so a focal word predicts its context words within a window of $m$.

Objective: maximise the likelihood $L(\theta) = \prod_t \prod_{j \ne 0} P(w_{t+j} \mid w_t; \theta)$; take the negative log (minimise; products become sums; stable) and average. Multiplying assumes every context word is independent.

$P(o \mid c) = \exp(u_o^\top v_c) / \sum_w \exp(u_w^\top v_c)$: the dot product measures similarity; exp makes the propensities positive; dividing by the sum normalises over the vocabulary.

Negative sampling: the sum over the vocabulary is too slow, so each update raises $\sigma(u_o^\top v_c)$ for the true pair and lowers $\sigma(u_{w_k}^\top v_c)$ for $K$ random negatives: several binary logistic decisions instead of one huge softmax. Afterwards the context vectors are usually discarded.

rubric.point: Distributional hypothesis; focal and context vectors are the parameters
Likelihood over windows; why negative and log
Independence assumption stated
Softmax over dot products, with why exp
Negative sampling: K negatives, avoids summing over the vocabulary
Softmax becomes sigmoid / binary logistic decisions

questions.question: Label the five stages of a text CNN classifier.

image.alt: A five-stage text CNN from word vectors to class scores, with boxes numbered 1–5.

questions.explanation: Filters detect local phrases at every position. Their feature maps vary with sentence length; global pooling makes one fixed-size sentence vector, which the classifier turns into class probabilities.

questions.question: Match each example to its classification type.

pairs.prompt: Which of 20 news topics an article is about
Choosing all the hashtags that fit a tweet

questions.explanation: Multi-label: several labels can be correct at once, so each label gets its own yes/no decision (sigmoid), unlike a single softmax.

questions.question: Which output layer suits a multi-label problem (several labels can be correct)?
choices: A sigmoid per label with binary cross-entropy for each
One softmax over all labels with multiclass cross-entropy
A single sigmoid
An argmax with no probabilities
questions.explanation: A softmax forces the labels to compete and sum to 1, which suits exactly one correct label. Contrast next-token prediction (L5), where one softmax and multiclass CE is right.

questions.question:
A classifier's linear layer outputs scores $(2,0.5,-1)$ for classes (pos, neu, neg). The true class is "neu".
(a) $P(neu)$ after the softmax. (b) The cross-entropy loss (natural log). (c) The loss if the true class were "pos".
questions.explanation: With a one-hot target, cross-entropy is $-\log p(\text{correct class})$: low when the model is confident and right, high when it is confident and wrong.

questions.question: Which statements about the final linear layer + softmax of a neural classifier are true?
choices: It is logistic regression on the feature vector $h$
Each class $k$ has a weight vector $w_k$, and its score is $w_k \cdot h + b_k$
Training makes text vectors point in the direction of their class vectors
It maps from $K$ classes back to $d$ features
questions.explanation: It maps $d \to K$. The class weight vectors are "vector representations of classes" (slide 37).

questions.question: Which statements describe the "features + classifier" view?
choices: A feature extractor turns the text into a vector $h$; a classifier turns $h$ into a probability distribution over classes
In classical methods, a human designs the features (e.g. bag of words, n-grams)
In neural methods, the network learns which features matter
Neural features are always easier to interpret than hand-crafted ones
questions.explanation: Interpretability is a weakness of learned features (Quiz 1 Q23).

questions.question:
Three documents: D1 "the cat sat on the mat", D2 "the dog sat", D3 "a cat and a dog". Use $\text{tf-idf}(w, d) = N(w, d) \times \ln\frac{|D|}{|\{d \in D: w \in d\}|}$ (natural log).
(a) tf-idf(the, D1)  (b) tf-idf(cat, D1)  (c) tf-idf(mat, D1)  (d) tf-idf(a, D3)
questions.explanation: A word that appears in every document gets idf $\ln 1 = 0$. tf-idf weights are one way to weight a bag of embeddings (slide 47). The slide does not fix the log base; state the one you use.

questions.question: A word appears in every document of the corpus. What is its idf?
choices: The number of documents
Undefined
questions.explanation: $\log(|D|/|D|) = \log 1 = 0$, so it gets no weight however often it appears.

questions.concept: Bag of embeddings and weighted BOE
questions.question:
A 3-word text has embeddings $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(3,3)$.
(a)–(b) The bag of embeddings (sum). (c)–(d) The weighted BOE with weights $(0.5,0.25,0.25)$.
questions.explanation: Word order is lost in both: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" give the same vector.

questions.concept: Convolution as a linear layer on windows
questions.question: True or False: A convolution with $m$ filters and kernel size $k$ over $d$-dimensional embeddings is a linear layer from $k \cdot d$ to $m$, applied to every window.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 78: concatenate the $k$ vectors in the window (size $k \cdot d$) and multiply by a $(k \cdot d) \times m$ matrix.

questions.concept: CNN output shapes, stride and padding
questions.question:
A 1D convolution runs over a sentence of 12 tokens with 100-dimensional embeddings, using 64 filters of width 3.
Give the number of output positions for (a) stride 1, no padding, (b) stride 1 with 1 padding token on each side, (c) stride 2, no padding. (d) How many channels does each output position have?
questions.solution:
Output length $= \lfloor (n + 2p - k)/s \rfloor + 1$.
(a) $12 - 3 + 1 = 10$. (b) $12 + 2 - 3 + 1 = 12$ (padding keeps the length, like the slide's <pad> tokens). (c) $\lfloor 9/2 \rfloor + 1 = 5$. (d) One channel per filter: 64.

questions.question: Same layer: 64 filters of width 3 over 100-dimensional embeddings. (a) Weights per filter. (b) Total parameters including one bias per filter. (c) Total if the kernel width is 5 instead.
questions.explanation: The count does not depend on the sentence length: the same weights are reused at every position (parameter sharing).

questions.question:
A sentence classifier (as in "CNNs for Sentence Classification") uses three convolutions with kernel sizes 2, 3, 4, each with 100 filters, over 300-dimensional embeddings, then max-over-time pooling and concatenation, then a linear layer to 5 classes.
(a) Convolution parameters (with biases). (b) Size of the concatenated vector $h$. (c) Parameters of the final linear layer (with biases).
questions.solution: (a) $100(2 \times 300 + 1)$ + $100(3 \times 300 + 1)$ + $100(4 \times 300 + 1)$ = 270,300. (b) Each convolution gives 100 pooled features: $3 \times 100 = 300$. (c) $300 \times 5 + 5 = 1505$.

questions.concept: Several kernel sizes, stacking and receptive field
questions.question:
How many input tokens does one output of the last layer see (its receptive field)?
(a) Two stacked width-3 convolutions, stride 1.
(b) Three stacked width-3 convolutions, stride 1.
(c) Width-3 convolution, then width-2 pooling with stride 2, then a width-3 convolution (all other strides 1).
questions.solution:
$r = 1 + \sum_l (k_l - 1)\prod_{i<l} s_i$.
(a) $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$. (b) $1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7$. (c) $1 + 2 + 1 + 2 \times 2 = 8$: pooling with stride doubles how far the next layer reaches.
questions.explanation: Stacking blocks lets later layers see longer phrases; a larger kernel also grows the receptive field (Quiz 1 Q10).

questions.question: Which statements about invariance and equivariance are true?
choices: Convolution is translation equivariant: shifting the input shifts the feature map
Global max pooling over the feature map makes the result translation invariant
A CNN classifier with global pooling still depends on the order of words inside each window
Global pooling makes the model care exactly where in the text a phrase occurs
questions.explanation: "We don't care where the cat is, we care that it is somewhere."

questions.question: Why is global pooling needed before the linear layer in a CNN text classifier?
choices: It turns a variable-length sequence of feature vectors into one fixed-size vector
It adds non-linearity
It increases the number of filters
It makes the model recurrent
questions.explanation: The final block is always global pooling: "you need it to get a single vector".

questions.concept: CNN output shapes, stride and padding
questions.question: A width-5 convolution (stride 1, 2 padding tokens on each side) runs over 20 tokens with 50 filters, followed by local max pooling of size 2 with stride 2. What is the output shape (positions × channels)?
questions.explanation: Convolution: $(20 + 4 - 5)/1 + 1 = 20$ positions × 50 channels. Pooling 2 with stride 2 halves the positions: 10 × 50. Pooling never changes the number of channels.

questions.question: Which statements about bag-of-words and n-gram features are true?
choices: Bag of words loses word order: "I don't like the cat, wake it up" and "I like the cat, don't wake it up" look almost the same
Adding bigrams such as "don't like" as their own features recovers some local word order
Using large n-grams makes the feature vector explode (curse of dimensionality) and they still carry no semantics
Bag of words is a neural feature extractor
questions.explanation: These were Devon's three in-class questions on L3: why counting is bad, how bigrams fix it, and why not just use big n-grams. BoW + bigrams was the popular trade-off for SVMs.

questions.question: In a text classifier's final layer, class $k$ gets the score $w_k^\top h + b_k$. If the sentence vector $h$ were all zeros, what would decide the prediction?
choices: Only the biases $b_k$: the model's prior preference for each class (e.g. the most common class)
Nothing: every class gets probability zero
The largest weight vector $w_k$
The softmax temperature
questions.explanation: Devon's Harry Potter example: with a meaningless $h$, the best guess is the class prior (book 5 has the most pages). Each $w_k$ is a direction "searching" the semantic space for its class.

questions.question: Why is max pooling usually preferred to mean pooling in CNN text classifiers?
choices: A following linear layer can already learn an average, but it can't learn a maximum; max adds a useful non-linearity ("did this phrase appear anywhere?")
Mean pooling isn't translation invariant
Max pooling uses fewer parameters
Mean pooling can't handle variable-length input
questions.explanation: L3 recording. Both pool over positions, so both handle variable length; max keeps the strongest filter response wherever it occurs.

questions.question: Label the BPE training stages and the result used to tokenize new words.

image.alt: A four-stage BPE flow from characters through pair counting and learned rules to a new tokenization, numbered 1–4.

questions.explanation: During training, repeatedly count adjacent pairs and merge the most frequent one, saving each merge in order. At inference, start from characters and apply those learned merges in order; do not recalculate pair frequencies on the new word.

questions.question:
A vanilla RNN computes $h_t = \tanh(h_{t-1}W_h + x_t W_x)$ (row vectors), with $W_h = \begin{bmatrix}0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}$, $W_x = \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $h_0 = (0, 0)$. The inputs are $x_1 = (1, 0)$, $x_2 = (0, 1)$.
(a)–(b) $h_1$. (c)–(d) $h_2$.
questions.explanation: The same $W_h$ and $W_x$ are used at every step. For classification the final state $h_T$ is the text representation.

questions.question: A vanilla RNN has input size 100 and hidden size 50, $h_t = \tanh(h_{t-1}W_h + x_tW_x + b)$. How many parameters does it have (a) in $W_h$, (b) in $W_x$, (c) in total with the bias?
questions.solution: (a) $50 \times 50 = 2500$. (b) $100 \times 50 = 5000$. (c) $2500 + 5000 + 50 = 7550$, the same however long the sentence is.

questions.question: True or False: The simplest RNN classifier reads the whole text and uses the final hidden state as the text representation $h$.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 5: the final state "knows" everything because it saw all tokens (though it is biased towards recent ones).

questions.question: Back-propagating through an RNN multiplies the gradient by roughly the same factor at every time step. Over 50 steps, what does a factor of (a) 0.9 and (b) 1.1 do to a gradient of size 1?
questions.explanation: "Lots of matrix multiplications either blow up or diminish the activity going through the network" (slide 6). The tanh derivative is at most 1, which pushes towards vanishing.

questions.question: Which are the problems with recurrence listed in Lecture 4?
choices: Vanishing and exploding gradients
Credit assignment: position information is subtle and often lost; recency bias
A fixed vector size that does not grow with the sentence
RNNs cannot handle variable-length input
questions.explanation: RNNs do handle variable-length input; the problem is that the summary vector has a fixed size.

questions.question: What does a bidirectional RNN classifier use as its text representation?
choices: The final states of a forward and a backward RNN (concatenated)
Only the backward RNN's first state
The average of the input embeddings
The output of a softmax
questions.explanation: Each direction is biased towards the words it read last, so combining them covers both ends of the sentence.

questions.question: True or False: In a multi-layer RNN the states of one RNN are fed as the inputs of the next.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 9.

questions.concept: Word embeddings: scratch, pretrained or fine-tuned
questions.question: Match each way of getting word embeddings to what it knows (slide 15).

pairs.answer: May not be enough to learn relationships between words
Know relationships between words, but are not specific to the task
Know relationships between words and are adapted for the task

options: May not be enough to learn relationships between words
Know relationships between words, but are not specific to the task
Know relationships between words and are adapted for the task
Know the meaning of every word in every context
questions.explanation: The third option "transfers" knowledge from a huge unlabelled corpus: a preview of Lecture 8.

questions.question: Which are text data-augmentation methods from Lecture 4?
choices: Word dropout: replace random words with UNK or random words
Replace words with synonyms from a thesaurus
Back-translation: translate to another language and back to get a paraphrase
Flipping the text backwards
questions.explanation: Augmentation should change the text while keeping its meaning; reversing word order destroys it. Word dropout is "the most simple and popular".

questions.question: How does Lecture 4 find out what a convolutional filter has learned?
choices: Find the positions where the filter activates most and trace them back to the n-grams in the input
Read the filter weights as words
Remove the filter and retrain
Look at the gradient of the loss
questions.explanation: Top n-grams per filter: e.g. one filter fires on "poorly designed junk", "utterly useless .".

questions.question: True or False: A single convolutional filter tends to activate for a family of n-grams with similar meaning (e.g. "still working perfect", "works … perfect", "still near perfect").
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 30: "a filter activates for a family of n-grams with similar meaning".

questions.question: What are the problems with splitting text into whole words?
choices: The model has a predefined vocabulary
Unseen words become the meaningless UNK token
Rare word forms get poor representations
Frequent words are split into characters
questions.explanation: The fix is to represent rare or unknown words by subwords (morphemes are the smallest units of meaning).

questions.question: True or False: In BPE, frequent words are kept intact while rare words are split into subwords.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 35; this is adaptive, unlike a fixed character or word vocabulary.

questions.question:
This is the slide example. A BPE tokenizer is trained on the word counts cat ×4, mat ×5, mats ×2, mate ×3, ate ×3, eat ×2, starting from characters (pairs are counted only inside words).
(a) How many times does the most frequent pair occur at the first step?
(b) After merging it, how many times does the most frequent pair occur at the second step?
(c) How many tokens is "mats" after these two merges?
questions.solution:
Merges: 1. a+t (19), 2. m+at (10), 3. c+at (4).
(a) "a"+"t" occurs in every word: $4 + 5 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 19$.
(b) "m"+"at": mat 5 + mats 2 + mate 3 = 10.
(c) "mats" → mat · s: 2 tokens.
questions.explanation: The slide then merges "c"+"at". Frequent words such as "cat" and "mat" end up as single symbols, while plurals ("mats") stay split longer.

questions.question:
Train BPE on the word counts low ×5, lower ×2, newest ×6, widest ×3, starting from characters. Count pairs only inside words, and break ties by choosing the alphabetically first pair.
(a)–(d) Give the count of the pair merged at each of the first four steps.
(e) Using these four merges in order, how many tokens is the new word "lowest"?
questions.solution:
Merges in order: 1. e+s (9); 2. es+t (9); 3. l+o (7); 4. lo+w (7).
Words after four merges: low ×5, low · e · r ×2, n · e · w · est ×6, w · i · d · est ×3.
(e) Apply the merges in order to l o w e s t: low · est → 2 tokens.
questions.explanation: Inference applies the learned merges in the order they were learned (the merge table is ordered), so BPE is deterministic. A word never seen in training still gets segmented into known pieces.

questions.question: How does a trained BPE tokenizer segment new text?
choices: Split words into characters, then apply the merges from the merge table in order, wherever they occur
Look each whole word up in the vocabulary and use UNK if it is missing
Pick the longest vocabulary token at each position, greedily from the left
Sample a segmentation at random
questions.explanation: The merge table is ordered: merges higher in the table were more frequent and get priority. BPE is deterministic.

questions.question: True or False: In the slide's BPE implementation detail, a marker such as "@@" lets the tokenizer treat "mat" as a whole word differently from "mat" inside "mat s".
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 44: the marker distinguishes whole-word tokens from word-internal pieces.

questions.question: What is the difference between a kernel's receptive field and its effective receptive field?
choices: The receptive field is what the kernel sees in its own input layer; the effective receptive field is how much of the original input it sees through the layers below
They are the same thing
The effective receptive field is the kernel size minus the stride
The receptive field is measured on the input; the effective one on the output
questions.explanation: Devon: "I do expect you know these words." Depth lets a small kernel see more of the sentence (a width-2 kernel after pooling might see about six words).

questions.question: Two width-3 convolutions (stride 1) are stacked over word embeddings. (a) What is the receptive field of one output of layer 2 on layer 1's outputs? (b) What is its effective receptive field on the input words?
questions.solution: (a) It sees 3 layer-1 outputs. (b) Each of those sees 3 words, overlapping by 2: $3 + (3-1) = 5$ words.
questions.explanation: Each extra width-$k$ layer (stride 1) adds $k - 1$ words to the effective receptive field.

questions.question: Devon: "If I asked you in a test, what are the two primary problems with the RNN?" Which two was he mainly looking for?
choices: Everything has to be squeezed into a fixed-size vector, so long sentences are hard to represent
Credit assignment: it is hard to know which earlier word (through which recurrent step) caused an error
RNNs can't be stacked
RNNs can't process words in order
questions.explanation: He said he would accept any of three (vanishing/exploding gradients is the third), but these two were the ones he wanted. The tutorial's "unstable to train" version wants vanishing and exploding gradients.

questions.question: In $h_t = \tanh(W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b)$, why can't $W_h$ simply be the identity matrix?
choices: Addition is commutative ($h + x = x + h$), so without processing the memory the cell would lose the order of the words
The identity matrix has no inverse
It would make the hidden state too small
Because tanh needs a square matrix
questions.explanation: L4 recording: $W_h$ processes the previous memory so it can absorb the new word in an order-sensitive way.

questions.question: Why does the RNN cell use tanh rather than ReLU, and what does it cost?
choices: tanh saturates, so "really really really … like" doesn't keep growing in magnitude across a long sequence
Saturation is an inductive bias that groups very positive (or negative) sentences together
The flat regions give very small (vanishing) gradients, which slows training
tanh only outputs positive values
questions.explanation: L4 recording: ReLU fits CNN filters (fire or not), but a recurrent sum over a long sentence needs a bounded activation.

questions.question: Why do embeddings trained from scratch on a classification task tend to be worse than Word2Vec embeddings?
choices: Classification is an easier, lower-rank task: many embeddings give the right label, so the model never needs to separate words like "happy" and "ecstatic"
Classification datasets have no vocabulary
Back-propagation can't reach the embedding layer
Word2Vec embeddings are larger
questions.explanation: Devon: "The harder the task, if it's trainable, the better the representations." Usual fix: start from pre-trained embeddings and fine-tune them.

questions.question: Training first on all of arXiv, then on bioRxiv, then on cancer papers (general, hard task first, becoming more specific) is called:
choices: An anti-curriculum, a form of transfer learning
A curriculum, because it ends with the easiest data
Data augmentation
Word dropout
questions.explanation: L4 recording: a curriculum goes easy → hard; an anti-curriculum starts with the hard, general task. Transfer learning returns in L8.

questions.question: Which statements about Byte Pair Encoding are true?
choices: Training outputs an ordered merge table and a token vocabulary
At inference the merges are applied in merge-table order, so BPE is deterministic
The tokenizer can be trained on different data from the model
The tokenizer and the embedding layer are the same thing
Pairs are merged across word boundaries
questions.explanation: Devon: "In a test I may ask you to do either one [training or inference]. I may ask you to do both." Don't confuse the tokenizer (symbols) with the embeddings (their vectors).

questions.question: True or False, a trigram language model predicts the next token from the previous three tokens.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: A trigram uses $n - 1 = 2$ context tokens plus the predicted token. The lecturer warned that this naming mix-up 'sometimes comes up'.

questions.question: Under the Markov assumption, a 4-gram language model approximates $P(y_t \mid y_1, \ldots, y_{t-1})$ by:
choices: $P(y_t \mid y_{t-1})$
questions.explanation: An n-gram model keeps the previous $n - 1$ tokens, so a 4-gram uses three tokens of context.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about sampling with temperature $\tau$ are True?
choices: As $\tau \to 0$ sampling approaches greedy decoding (always the most probable token)
$\tau = 1$ gives the ordinary softmax distribution
$\tau > 1$ makes the distribution sharper and the text more coherent
Changing $\tau$ can change which token is the most probable
questions.explanation: $\tau < 1$ sharpens (more coherent, less diverse), $\tau > 1$ flattens (more diverse, less coherent). Dividing every logit by the same positive $\tau$ never changes their order, so the argmax stays the same.

questions.question: True or False, a language model that assigns probability 1/|V| to every token, regardless of context, has a perplexity of |V|.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: $\mathrm{PPL} = 2^{-\frac{1}{M}\sum \log_2 (1/|V|)} = 2^{\log_2 |V|} = |V|$, the 'knows nothing' baseline.

questions.question: What is the best (lowest) possible perplexity of a language model?
choices: It has no lower bound
questions.explanation: A perfect model gives probability 1 to every correct token, so every log term is 0 and the perplexity is 2⁰ = 1. Lower perplexity is better.

questions.question: Which of the following are True about Laplace (add-$\delta$) smoothing for an n-gram model?
choices: It adds $\delta$ to every n-gram count
It adds $\delta \cdot |V|$ to the context count in the denominator
It gives every n-gram, including unseen ones, a non-zero probability
Its weights $\lambda$ are chosen by cross-validation
questions.explanation: $P = \dfrac{\delta + N(context, w)}{\delta \cdot |V| + N(context)}$. The $\lambda$ weights chosen by cross-validation belong to linear interpolation, not Laplace smoothing.

questions.question: Which loss function is used to train a neural language model whose output is a softmax over the vocabulary?
choices: Cross-entropy (multiclass)
Binary cross-entropy
Mean squared error
Hinge loss
questions.explanation: The model outputs one distribution over |V| classes, so the loss is multiclass cross-entropy: with a one-hot target it is $-\log p(\text{correct token})$. The lecturer specifically warned against mixing it up with binary cross-entropy.

questions.question: True or False, weight tying reuses the input word embedding matrix as the output word embedding matrix, which roughly halves the parameters in those matrices.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: That's the saving. The cost is less freedom: the same vector has to work for reading a word and for predicting it.

questions.question: With nucleus (top-p) sampling and p = 0.9, the next-token distribution is: 'on' 0.60, 'off' 0.35, 'blue' 0.03, other tokens 0.02 in total. How many tokens are in the nucleus?
choices: Every token in the vocabulary
questions.explanation: Add the most probable tokens until the total reaches p: $0.60 < 0.9$, then $0.60 + 0.35 = 0.95 \geq 0.9$, so the nucleus is {on, off}.

questions.question: True or False, top-k sampling adapts the number of candidate tokens to the shape of the probability distribution.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Top-k always keeps a fixed k tokens. The adaptive one is top-p (nucleus) sampling.

questions.question: What is the name of the decoding strategy that always picks the single most probable next token? Write one word.
questions.explanation: Greedy decoding. The class 'shout the next word' game was an example of it.

questions.question: True or False, with a one-hot target, the cross-entropy loss reduces to the negative log-probability of the correct token.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Every other term in $-\sum_j p^*_j \log \hat{p}_j$ is multiplied by 0.

questions.question: In the neural language model pipeline, which part is model-agnostic (the same whether the context is processed by an RNN, a CNN or a Transformer)?
choices: The linear layer from size d to |V| followed by softmax
The input word embeddings
The network that processes the context
The hidden state h
questions.explanation: Processing the context is model-specific; turning h into a distribution over the next token (a linear layer, or dot products with the output embeddings, then softmax) is the same for every model.

questions.question: True or False, an RNN language model has to re-process the whole prefix every time it generates a new token.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The RNN carries the past in its hidden state, so each new token is cheap. It's a CNN LM that has to rerun the convolutions and global pooling over the whole sequence for every new token.

questions.question: A language model reads a 4-token test text and assigns the correct tokens the probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.125. Calculate the perplexity of the model on this text (use log base 2).
questions.solution:
$\log_2$ probabilities: $-1, -2, -1, -3$ → sum $-7$ → average $-1.75$.
$$\mathrm{PPL} = 2^{-\frac{1}{M}\sum_t \log_2 p(y_t)} = 2^{1.75} \approx 3.3636$$
Check: it sits between 1 (perfect) and $|V|$ (uniform).
questions.inputHint: Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

questions.question: A language model outputs the scores (logits) [2, 1, 0] for three candidate tokens. Apply softmax with temperature $\tau = 2$ and give the three probabilities. Is the result more or less diverse than ordinary softmax?
questions.solution:
Divide the logits by $\tau = 2$: $[1, 0.5, 0]$.
Exponentiate: $e^{1} = 2.7183,\ e^{0.5} = 1.6487,\ e^{0} = 1$ → sum $5.3670$.
$$\begin{aligned}p_i &= \frac{e^{z_i/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}} \\ &= [0.5065,\ 0.3072,\ 0.1863]\end{aligned}$$
Ordinary softmax ($\tau = 1$) gives $[0.6652, 0.2447, 0.0900]$, so $\tau = 2$ flattens the distribution: MORE diverse, less coherent. The ranking stays the same.
questions.inputHint: Give each probability to 4 decimal places.

questions.question: A bigram model is trained on the corpus 'the cat sat on the mat the cat ran' (9 tokens; vocabulary: the, cat, sat, on, mat, ran, so $|V| = 6$). Calculate (a) the maximum-likelihood estimate of $P(cat \mid the)$ and (b) $P(cat \mid the)$ with Laplace smoothing, $\delta = 1$.
questions.solution:
Count 'the' as a context: it appears 3 times, and is followed by 'cat' 2 times (and 'mat' once).
(a) $$P = \frac{N(the\ cat)}{N(the)} = \frac{2}{3} \approx 0.6667$$
(b) $$\begin{aligned}P &= \frac{N(the\ cat) + \delta}{N(the) + \delta |V|} \\ &= \frac{2 + 1}{3 + 6} = \frac{3}{9} \approx 0.3333\end{aligned}$$
Smoothing moves probability mass from seen to unseen bigrams.

questions.question: A 4-gram model uses linear interpolation with $\lambda_4 = 0.6,\ \lambda_3 = 0.3,\ \lambda_2 = 0.08,\ \lambda_1 = 0.02$ for the 4-gram, trigram, bigram and unigram estimates. For a word w the estimates are $P_4 = 0$ (unseen), $P_3 = 0.2$, $P_2 = 0.1$ and $P_1 = 0.05$. Calculate the interpolated probability.
questions.solution:
$$\begin{aligned}P &= \lambda_4 P_4 + \lambda_3 P_3 + \lambda_2 P_2 + \lambda_1 P_1 \\ &= 0.6 \cdot 0 + 0.3 \cdot 0.2 \\ &\quad + 0.08 \cdot 0.1 + 0.02 \cdot 0.05 \\ &= 0.069\end{aligned}$$
(The $\lambda$s sum to 1, so the result is still a probability, and an unseen 4-gram no longer gives 0.)
questions.inputHint: Give your answer to 3 decimal places.

questions.question: Explain why a count-based n-gram language model can assign zero probability to a perfectly valid sentence, and describe two techniques that address this. (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Language is compositional, so most n-grams (especially long ones) never appear in the training corpus. The MLE $P(w \mid context) = N(context, w)/N(context)$ is then 0 for an unseen n-gram, and because the sentence probability is a product, a single 0 makes the whole sentence 0. If the context itself is unseen, the estimate is 0/0, undefined.
Fixes (any two):
• Backoff: if the longer context has no counts, use a shorter one (trigram → bigram → unigram).
• Linear interpolation: mix the estimates of every order, $\sum_i \lambda_i P_i$ with $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$, $\lambda$s chosen on a validation set.
• Laplace (add-$\delta$) smoothing: $\dfrac{N + \delta}{N(context) + \delta |V|}$, so nothing is ever 0.

rubric.point: Unseen n-grams have count 0 (sparsity / compositionality)
The product over tokens means one zero makes the whole sentence probability 0 (or 0/0 for an unseen context)
First technique correctly described
Second technique correctly described

questions.question: Explain the coherence–diversity trade-off in text generation and how sampling temperature controls it. Why is temperature alone not a complete solution? (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Generated text should be coherent (make sense, stay consistent with what came before) and diverse (different samples, not always the most likely, short, repetitive output).
Temperature divides the logits by $\tau$ before the softmax. $\tau < 1$ sharpens the distribution: more coherent but repetitive and less diverse ('the new version of the new version…'). $\tau > 1$ flattens it: more diverse but incoherent. $\tau = 1$ is the ordinary softmax.
It isn't enough because it is one global knob: moving it in either direction improves one property and hurts the other, and it ignores how many plausible candidates there are at each step. Top-k and especially top-p (nucleus) sampling adapt to the distribution.

rubric.point: Defines coherence and diversity
Temperature divides the logits before softmax: $\tau<1$ sharper/more coherent, $\tau>1$ flatter/more diverse
States the trade-off: improving one hurts the other
Why not enough: one global knob that doesn't adapt to the distribution; mentions top-k/top-p

questions.question: Define perplexity for a language model, state its best and worst values, and explain why a lower perplexity is better. (3 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
$$\mathrm{Perplexity}(y_{1:M}) = 2^{-\frac{1}{M}\sum_{t} \log_2 p(y_t \mid y_{<t})}$$ 2 to the power of the average negative log-likelihood (cross-entropy in bits). It measures how 'surprised' the model is by the text.
Best: 1, when the model gives probability 1 to every correct token. Worst (uniform model): $|V|$, when it gives $1/|V|$ to every token.
Lower perplexity means higher likelihood of real text, i.e. the model predicts the data better.

rubric.point: Formula / definition: exponentiated average negative log-likelihood ('surprise')
Best = 1 and worst (uniform) = |V|
Lower = higher likelihood of real text = better prediction

questions.question: Explain why recurrent networks were preferred over CNNs for generating text with a language model. (3 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Generation is autoregressive: after every new token the model must predict again with a longer context.
An RNN keeps a hidden state summarising everything so far, so each new token needs only one recurrent step: no recomputation.
A CNN (with global pooling) has no running memory: to predict the next token it must rerun the convolutions and pooling over the whole growing sequence, redoing work every step. The lecturer's wider point: in NLP, faster training/generation with a small memory footprint wins because it lets you use more data.

rubric.point: Generation is autoregressive: predict, append, predict again
RNN hidden state carries the past, so each new token is one cheap step
CNN must recompute convolutions/pooling over the whole prefix for every token

questions.question: What is weight tying in a neural language model, and what is its trade-off? (2 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Weight tying uses the same matrix for the input word embeddings and the output word embeddings (the final layer that scores every token). It roughly halves those (very large) parameter matrices. The trade-off is less flexibility: one vector per word has to serve both for reading the word and for predicting it.

rubric.point: Same matrix for input and output embeddings, reducing parameters
Trade-off: less freedom/flexibility for separate input and output representations
