options: h: vector representation of the context
Get probability distribution for the next token
questions.explanation: Two halves: (1) process the context with a model-specific network (RNN, CNN…) into a d-sized vector h; (2) a model-agnostic part: a linear layer d → |V| and softmax give P(next token | context). Equivalently, take dot products of h with the output word embeddings.

questions.question: What does a language model estimate?
choices: The probability of linguistic units: a sentence, or the next token given the previous ones
The grammatical parse tree of a sentence
The sentiment label of a text
A fixed embedding for every word in the vocabulary
questions.explanation: Lecture 5: LMs estimate the probability of different linguistic units (texts, sentences, tokens). In practice, via $P(y_t \mid y_{<t})$.

questions.question: True or False: The lecturer compared a language model to a model train: it must reproduce the properties of language that matter for prediction, not copy how humans actually produce language.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: From the recording: a language model is an approximation of language, like a model train or a physics model of the world.

questions.question: True or False: We can estimate the probability of a whole sentence by counting how often that exact sentence occurs in a large corpus.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Language is compositional: almost every sentence has a count of 0, so we cannot treat sentences as atomic units. Instead we decompose them with the chain rule.

questions.question: Which expression is the left-to-right factorisation used by language models?
choices: $P(y_1, \dots, y_n) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} P(y_t \mid y_1, \dots, y_{t-1})$
$P(y_1, \dots, y_n) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} P(y_t)$
$P(y_1, \dots, y_n) = \sum_{t=1}^{n} P(y_t \mid y_{t-1})$
$P(y_1, \dots, y_n) = \frac{N(y_1, \dots, y_n)}{N(\text{all sentences})}$
questions.explanation: The product rule of probability, applied left to right. It is exact; the Markov assumption is what makes it approximate.

questions.question: Which statements about the left-to-right framework are true?
choices: It is exact before any Markov assumption is made
N-gram and neural LMs differ only in how they compute $P(y_t \mid y_{<t})$
To generate text you sample a token, append it to the context and repeat
It requires the model to see the future tokens
questions.explanation: The slides: "models differ in how they evaluate the probabilities". Generation feeds each predicted token back in, so it never looks ahead.

questions.question: Under the Markov assumption, a 5-gram model predicts $y_t$ from how many previous tokens?
questions.explanation: The $n$ in n-gram includes the predicted word, so a 5-gram uses $n - 1 = 4$ context words. The lecturer warned this naming is an easy mistake.

questions.question: For the sentence "I saw a cat on a mat", match each model to the factor it uses for the word "mat".
options: $P(mat \mid I\ saw\ a\ cat\ on\ a)$
questions.explanation: An n-gram keeps $n - 1$ previous words. Only the full (no Markov) model uses the whole history.

questions.concept: N-gram MLE and the zero problem
questions.question: For a count-based estimate $P(mat \mid cat\ on\ a) = \frac{N(cat\ on\ a\ mat)}{N(cat\ on\ a)}$, which statements are true?
choices: If the numerator is 0, one unseen n-gram makes the whole sentence probability 0
If the denominator is 0, the probability is undefined
The estimate can never exceed 1, because $N(\text{prefix} + w) \le N(\text{prefix})$
Using a longer context always reduces the number of zero counts
questions.explanation: Longer contexts are rarer, so they make zeros more likely, not less. That is why backoff shortens the context.

questions.concept: N-gram MLE and the zero problem
questions.question:
A bigram model is trained on:
<s> I like green tea </s>
<s> I like black tea </s>
<s> I drink green tea </s>
<s> you like tea </s>
(a) $P(like \mid I)$  (b) $P(green \mid like)$  (c) $P(tea \mid green)$, all maximum-likelihood estimates.
(d) The MLE probability of "<s> you drink tea </s>" (predict the 4 tokens after <s>).
questions.solution:
$P(w \mid v) = N(v\,w) / N(v)$ where $N(v)$ counts $v$ as a context.
(a) $2/3 = 0.6667$  (b) $1/3 = 0.3333$  (c) $2/2 = 1$
(d) "you drink" never occurs, so $P(drink \mid you) = 0$ and the whole product is $0$: one unseen bigram zeroes the sentence, even though every word was seen.
questions.explanation: This is the zero problem that backoff, interpolation and smoothing fix.

questions.question:
Same corpus:
<s> I like green tea </s>
<s> I like black tea </s>
<s> I drink green tea </s>
<s> you like tea </s>
The prediction vocabulary is {I, like, green, tea, black, drink, you, </s>}, so $|V| = 8$. With Laplace (add-one, $\delta = 1$) smoothing compute:
(a) $P(drink \mid you)$  (b) $P(like \mid I)$  (c) the probability of "<s> you drink tea </s>" (4 predicted tokens).
questions.solution:
$$\hat P(w \mid v) = \frac{N(v\,w) + \delta}{N(v) + \delta|V|}$$
(a) $\frac{0 + 1}{1 + 8} = 0.1111$
(b) $\frac{2 + 1}{3 + 8} = 0.2727$: smoothing takes mass away from seen bigrams.
(c) Factors: $P(\text{you} \mid \text{<s>}) = \frac{1+1}{4+8}$, $P(\text{drink} \mid \text{you}) = \frac{0+1}{1+8}$, $P(\text{tea} \mid \text{drink}) = \frac{0+1}{1+8}$, $P(\text{</s>} \mid \text{tea}) = \frac{4+1}{4+8}$; product $\approx 0.0008573$.
questions.inputHint: A decimal; scientific notation such as 1.2e-4 is fine.

questions.question:
A trigram model is trained on three sentences, each padded with two start tokens:
<s> <s> the cat sat on the mat </s>
<s> <s> the cat ate the fish </s>
<s> <s> the dog sat on the cat </s>
The prediction vocabulary is every token except <s>, so $|V| = 9$.
(a) How many context words does this model use?
(b) MLE $P(sat \mid the\ cat)$  (c) MLE $P(the \mid sat\ on)$
(d) Add-$\delta$ with $\delta = 0.5$: $P(sat \mid the\ cat)$  (e) Add-$\delta$: $P(ran \mid the\ cat)$
questions.solution:
(a) A trigram is $n = 3$ including the predicted word, so $n - 1 = 2$ context words.
(b) "the cat" occurs 3 times as a context ("the cat sat", "the cat ate"; the last "the cat" is followed by </s>, so it counts too): $1/3 = 0.3333$.
(c) "sat on" is followed by "the" both times: $2/2 = 1$.
(d) $\frac{1 + 0.5}{3 + 0.5 \times 9} = 0.2$
(e) $\frac{0 + 0.5}{3 + 0.5 \times 9} = 0.0667$: an unseen trigram now gets a small non-zero probability.
questions.explanation: With a large $|V|$ (around a million in practice), the $\delta|V|$ term dominates the denominator and drags every probability down, which is the downside the lecturer pointed out.

questions.question: True or False: Laplace smoothing can be seen as a uniform prior over the vocabulary, and with a very large vocabulary the $\delta|V|$ term can dominate the denominator.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: From the recording: Laplace comes from Naive Bayes and acts as a uniform Bayesian prior; with $|V|$ around a million, even a tiny $\delta$ drags every probability down.

questions.question: Stupid backoff (as on the slides) estimates $P(mat \mid cat\ on\ a)$ when $N(cat\ on\ a) = 0$ by:
choices: Trying $P(mat \mid on\ a)$ instead, then $P(mat \mid a)$, then $P(mat)$, until the context has been seen
Adding 1 to every count
Averaging all four estimates with weights that sum to 1
Returning 0
questions.explanation: Backoff uses less context for contexts we don't know much about. (The original "stupid backoff" also multiplies each step down by a constant such as 0.4; the slides leave this out.) Option (c) is linear interpolation.

questions.question: Which statements about backoff are true?
choices: It fixes the problem that larger n-grams are rarer
Shrinking the context removes constraints, so the prediction becomes less specific
It always uses the longest context available that has been seen
It guarantees that probabilities sum to exactly 1 without any extra normalisation
questions.explanation: The lecturer's trade-off: avoiding zero counts by dropping context also drops constraints. Plain (stupid) backoff scores do not form a normalised distribution: that needs discounting (Katz backoff), which was not covered.

questions.question:
A model is trained on:
<s> the cat sat on a mat </s>
<s> a dog sat on a rug </s>
<s> the mat was on a table </s>
Use backoff exactly as on the slides (no discount factor): use the trigram if its context has been seen, otherwise the bigram, otherwise the unigram.
(a) $\hat P(a \mid cat\ on)$
(b) $\hat P(mat \mid on\ a)$
questions.solution:
(a) $N(cat\ on) = 0$: the context was never seen ("cat sat on", not "cat on"), so back off to the bigram: $P(a \mid on) = N(on\ a)/N(on) = 3/3 = 1$.
(b) $N(on\ a) = 3$, so the trigram can be used: $N(on\ a\ mat)/N(on\ a) = 1/3 = 0.3333$. (The bigram would give $P(mat \mid a) = 1/4 = 0.25$, but backoff only drops context when it has to.)

questions.question: In linear interpolation $\hat P(mat \mid cat\ on\ a) = \lambda_3 P(mat \mid cat\ on\ a) + \lambda_2 P(mat \mid on\ a) + \lambda_1 P(mat \mid a) + \lambda_0 P(mat)$, which are true?
choices: The $\lambda$s must sum to 1
The $\lambda$s are chosen by cross-validation on held-out data
It turns the backoff algorithm into a hyperparameter problem
The $\lambda$s are learned on the training set by maximising its likelihood
questions.explanation: Fitting the $\lambda$s on the training data would just put all the weight on the longest n-gram (which fits the training data best). They must be tuned on a validation set.

questions.question:
(a) A trigram LM is interpolated with weights $\lambda_3 = 0.6, \lambda_2 = 0.3, \lambda_1 = 0.1$. The estimates are $P(tea \mid drink\ green) = 0$ (unseen), $P(tea \mid green) = 0.25$ and $P(tea) = 0.04$. Give $\hat P(tea \mid drink\ green)$.
(b) A 4-gram model uses $\lambda = (0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05)$ for the 4-gram, trigram, bigram and unigram estimates $(0.5, 0.4, 0.1, 0.01)$. Give the interpolated probability.
In a neural LM, what happens after the network turns the context into a vector $h$ of size $d$?
choices: A linear layer maps $h$ to $|V|$ scores, and a softmax turns them into $P(y_t \mid y_{<t})$
The network counts n-grams in $h$
A sigmoid is applied to each of the $|V|$ scores independently
The most similar training sentence is retrieved
questions.explanation: process context → $h$ → linear layer ($d \to |V|$) → softmax. One softmax over the whole vocabulary: that is why cross-entropy, not BCE, is the right loss.

questions.question: True or False: In the "output embeddings" view of the final layer, the score of each token is the dot product of $h$ with that token's output embedding.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The rows of the output matrix are output embeddings; a token scores highly when its embedding points in the same direction as $h$. The lecturer said the field mostly uses this view.

questions.question: True or False: A neural LM can give a sensible probability to a context it never saw in training because it works in a continuous vector space where similar contexts get similar representations.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Counting cannot generalise to an unseen n-gram; a neural LM interpolates between nearby points. The cost: it needs a lot of data, and gaps in the space are where odd behaviour (e.g. jailbreaks) comes from.

questions.question: The model gives $p(cat \mid I\ saw\ a) = 0.2$ and the target is "cat". With a one-hot target, what is the cross-entropy loss at this step (natural log)?
questions.explanation: $\text{CE} = -\sum_j p^*_j \log \hat p_j$ and the one-hot target kills every term but the correct one, leaving $-\log \hat p(cat)$. Option (d) is the binary cross-entropy form, which is the wrong loss for a softmax over $|V|$.

questions.question: Which statements about the training loss of an LM are true?
choices: It is multiclass cross-entropy over one softmax across the vocabulary
With a one-hot target it reduces to $-\log \hat p(\text{observed token})$
Using binary cross-entropy (e.g. BCEWithLogits) on the $|V|$ outputs is a common bug
Lowering the loss on the correct token cannot change the other probabilities
questions.explanation: Because the softmax sums to 1, raising the correct token's probability lowers the others (Quiz 1 Q2 makes the same point).

questions.question: Which statements about RNN language models are true?
choices: The simplest version reads the text and predicts the next token from the hidden state at each step
In a multi-layer RNN, the states of one RNN are fed as inputs to the next
Roughly, lower layers capture local phenomena and higher layers longer dependencies
An RNN LM must recompute every previous step from scratch to generate each new token
questions.explanation: The hidden state caches the past, so generating a token costs one step. That is the lecturer's reason for using RNNs rather than CNNs for generation.

questions.question: True or False: The lecturer argued that RNNs suit generation better than CNNs because the hidden state caches the past, whereas a CNN must rerun convolution and pooling over the whole sequence for every new token.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: His wider point: in NLP, fast training with a small memory footprint (so you can show the model more data) beats mathematical elegance.

questions.question: Why can't a language model simply always output its most probable continuation?
choices: The most probable continuation is often short and generic ("I like the cat."), so the text is coherent but not diverse and communicates little
Because the most probable token is always <eos>
Because computing the most probable token is intractable
Because it would make the text incoherent
questions.explanation: Real language communicates something, so it can't always take the most likely path. We need both coherence and diversity.

questions.question: True or False: Changing the softmax temperature can improve coherence and diversity at the same time.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Temperature is a single knob: moving it either way helps one of coherence/diversity and hurts the other (slide 77).

questions.question:
A language model outputs logits $(3, 1, 0.5, 0)$ for the tokens (cat, dog, mat, the). Give the probability of "cat" with softmax temperature:
(a) $\tau = 1$  (b) $\tau = 0.5$  (c) $\tau = 2$
(d) The probability of "the" with $\tau = 2$.
questions.solution:
$$p_i = \frac{e^{z_i/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}}$$
(a) $e^{3}/(e^{3}+e^{1}+e^{0.5}+e^{0}) = 0.7891$
(b) logits become $(6, 2, 1, 0)$: $0.9732$ (sharper: more coherent, less diverse)
(c) logits become $(1.5, 0.5, 0.25, 0)$: $0.5326$ (flatter: more diverse, less coherent)
(d) $e^{0}/\sum = 0.1188$, up from $0.0393$ at $\tau = 1$.
questions.explanation: Dividing every logit by the same $\tau > 0$ never changes their order, so the argmax (and greedy decoding) is unchanged. As $\tau \to 0$ sampling becomes greedy; as $\tau \to \infty$ it becomes uniform.

questions.question: Logits $(2, 1, 0)$. Give the probability of the top token at (a) $\tau = 0.25$ and (b) $\tau = 3$, and (c) the ratio $p_1 / p_3$ (top token over bottom token) at $\tau = 3$.
questions.solution:
(a) logits $(8, 4, 0)$: $0.9817$, almost greedy.
(b) logits $(0.667, 0.333, 0)$: $0.4484$, close to uniform ($1/3$).
(c) The ratio of two softmax outputs is $e^{(z_1 - z_3)/\tau} = e^{2/3} = 1.9477$.

questions.question: Which statements about temperature are true?
choices: $\tau < 1$ gives more repetitive, safer text (e.g. "the new version of the new version…")
$\tau > 1$ behaves a little like a uniform prior, similar in spirit to Laplace smoothing
Temperature changes which token has the highest probability
$\tau = 1$ is ordinary sampling from the softmax
questions.explanation: The lecturer's examples and his Laplace comparison. Dividing by $\tau$ keeps the order of the logits, so the most probable token stays the same.

questions.question:
The next-token distribution (sorted) is $(0.42, 0.23, 0.15, 0.1, 0.06, 0.04)$.
(a) Top-k with $k = 3$: the renormalised probability of the most likely token.
(b) Top-p with $p = 0.75$: how many tokens are in the nucleus?
(c) The renormalised probability of the most likely token inside that nucleus.
(d) Nucleus size with $p = 0.9$.
questions.explanation: The standard nucleus method renormalises inside the set and samples in proportion. (The lecturer said "pick uniformly"; write the standard version.)

questions.question:
Two steps of generation give these sorted distributions:
Peaked: 0.88, 0.05, 0.03, 0.02, 0.02
Flat: 0.12, 0.11, 0.11, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.09, 0.09, 0.09, 0.09
With top-p, $p = 0.8$, how many tokens are in the nucleus (a) for the peaked step and (b) for the flat step? (c) With top-k, $k = 4$, what total probability mass is kept at the peaked step?
questions.solution:
(a) $0.88 \ge 0.8$ already: 1 token.
(b) The flat distribution needs 8 tokens to reach $0.82$.
(c) $0.88 + 0.05 + 0.03 + 0.02 = 0.98$: top-4 keeps three tokens the model barely believes in, while for the flat step it would cut off plausible words.
questions.explanation: This is the slide-79 problem with fixed $k$ (too many candidates for a peaked distribution, too few for a flat one) and why top-p is called adaptive.

questions.question: What is the main problem with top-k sampling according to Lecture 5?
choices: A fixed $k$ is not good: the shape of the distribution changes from step to step
It can only be used with RNNs
It always picks the most probable token
It needs the probabilities to be renormalised over the whole vocabulary
questions.explanation: For a flat distribution $k$ may be too small; for a peaked one it lets in tokens the model rejects. Usually $k \approx 10$–$50$.

questions.question:
(a) A model assigns probabilities $(0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.5)$ to the 4 tokens of a test text. Compute its perplexity.
(b) Another model assigns $(0.2, 0.1, 0.4, 0.25, 0.05)$ to 5 tokens. Compute its perplexity.
(c) What is the perplexity of a uniform model over a vocabulary of 50,000 tokens?
questions.solution:
$$\text{PP} = 2^{-\frac{1}{M}\sum_t \log_2 p(y_t \mid y_{<t})}$$
(a) $\log_2$ values: $-1, -2, -3, -1$, mean $-1.75$, so $\text{PP} = 2^{1.75} = 3.3636$.
(b) mean $\log_2 p = -2.6575$, so $\text{PP} = 6.3096$ (equivalently the inverse geometric mean of the probabilities).
(c) $p = 1/|V|$ everywhere gives $2^{\log_2 |V|} = |V| = 50000$.

questions.question:
A model over a vocabulary of $|V| = 4$ tokens is confidently wrong: it gives the correct token probability $0.1$ at every one of 10 test positions.
(a) What is its perplexity?
(b) What is the perplexity of a uniform model on the same text?
(c) Recompute (a) with natural logs: $e^{-\frac{1}{M}\sum \ln p}$.
questions.solution:
(a) $2^{-\log_2 0.1} = 10$, which is above $|V| = 4$.
(b) 4.
(c) The same, 10: perplexity is base-independent as long as the log and the power use the same base.
questions.explanation: The slides say perplexity is "always between 1 and |V|". That holds for the uniform worst case they derive, but a confidently wrong model (p(correct) < 1/|V|) goes above |V|. In a test use the slides' framing unless asked for a critique.
questions.keyDispute: The slides state perplexity is always between 1 and |V|; this question shows the strict exception.

questions.question: Which statements about perplexity are true?
choices: Lower perplexity means higher data likelihood, which is better
A perfect model that gives the correct token probability 1 has perplexity 1
It measures how surprised a model is by a text
Over-optimising perplexity is always good, because language should be as predictable as possible
questions.explanation: The lecturer warned that some surprise is necessary for language to carry information, so over-optimising perplexity is a trap.

questions.question: True or False: Cross-entropy (the training loss) is the negative log-likelihood, and perplexity is the exponent of the average negative log-likelihood per token.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 85: "cross-entropy (our loss) is negative log-likelihood". Perplexity $= 2^{\text{average NLL in bits}}$.

questions.question:
An LM has vocabulary $|V| = 50,000$ and embedding size $d = 512$. Ignore biases.
(a) How many parameters do the input embedding matrix and the output layer have together without weight tying?
(b) How many parameters are saved by tying them?
questions.solution:
(a) Input embeddings $|V| \times d$ plus output layer $d \times |V|$: $2 \times 50000 \times 512 = 51,200,000$.
(b) Tying reuses one matrix for both, saving $50000 \times 512 = 25,600,000$ parameters.
questions.explanation: Slide 93: a large part of the parameters comes from these matrices. The cost (lecturer): you lose the "semantic freedom" of separate input and output representations. It needs the vector fed to the output layer to have size $d$ (or a projection).

questions.question: What is weight tying in a language model?
choices: Using the same matrix for the input embeddings and the output (scoring) layer
Freezing the embeddings so they are not recomputed
Sharing weights between the layers of a multi-layer RNN
Tying the temperature to the learning rate
questions.explanation: It is not about avoiding recomputation (a correction to your notes): one matrix serves as both the input embeddings and the output embeddings.

questions.question: What did the Lecture 5 slides show about individual neurons in character-level LSTM language models?
choices: Some neurons track interpretable things such as line length, being inside quotes, or the depth of an expression
A "sentiment neuron" could be found and used to control the sentiment of generated text
Every neuron corresponds to exactly one word
No neuron can be interpreted at all
questions.explanation: Karpathy's visualisations and the sentiment neuron (Radford et al.). You can probe a unit by training a simple classifier on its activation.

questions.question: True or False: Once an interpretable neuron (such as a sentiment neuron) is found, fixing its value can steer what the model generates.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 104 "Use interpretable neurons to control generated texts".

questions.question: In contrastive evaluation of an LM on "The roses in the vase by the door ___", what is compared?
choices: P(... are) against P(... is): is the grammatical form ranked higher?
The perplexity of two different models on the whole corpus
The BLEU score of two translations
The number of tokens in each continuation
questions.explanation: You pick the tokens of interest from the model's distribution and check the ranking.

questions.question: For subject–verb agreement tests, which statements are true?
choices: Attractors are nouns between the subject and the verb with a different number from the subject
Adding attractors makes the test harder
"The roses ___" has no attractors; "The roses in the vase by the door ___" has two
Contrastive evaluation needs labelled training data for the model
questions.explanation: "vase" and "door" are singular, while "roses" is plural. The test only needs the LM's probabilities.

questions.concept: N-gram MLE and the zero problem
questions.question:
A bigram LM is trained on:
<s> she reads books </s>
<s> she writes books </s>
<s> he reads papers </s>
<s> he reads books </s>
The prediction vocabulary is {she, he, reads, writes, books, papers, </s>} ($|V| = 7$; <s> is never predicted).
(a) Give the MLE factors and probabilities of "<s> she reads papers </s>" and "<s> she writes papers </s>". Neither sentence is in the corpus. Explain what the two results show about count-based LMs. (3)
(b) Recompute the four factors of "<s> she writes papers </s>" with Laplace ($\delta = 1$) smoothing, its probability, and its perplexity over the 4 predicted tokens. Is the perplexity sensible compared with $|V|$? (4)
(c) Explain, in terms of continuous representations, why a neural LM could give "she writes papers" a reasonable probability without smoothing, and name one cost of the neural approach. (3) (10 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) "she reads papers": $P(\text{she} \mid \text{<s>}) = 2/4$, $P(\text{reads} \mid \text{she}) = 1/2$, $P(\text{papers} \mid \text{reads}) = 1/3$, $P(\text{</s>} \mid \text{papers}) = 1/1$; product $= 0.0833$. "she writes papers": $P(\text{she} \mid \text{<s>}) = 2/4$, $P(\text{writes} \mid \text{she}) = 1/2$, $P(\text{papers} \mid \text{writes}) = 0/1$, $P(\text{</s>} \mid \text{papers}) = 1/1$; product $= 0$.
The first sentence never occurs, yet gets a non-zero probability: the Markov assumption lets a count model combine bigrams seen in different sentences. The second gets exactly 0 because one bigram ("writes papers") was never counted, even though every word is known: a single unseen n-gram in the numerator zeroes the whole product.

(b) $\hat P = \frac{N + 1}{N(\text{ctx}) + 7}$: $\frac{2+1}{4+7} = 0.2727$, $\frac{1+1}{2+7} = 0.2222$, $\frac{0+1}{1+7} = 0.125$, $\frac{1+1}{1+7} = 0.25$. Product $\approx 0.001894$. Perplexity $= (\prod p)^{-1/4} = 4.7936$. Since $1 \le 4.79 \le 7$, it is better than a uniform model (7) but far from perfect (1); smoothing moved mass to unseen bigrams, which also lowered the seen ones.

(c) A neural LM maps the context to a vector $h$ in a continuous space and scores every token by a dot product with its output embedding. "reads" and "writes" appear in similar contexts (after she/he, before books), so they get similar representations; the same holds for "papers" and "books". The model can therefore interpolate: "writes papers" sits near "reads papers" and "writes books", which it has seen, so it gets a reasonable probability without explicit smoothing. Cost: it needs a lot of data and compute, is harder to interpret, and gaps in the space can give odd predictions.

rubric.point: (a) Correct MLE factors and both products
(a) Explains Markov generalisation and the zero problem
(b) Correct Laplace factors
(b) Correct perplexity
(b) Interprets it against 1 and |V|
(c) Similar contexts → similar vectors, so the model interpolates to unseen combinations
(c) A cost of neural LMs

questions.explanation: Numbers: MLE 0.0833 and 0, Laplace 0.001894, perplexity 4.7936.

questions.question:
At one decoding step an LM gives logits $(2, 1.2, 0.8, 0.2, -0.5)$ for the tokens (the, a, this, my, his).
(a) Compute the softmax probabilities at $\tau = 1$ and $\tau = 0.5$. (3)
(b) Give the top-k ($k = 2$) and top-p ($p = 0.8$) candidate sets at $\tau = 1$, with the renormalised probabilities you would sample from. (3)
(c) Explain the coherence–diversity trade-off of temperature, and why top-p is called adaptive while top-k is not. (2)
(d) Explain why greedy decoding, which this step would turn into argmax, tends to produce short generic sentences. (2) (10 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\tau = 1$: (0.501, 0.225, 0.151, 0.083, 0.041). $\tau = 0.5$ (logits doubled): (0.754, 0.152, 0.068, 0.021, 0.005). Lower $\tau$ sharpens the distribution; the order stays the same.

(b) Top-2: {the, a} with renormalised $(0.69, 0.31)$. Top-p 0.8: cumulative (0.501, 0.725, 0.876, 0.959, 1), so the nucleus is the first 3 tokens {the, a, this} with mass 0.876; renormalised (0.571, 0.257, 0.172).

(c) $\tau < 1$: more coherent, less diverse (repetitive); $\tau > 1$: more diverse, less coherent; $\tau = 1$ is ordinary sampling. One knob, so improving one hurts the other. Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens whatever the shape of the distribution; top-p keeps the smallest set covering mass $p$, so it takes few tokens when the model is confident and many when the distribution is flat.

(d) Greedy takes the most probable token each step. Frequent function words and the end-of-sentence token are often the most probable choices, so it produces safe, short, repetitive text ("the hotel is located in the heart of the city <eos>"): high coherence, no diversity. It also is not the most probable sentence overall (L6).

questions.question:
A student builds a neural LM with an embedding layer, an LSTM, a linear layer of size $d \to |V|$ and a sigmoid on each output, trained with binary cross-entropy against the one-hot next token.
(a) Explain what is wrong with the output and loss, and give the correct choice with its formula for one step. (3)
(b) Show that the correct loss reduces to $-\log \hat p(\text{target})$ for a one-hot target, and explain why pushing this down also pushes the other tokens' probabilities down. (2)
(c) The student wants to cut parameters. Explain weight tying, what it requires, and its cost. (3) (8 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Next-token prediction is one multiclass decision over the vocabulary: exactly one token comes next. Independent sigmoids with BCE treat it as $|V|$ separate yes/no problems (multi-label), so the outputs need not sum to 1 and are not a distribution over the next token. Correct: one softmax over the $|V|$ scores, $\hat p = \text{softmax}(W h + b)$, with multiclass cross-entropy $\mathcal{L} = -\sum_j p^*_j \log \hat p_j$.

(b) With a one-hot target $p^*$ only the correct index $c$ has $p^*_c = 1$, so $\mathcal{L} = -\log \hat p_c$. The softmax outputs sum to 1, so increasing $\hat p_c$ necessarily decreases the other probabilities; the gradient raises the correct logit and lowers the others in proportion to their probability.

(c) Use one matrix for both the input embedding ($|V| \times d$) and the output layer ($d \times |V|$, transposed). It saves $|V| \cdot d$ parameters (a large share of a small LM). It requires the vector fed to the output layer to have the same size $d$ as the embeddings (or a projection). Cost: the input and output representations of a word are forced to be the same, losing their "semantic freedom".

rubric.point: (a) Identifies the multi-label (sigmoid/BCE) vs multiclass error
(a) Softmax + multiclass CE with formula
(b) One-hot reduces CE to −log p(target)
(b) Softmax coupling pushes the others down
(c) Explains weight tying
(c) States the dimension requirement
(c) States the cost

questions.question: Critically discuss perplexity as an evaluation metric for language models. Define it, derive its value for a perfect model and for a uniform model, explain the slides' claim that it lies between 1 and $|V|$ and when that claim fails, and give two limitations of using it. (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
$\text{PP}(y_{1:M}) = 2^{-\frac{1}{M}\sum_t \log_2 p(y_t \mid y_{<t})}$: the exponent of the average negative log-likelihood (cross-entropy) per token; it measures how surprised the model is. Lower is better.

Perfect model: every $p = 1$, every log is 0, so $\text{PP} = 2^0 = 1$. Uniform model: $p = 1/|V|$, so the average log is $-\log_2|V|$ and $\text{PP} = |V|$.

The "between 1 and $|V|$" claim treats the uniform model as the worst case. A model that is confidently wrong (gives the correct token less than $1/|V|$ on average) scores above $|V|$, e.g. $p = 0.1$ with $|V| = 4$ gives 10.

Limitations: (i) it only compares models with the same vocabulary/tokenization (a different tokenizer changes $M$ and $|V|$); (ii) it measures likelihood of a test text, not quality of generated text: a model can have low perplexity yet generate dull text, and some surprise is necessary for language to carry information, so over-optimising it is a trap; (iii) it depends on the test domain.

rubric.point: Correct definition and interpretation (lower = better)
Derives 1 for a perfect model
Derives |V| for a uniform model
Explains when PP exceeds |V|
Two valid limitations

questions.question: Compare CNN language models with RNN language models. Explain the role of global pooling in a CNN LM, why the lecturer preferred RNNs for generation, and why stacking RNN layers helps. (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
CNN LM: convolution filters slide over the previous tokens (the sequence laid out spatially); to predict the next token the variable-length sequence of feature maps is collapsed by global pooling into one fixed-size vector, keeping each filter's strongest response wherever it occurred, which then feeds the linear layer and softmax. (To stay causal, the filters may only see past tokens.)

Generation: each new token changes the input, so a CNN LM has to rerun convolution and global pooling over the whole sequence for every token (it repeatedly processes the same words). An RNN keeps a hidden state that caches the past, so each new token costs one update. Fast training and generation with a small memory footprint let you show the model more data, which the lecturer valued over mathematical elegance.

Stacked RNNs: the states of one layer are the inputs of the next; roughly, lower layers capture local phenomena (e.g. parts of speech) and higher layers longer-range structure (sentence structure).

rubric.point: Explains global pooling in a CNN LM (variable length → fixed vector)
Explains the inefficiency of CNNs for generation vs the RNN cache

questions.question: Describe two ways of analysing what a language model has learned, as shown at the end of Lecture 5. For each, explain what it can and cannot tell you. (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Looking at neurons: visualise activations of individual units while the model reads text (e.g. char-level LSTM units that track line length, quotes, or expression depth; the sentiment neuron). You can also probe a unit by training a binary classifier on its activation. Can: show interpretable features are represented and even steer generation (fix the sentiment neuron). Cannot: most units are not interpretable, and correlation does not prove the model uses the feature.

2. Contrastive evaluation: compare the LM's probabilities for minimal pairs, e.g. P(The roses in the vase by the door are) vs P(… is). Attractors (nouns of a different number between subject and verb) make it harder. Can: test a specific linguistic ability with no extra training and graded difficulty. Cannot: it only tests the phenomena you design pairs for, and ranking the right form higher on a test set does not show how the model represents the rule.

Its strength and limitation

Its strength and limitation

questions.question:
A trigram LM is trained on:
<s> the cat sat on the mat </s>
<s> the cat sat on the rug </s>
<s> a dog lay on the mat </s>
The prediction vocabulary is every token except <s> ($|V| = 10$), and the unigram estimate is $P(on) = N(on)/N(\text{all predicted tokens})$.
(a) Why can't the MLE trigram estimate $P(on \mid dog\ sat)$ be used? (1)
(b) Give the stupid-backoff estimate as on the slides (use the longest context that has been seen; no discount). (2)
(c) Give the linearly interpolated estimate with $\lambda_3 = 0.6, \lambda_2 = 0.3, \lambda_1 = 0.1$ (use 0 for an undefined trigram). How should the $\lambda$s be chosen? (3)
(d) Give the Laplace ($\delta = 1$) trigram estimate and explain its main weakness for a realistic vocabulary. (2)
(e) Which of the three would you choose, and why? (2) (10 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $N(dog\ sat) = 0$ ("a dog lay", never "dog sat"), so the estimate is $0/0$: undefined (a zero in the denominator).

(b) Back off to the bigram: $P(on \mid sat) = N(sat\ on)/N(sat) = 2/2 = 1$.

(c) $P(on) = 3/21 = 0.1429$. $\hat P = 0.6(0) + 0.3(1) + 0.1(0.1429) = 0.3143$. The $\lambda$s must sum to 1 and are tuned by cross-validation on held-out data (not on the training data, which would favour the trigram).

(d) $\frac{0 + 1}{0 + 10} = 0.1$. Weakness: with a realistic $|V|$ (around a million) the $\delta|V|$ term dominates every denominator, so seen events lose most of their mass and estimates become nearly uniform; it treats all unseen continuations as equally likely.

(e) Interpolation is usually best: it always mixes in the more specific estimate when available, never gives 0 when a lower order has seen the word, and its weights are tuned on data. Backoff is simple but jumps between orders and drops constraints (less specific, less reasonable continuations); Laplace distorts the probabilities too much for large vocabularies. (Any well-argued choice gets the marks.)

rubric.point: (a) Identifies the zero denominator / undefined estimate
(b) Correct backoff estimate
(c) Correct interpolated value
(c) λs sum to 1, tuned on held-out data
(d) Correct Laplace value
(d) Weakness with large |V|
(e) Reasoned choice comparing the methods

questions.explanation: Numbers: backoff 1, interpolation 0.3143, Laplace 0.1.

questions.question: Explain what a language model is and how it assigns a probability to a sentence. Your answer should cover: the left-to-right (chain rule) factorisation, why whole sentences cannot simply be counted, what the Markov assumption changes and why, and how a neural LM differs from an n-gram LM in computing each factor. (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
A language model estimates the probability of linguistic units: a sentence, or the next token given the previous ones. It is an approximation of language that only needs to reproduce the properties that matter for prediction.

Chain rule: $P(y_1, \dots, y_n) = \prod_t P(y_t \mid y_{<t})$, which is exact. Counting whole sentences fails because language is compositional: almost every sentence has count 0, so we must decompose.

Markov assumption: $P(y_t \mid y_{<t}) \approx P(y_t \mid y_{t-n+1}, \dots, y_{t-1})$: only the $n - 1$ previous tokens matter (the $n$ includes the predicted word). It makes the counts dense enough to estimate, at the price of forgetting anything outside the window; zeros still appear and need backoff, interpolation or smoothing.

Neural LM: instead of counts, a network turns the whole (or a long) context into a vector $h$, then a linear layer + softmax gives a distribution over $|V|$; trained with cross-entropy. It works in a continuous space so it generalises to unseen contexts and can use longer contexts.

rubric.point: Definition of an LM
Chain-rule factorisation
Why sentences cannot be counted (compositional, zero counts)
Markov assumption: n − 1 context words, why and its cost
Neural LM computes each factor via h → linear → softmax, generalising

questions.question: An RNN decoder state is $h_t = [1, 0]$ and the encoder states are $s_1 = [2, 1]$, $s_2 = [0, 1]$, $s_3 = [1, 1]$. Using dot-product attention, calculate the three attention weights and the attention output (source context) $c^{(t)}$.
questions.solution:
Scores: $h_t \cdot s_1 = 2,\ h_t \cdot s_2 = 0,\ h_t \cdot s_3 = 1$.
Softmax: $e^2 = 7.389,\ e^0 = 1,\ e^1 = 2.718$ → sum $11.107$ → $a = [0.6652,\ 0.0900,\ 0.2447]$.
$$\begin{aligned}c^{(t)} &= a_1 s_1 + a_2 s_2 + a_3 s_3 \\ &= 0.6652\,[2, 1] + 0.0900\,[0, 1] \\ &\quad + 0.2447\,[1, 1] \\ &= [1.5752,\ 1.0000]\end{aligned}$$
(The second component is 1 because every encoder state has 1 there and the weights sum to 1.)

questions.question: Explain the 'fixed source representation' problem of a seq2seq model without attention, from the point of view of both the encoder and the decoder, and how attention solves it. (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Encoder: it must compress the whole source sentence into one fixed-size vector. That gets harder (noisier) as sentences get longer, and early tokens fade through the recurrence.
Decoder: it needs different, specific information at different steps (the word for 'cat' now, the word for 'mat' later), but only has one summary vector, set once at the start.
Attention: at every decoder step, score all encoder states against the current decoder state, softmax the scores into weights, and take the weighted sum as a source context vector. The decoder can then retrieve the relevant source details at each step instead of relying on the single bottleneck vector.

rubric.point: Encoder must squeeze the entire source into one fixed-size vector (worse for long sentences)
Decoder needs different source details at different steps
Attention: scores against all encoder states → softmax weights → weighted sum (context) at each step
So the decoder can look up relevant source information at each step: no single bottleneck

questions.question: Describe beam search for decoding, and give one advantage and one disadvantage compared with greedy decoding. (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Beam search keeps the k (beam size) best partial hypotheses at each step. Start from <bos>; extend every hypothesis with candidate next tokens; score the extensions by their total (log-)probability; keep only the top k; repeat until the hypotheses end with <eos>; return the most probable complete one.
Advantage: it explores more than one path, so it gets closer to the most probable whole sentence than greedy decoding, which can commit early to a token that ruins the rest.
Disadvantage: much more computation and memory (k hypotheses, and large beams for big models), and it is still not guaranteed optimal. It also tends to reduce diversity. Modern open-ended LLMs use sampling instead.

rubric.point: Keeps the top-k partial hypotheses at each step
Extend, score by total (log-)probability, prune to k, until <eos>; pick the best
Advantage: closer to the most probable sentence than greedy
Disadvantage: memory/compute cost, still not optimal (or less diverse)

questions.question: Compare the Bahdanau and Luong attention models. Give four differences or defining features. (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
• Encoder: Bahdanau uses a bidirectional RNN (forward and backward states concatenated); Luong uses a unidirectional RNN.
• Which decoder state attends: Bahdanau uses the previous state $h_{t-1}$; Luong uses the current state $h_t$.
• Score function: Bahdanau uses an MLP (additive) score; Luong uses a bilinear score.
• How the context is used: Bahdanau feeds $c^{(t)}$ (with $h_{t-1}$) into the next decoder step; Luong combines $c^{(t)}$ and $h_t$ ($\tilde{h}_t = \tanh(W_c[h_t, c^{(t)}])$) to make the prediction.
The lecturer framed them as two variants of the same general mechanism, differing mainly in the score function and in $h_t$ vs $h_{t-1}$.

rubric.point: Encoder: bidirectional (Bahdanau) vs unidirectional (Luong)
Attending state: $h_{t-1}$ (Bahdanau) vs $h_t$ (Luong)
Score function: MLP (Bahdanau) vs bilinear (Luong)
Use of the context: fed into the next step vs combined with $h_t$ for the prediction

questions.question: Explain why greedy decoding does not necessarily produce the most probable output sentence. (2 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Greedy picks argmax at each step, i.e. it maximises $\prod_t \max p(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x)$ step by step, which is not the same as the argmax over whole sequences of $\prod_t p(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x)$. A locally most probable token can lead into a continuation where every later token has low probability ('The Sistine Chapel is in London…'), so the overall sentence probability ends up lower than an alternative that started with a less probable token.

rubric.point: Greedy is a local choice per step; the product of local maxima $\neq$ the global maximum over sequences

questions.question: Which statement is the key lecture point about greedy decoding?
choices: $\prod_t \arg\max p(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x) \neq \arg\max \prod_t p(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x)$: the best token at each step need not give the most probable sentence
Greedy decoding always finds the most probable sentence
Greedy decoding samples from the full distribution
Greedy decoding keeps $k$ hypotheses
questions.explanation: The lecturer spelled this out as something to remember. An early choice can lock in a bad sentence ("The Sistine Chapel is in London").

questions.question: True or False: Beam search with a beam size of 1 is the same as greedy decoding.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: With one hypothesis kept, each step simply extends it with the most probable token.

questions.question: Which statements about beam search are true?
choices: It keeps the beam_size most probable partial hypotheses at each step
It usually finds a more probable sentence than greedy decoding, but is not guaranteed to find the best one
It is memory-hungry, especially for Transformers
Modern open-ended LLMs mostly use beam search rather than sampling
questions.explanation: Pros and cons, as the lecturer asked: closer to the best whole sentence, but costly. He said open-ended LLMs use sampling instead; beam search works well for short, constrained outputs.

questions.question:
A decoder has this toy distribution; after any two tokens it always outputs </s> with probability 1.
Step 1: The 0.5, A 0.4, </s> 0.1
After "The": cat 0.4, dog 0.35, </s> 0.25
After "A": cat 0.9, dog 0.05, </s> 0.05
(a) Probability of the greedy output.
(b) Probability of the beam-search output with beam size 2.
(c) Probability of the most probable sentence overall.
questions.solution:
(a) Greedy picks "The" (0.5), then "cat" (0.4): "The cat </s>", $0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.2$.
(b) Beam after each step: step 1: The (0.5); A (0.4)
step 2: A cat (0.36); The cat (0.2)
step 3: A cat </s> (0.36); The cat </s> (0.2)
Result: "A cat </s>" with $0.36$.
(c) "A cat </s>" with $0.36$. The lower-probability first word "A" leads to a much better sentence, which greedy throws away at step 1.
questions.explanation: This is exactly why $\prod_t \arg\max \neq \arg\max \prod_t$.

questions.question:
A decoder has these next-token probabilities (every sequence ends after its third word with </s> probability 1):
Step 1: I 0.45, We 0.35, You 0.2
After I: saw 0.5, see 0.3, </s> 0.2 · After We: saw 0.8, </s> 0.2 · After You: saw 0.9, </s> 0.1
After "I saw": it 0.3, them 0.3, </s> 0.4 · After "I see": it 0.9, </s> 0.1 · After "We saw": it 0.7, </s> 0.3 · After "You saw": it 0.6, </s> 0.4
A finished hypothesis (ending in </s>) stays in the beam and competes on its probability.
Give the probability of the final output of (a) greedy decoding, (b) beam search with $k = 2$, (c) beam search with $k = 3$.
questions.solution:
(a) "I saw </s>": $0.09$.
(b) Step 1: I (0.45); We (0.35)
Step 2: We saw (0.28); I saw (0.225)
Step 3: We saw it (0.196); I saw </s> (0.09)
Step 4: We saw it </s> (0.196); I saw </s> (0.09)
Output "We saw it </s>": $0.196$.
(c) Step 1: I (0.45); We (0.35); You (0.2)
Step 2: We saw (0.28); I saw (0.225); You saw (0.18)
Step 3: We saw it (0.196); You saw it (0.108); I saw </s> (0.09)
Step 4: We saw it </s> (0.196); You saw it </s> (0.108); I saw </s> (0.09)
Output "We saw it </s>": $0.196$.
questions.explanation: Note how short hypotheses that end early keep a high probability: this is why real systems length-normalise beam scores (not on the slides).

questions.question: Why is a fixed source representation a problem, according to Lecture 6?
choices: For the encoder: compressing a whole sentence into one vector is hard
For the decoder: different information may be needed at different steps
Early source words tend to be lost first
The fixed vector makes training impossible to parallelise on GPUs
questions.explanation: Attention fixes both halves: the encoder no longer has to keep every detail in one vector, and the decoder can fetch a different detail at each step. Parallelism motivated the Transformer, not RNN attention.

questions.question: Match each term to its meaning at decoder step $t$.

pairs.answer: An unnormalised relevance of source token $k$ (a "propensity")
The score after the softmax over all source tokens
The weighted sum of the encoder states

options: An unnormalised relevance of source token $k$ (a "propensity")
The score after the softmax over all source tokens
The weighted sum of the encoder states
questions.explanation: Score → softmax → weights → weighted sum → context ("source context for decoder step $t$").

questions.question: True or False: Because the attention weights come from a softmax, they are all positive and sum to 1, so the attention output keeps roughly the same magnitude as the encoder states.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The softmax is a differentiable "soft argmax" that usually concentrates on one or two tokens. Weights are close to, but never exactly, zero.

questions.question: True or False: The attention scores for all source tokens at one decoder step can be computed in parallel, even though the decoder itself is still recurrent.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Computing attention is parallel across encoder states; generation is still bottlenecked by the recurrence.

questions.question:
A decoder state is $h = (1,2)$ and the three encoder states are $s_1 = (1,0)$, $s_2 = (0,1)$, $s_3 = (1,1)$. Use dot-product scores.
(a)–(c) The attention weights $a_1, a_2, a_3$.
(d)–(e) The two components of the attention output $c$.

Luong-style attention uses the current decoder state $h_t = (1,-1)$ and a bilinear score $h_t^\top W s_k$ with $W = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$. The encoder states are $s_1 = (2,0)$, $s_2 = (0,1)$, $s_3 = (1,1)$.
(a)–(c) The scores. (d)–(f) The attention weights. (g) The first component of the attention output.
questions.solution:
$W s_k$: $W s_1 = (2,2)$, $W s_2 = (0,1)$, $W s_3 = (1,2)$.
Scores $h_t^\top W s_k$: $(0, -1, -1)$.
Weights: $(0.5761, 0.2119, 0.2119)$.
$c = (1.3642, 0.4239)$. Luong then combines $[h_t; c]$ through a tanh layer to predict the next token.

questions.question:
Bahdanau-style (MLP) attention: $\text{score}(h, s_k) = w_2^\top \tanh(W_1 [h; s_k])$ with $[h; s_k]$ the concatenation. The previous decoder state is $h_{t-1} = (1,0)$, the encoder states are $s_1 = (0,1)$ and $s_2 = (1,1)$, and
$W_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, $w_2 = (1,-1)$.
Give (a) score₁, (b) score₂, (c) the attention weight $a_1$.
Match each attention score function to its formula.
questions.explanation: The softmax turns scores into weights; it is not a score function (Quiz 2 Q1 and Q8).

questions.question: Which statements about score functions are true?
choices: Dot-product attention is bilinear attention with $W = I$
The dot product needs $h$ and $s_k$ to have the same dimension; bilinear and MLP scores do not
The MLP score is the most flexible: a small classifier deciding where to look
The dot product has the most trainable parameters
questions.explanation: Dot product has no parameters at all. A learned $W$ reshapes the comparison and can map between different sizes.

questions.question: Which features belong to the Bahdanau model as taught?
choices: A bidirectional encoder (forward and backward states concatenated)
The previous decoder state $h_{t-1}$ is used to compute attention
An MLP (additive) score function
The context vector is combined with $h_t$ only after the decoder step, through a tanh layer
questions.explanation: Option (d) is Luong. In Bahdanau the context, $h_{t-1}$ and the previous target embedding together produce the new state.

questions.question: Which features belong to the Luong model as taught?
choices: A unidirectional encoder
The current decoder state $h_t$ (after reading the previous word) is used to compute attention
A bilinear score function
$[h_t; c^{(t)}]$ goes through a tanh layer to make the prediction
questions.explanation: Nothing is missing from Luong (a correction to your notes): it updates $h_t$ first, then attends with it. (The Luong paper also proposed dot and concat scores; answer as taught.)

questions.question: True or False: The lecturer described Bahdanau's backward RNN as free to specialise in making attention precise, because it could not usefully initialise the decoder.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: He called this "deeply insightful": the backward states only matter through attention.

questions.question: What does the English–French attention plot ("European Economic Area" ↔ "zone économique européenne") show?
choices: Attention learns an (almost) word-level alignment, including reordering, without being told the alignment
Attention always looks at the same position in the source as the target
The decoder ignores the source after the first word
Attention weights are uniform
questions.explanation: The reversed block shows the model looked at the right words in the right (reversed) order. The lecturer called this the root of mechanistic interpretability: where is the network looking, and why?

questions.question: True or False: The alignment in the attention plot is learned only from translation pairs; no word alignments are given during training.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: That is why the slide says "Attention learned (almost) alignment".

questions.question:
Reference: "the cat is on the mat". Candidate: "the the cat on mat".
Using the standard BLEU ingredients:
(a) clipped unigram precision, (b) clipped bigram precision, (c) the brevity penalty $\text{BP} = e^{1 - r/c}$ (since $c < r$).
questions.solution:
(a) Candidate unigrams: the ×2, cat, on, mat. "the" appears twice in the reference, so both count: $5/5 = 1$.
(b) Bigrams: "the the", "the cat", "cat on", "on mat"; only "the cat" is in the reference: $1/4 = 0.25$.
(c) $c = 5$, $r = 6$: $e^{1 - 6/5} = 0.8187$.
questions.explanation: BLEU is the tutorial's Q5.1, not on the slides; this uses the standard definition. Clipping stops "the the the…" from scoring well; the brevity penalty stops very short candidates from getting perfect precision. BLEU still misses synonyms and paraphrases, and can be gamed.

questions.question: Which are genuine problems with BLEU as a translation metric?
choices: It only matches exact n-grams, so correct synonyms and paraphrases are penalised
It can be gamed (the lecturer mentioned longer outputs)
It needs one or more reference translations
It cannot be computed automatically
questions.explanation: BLEU is automatic, which is why it was popular. It is n-gram precision against references with a brevity penalty (tutorial 5.1).

questions.concept: Greedy decoding vs the best sentence
questions.question:
A decoder has this toy distribution; after any two tokens it outputs </s> with probability 1.
Step 1: Je 0.45, Il 0.40, </s> 0.15
After "Je": suis 0.35, mange 0.35, </s> 0.30
After "Il": mange 0.85, est 0.10, </s> 0.05
(a) Trace greedy decoding and give the output and its probability. (2)
(b) Trace beam search with $k = 2$, showing the beam after each step, and give the result. (3)
(c) Use (a) and (b) to explain why $\prod_t \arg\max p(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x) \neq \arg\max \prod_t p(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x)$, and give one advantage and one cost of beam search. (3)
(d) Explain the information bottleneck in a seq2seq model without attention, and both ways attention relieves it. (2) (10 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Step 1 takes "Je" (0.45). Step 2: "suis" and "mange" tie at 0.35 (either is accepted), then </s>. Output "Je suis </s>" (or "Je mange </s>"), probability $0.45 \times 0.35 = 0.1575$.

(b) Step 1: Je (0.45); Il (0.4)
Step 2: Il mange (0.34); Je suis (0.1575)
Step 3: Il mange </s> (0.34); Je suis </s> (0.1575)
Result "Il mange </s>" with 0.34, which is also the best sentence overall (0.34).

(c) Greedy maximises each factor separately; the most probable sentence maximises their product. "Il" is worse than "Je" at step 1 (0.40 < 0.45), but its continuation is far more certain (0.85), so the full sentence wins. Searching every sentence is intractable; beam search keeps $k$ hypotheses so it can recover from a locally worse choice. Advantage: closer to the best whole sentence than greedy. Cost: $k$ times the compute and memory (especially for Transformers), still no guarantee, and it reduces diversity; open-ended LLMs therefore sample instead.

(d) Without attention the whole source is squeezed into the encoder's final state, which initialises the decoder: hard for long sentences, early words fade (recency bias), and the decoder gets the same vector at every step. Attention: (1) encoder side: it no longer has to store every detail in one vector because every encoder state stays available; (2) decoder side: at each step it can fetch the specific source information it needs now, while its recurrent state keeps the overall intent and what it has already said.

rubric.point: (a) Correct greedy trace and probability
(b) Correct beams at each step
(b) Correct final output and probability
(c) Explains product of argmaxes vs argmax of product with the example
(c) An advantage and a cost of beam search
(d) Describes the bottleneck
(d) Both ways attention relieves it

questions.question:
A decoder state is $h = (0.5,1)$ and the encoder states are $s_1 = (1,0)$, $s_2 = (0,1)$, $s_3 = (1,1)$.
(a) Compute the dot-product attention weights and the attention output. (3)
(b) Compute the bilinear attention weights with $W = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, and explain in words what this $W$ does to the comparison. (3)
(c) State the three score functions and which one Bahdanau and Luong use (as taught). (2)
(d) Bahdanau attends with $h_{t-1}$ and Luong with $h_t$. Explain the difference in how each uses the attention output. (2) (10 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Scores $(0.5, 1, 1.5)$, weights $(0.1863, 0.3072, 0.5065)$, output $c = (0.6928, 0.8137)$.

(b) $W$ swaps the two coordinates of $s_k$, so the score compares $h_1$ with $s_{k,2}$ and $h_2$ with $s_{k,1}$. Scores $(1, 0.5, 1.5)$, weights $(0.3072, 0.1863, 0.5065)$: the focus moves from $s_2$ to $s_1$. A learned $W$ lets the model decide which features of the decoder state should match which features of the encoder state.

(c) Dot product $h^\top s_k$; bilinear $h^\top W s_k$; MLP $w_2^\top \tanh(W_1[h, s_k])$. Bahdanau: MLP. Luong: bilinear (the paper also proposed dot and concat).

(d) Bahdanau: $h_{t-1}$ scores the (bidirectional) encoder states; the context, $h_{t-1}$ and the previous target embedding together produce the new state $h_t$, which predicts the token. Luong: the RNN first updates to $h_t$ from the previous word, then $h_t$ attends; $\tilde h_t = \tanh(W_c [h_t; c^{(t)}])$ makes the prediction. Only the order of updating and attending differs.

rubric.point: (a) Correct dot-product weights
(a) Correct output
(b) Correct bilinear weights
(b) Interprets W
(c) Three formulas and who uses which
(d) Bahdanau vs Luong use of the context

questions.question: Explain why a seq2seq decoder is a conditional language model. Describe the RNN encoder–decoder (what the encoder outputs, how the decoder is initialised, what it receives at each step), how it is trained (including teacher forcing), and why conditioning on the source makes translation easier to learn than open-ended generation. (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
A seq2seq decoder models $P(y_t \mid y_{<t}, x)$: exactly an L5 language model, but conditioned on the source $x$. That is the only new idea.

Encoder: an RNN reads the source tokens; it produces no outputs, only states, and its final state summarises the sentence. Decoder: an RNN LM whose initial state is the encoder's final state; at each step it takes the previous target token, updates its state, and outputs a softmax over the target vocabulary; at inference it feeds its own prediction back in (autoregressive).

Training: cross-entropy, summing $-\log p(y^*_t \mid y^*_{<t}, x)$ over target positions, with the ground-truth previous token as the decoder input (teacher forcing), so all steps get a clean signal.

Conditioning lowers diversity and raises coherence: for a given source only a few targets are correct, which gives the task a notion of correctness and a clean, constrained learning signal. Open-ended generation has many valid continuations, so the one-hot labels conflict more.

rubric.point: States $P(y_t | y_{<t}, x)$: an LM conditioned on the source
Encoder: states only; final state initialises the decoder
Decoder step and autoregressive feedback
Cross-entropy with teacher forcing
Why conditioning helps (less diversity, correctness, clean signal)

questions.concept: Seq2seq tasks and argmax p(y given x)
questions.question: Lecture 6 frames seq2seq as three questions: modelling, learning and search. Explain each for an RNN-with-attention translation model, and explain why a better answer to "learning" does not remove the need for a good answer to "search". (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Modelling: what $p(y \mid x, \theta)$ looks like: an encoder RNN over the source, a decoder RNN (conditional LM) that at each step attends over the encoder states (scores → softmax → weighted sum) and predicts a softmax over target tokens.

Learning: how to find $\theta$: minimise cross-entropy $-\sum_t \log p(y_t^* \mid y^*_{<t}, x)$ over parallel sentence pairs by gradient descent (teacher forcing).

Search: how to find $\arg\max_y p(y \mid x, \theta)$: impossible exactly (exponentially many sentences), so use greedy decoding or beam search.

Even a perfect model only gives probabilities; the output still has to be found. Greedy picks the best token each step, but $\prod_t \arg\max \neq \arg\max \prod_t$, so a locally best token can lead to a worse sentence; beam search reduces (but does not remove) this search error. So modelling/learning errors and search errors are separate.

rubric.point: Modelling explained for this model
Learning: cross-entropy on parallel data
Search: intractable argmax; greedy/beam
Why search still matters (search error, product of argmaxes)

questions.question: Explain what BLEU measures and how it is computed at a high level, and give two problems with it. Why did the lecturer say the field moved away from it? (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
BLEU compares a candidate translation with one or more reference translations: it computes modified (clipped) n-gram precisions for $n = 1$ to $4$ (how many candidate n-grams appear in a reference, each counted at most as often as in the reference), combines them with a geometric mean, and multiplies by a brevity penalty for candidates shorter than the reference.

Problems: (1) exact n-gram matching misses synonyms and paraphrases, so a correct but differently worded translation scores low; (2) it can be gamed (the lecturer mentioned longer outputs), and it ignores meaning and grammaticality beyond local n-grams; it also needs reference translations. Because of this, the field moved to other evaluations.

rubric.point: Precision of n-grams against references (clipped)
Brevity penalty / combination
Two valid problems

questions.question: Attention in RNN seq2seq models has costs as well as benefits. Discuss: what attention fixes, what the alignment plots reveal, and what the lecturer said attention costs (diagnosis, data). (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Fixes: the bottleneck. The encoder no longer has to preserve every detail in one vector, and the decoder can fetch a different detail at each step; the recurrent state keeps the intent and history while attention supplies the detail.

Alignment plots: attention weights for each target word over source words form an almost one-to-one alignment, including reordering (European Economic Area ↔ zone économique européenne), learned without alignment labels. This makes the model partly interpretable: "where is the network looking, and why?", the root of mechanistic interpretability.

Costs: errors are harder to diagnose (bad encoding? lost track? attended to the wrong token?), it needs more data, gradient descent has to make the encoder states easy to find, and the extra computation per step.

rubric.point: What attention fixes
What alignment plots show
At least two costs from the lecture

questions.question: True or False, masked self-attention is used in the encoder of a Transformer to stop tokens attending to future tokens.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Masking is in the decoder; the encoder's self-attention is unmasked and can look in both directions.

questions.question: In the Transformer's encoder–decoder (cross) attention, the queries come from:
choices: The decoder states
The encoder states
The positional encodings
The output softmax
questions.explanation: Queries from the decoder; keys and values from the encoder output.

questions.question: Which of the following are True about multi-head attention in a Transformer?
choices: Each head has its own query, key and value projection matrices
The heads' outputs are concatenated and then multiplied by an output matrix $W_O$
Each head attends to a different chunk of the sentence
The output has the same dimension as the input, so layers can be stacked
questions.explanation: Every head sees all the tokens but uses its own projections (a different subspace). Concatenate → $W_O$ → back to $d_{model}$.

questions.question: Why are the attention scores divided by $\sqrt{d_k}$ in scaled dot-product attention?
choices: To stop large dot products from pushing the softmax into a saturated, near one-hot region with tiny gradients
To turn the scores into probabilities
To reduce the number of parameters
To encode the position of each token
questions.explanation: The variance of $q \cdot k$ grows with $d_k$; dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps it around 1, a bit like stopping the softmax from behaving as if it had a very low temperature.

questions.question: True or False, without positional encodings, self-attention is permutation equivariant: shuffling the input tokens just shuffles the outputs in the same way.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: That's why position has to be added explicitly.

questions.question: In masked self-attention, the scores for future positions are set to which value before the softmax?
choices: $-\infty$
The mean of the other scores
questions.explanation: $\exp(-\infty) = 0$, so the future weights become exactly 0. Setting a score to 0 would not mask anything, because $\exp(0) = 1$.

questions.question: True or False, in the original Transformer, sine is used for the even dimensions and cosine for the odd dimensions of the positional encoding.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: $PE_{pos,2i} = \sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})$, $PE_{pos,2i+1} = \cos(\ldots)$.

questions.question: Which activation function is used between the two linear layers of the Transformer's feed-forward block? Write its short name.
questions.explanation: ReLU: $\mathrm{FFN}(x) = \max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2$.

questions.question: Which of the following are found inside a single Transformer ENCODER layer?
choices: Multi-head self-attention
A position-wise feed-forward network
Residual connections with layer normalisation
Encoder–decoder (cross) attention
Masked self-attention
questions.explanation: Cross-attention and masked self-attention only appear in the decoder.

questions.question: True or False, layer normalisation in a Transformer normalises each token's vector across its feature dimensions.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Mean 0 / variance 1 over the $d_{model}$ features of one token, followed by a learned scale $\gamma$ and shift $\beta$. Normalising across the batch is BatchNorm.

questions.question: A residual (skip) connection around a sublayer F computes:
choices: $F(x) \cdot x$
$\mathrm{LayerNorm}(F(x))$ only
questions.explanation: The block learns an update to its input. It came from ResNet and smooths the loss landscape.

questions.question: True or False, the attention weights of a Transformer attention layer are computed as $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k})V$.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k})$ are the weights (the attention matrix). Multiplying by $V$ gives the attention OUTPUT. The lecturer said that if he asks for the attention matrix, don't multiply by $V$.

questions.question: A query $q = [1, 2, 0, 1]$ attends to two keys $k_1 = [1, 0, 1, 1]$ and $k_2 = [2, 1, 0, 0]$ in a Transformer attention layer ($d_k = 4$). Calculate the two attention weights.
questions.solution:
$q \cdot k_1 = 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 2$; $q \cdot k_2 = 2 + 2 + 0 + 0 = 4$.
Scale by $\sqrt{d_k} = 2$: scores $[1, 2]$.
$$\frac{e^1}{e^1 + e^2} = 0.2689, \qquad \frac{e^2}{e^1 + e^2} = 0.7311$$
These ARE the attention weights: don't multiply by $V$ unless the output is asked for.
questions.inputHint: Give each weight to 4 decimal places.

questions.question: A Transformer has $d_{model} = 512$ and 8 attention heads, with each head's key dimension $d_k = d_{model}/h$. Calculate (a) $d_k$ and (b) the total number of weights (no biases) in one multi-head attention block's projection matrices $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$ and $W_O$.
questions.solution:
(a) $d_k = 512 / 8 = 64$.
(b) Across all heads, $W_Q$, $W_K$ and $W_V$ are each $512 \times (8 \cdot 64) = 512 \times 512$, and $W_O$ is $512 \times 512$: $4 \times 262{,}144 = 1{,}048{,}576$.
Splitting into heads doesn't add parameters compared with one full-width head.

questions.question: Using $PE_{pos,2i} = \sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})$ and $PE_{pos,2i+1} = \cos(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})$, calculate the first two dimensions ($i = 0$) of the positional encoding for $pos = 1$, and the first dimension for $pos = 2$. Use radians.
questions.solution:
For i = 0 the denominator is 10000⁰ = 1, so the angle is just pos.
PE(1, 0) = sin(1) = 0.8415; PE(1, 1) = cos(1) = 0.5403; PE(2, 0) = sin(2) = 0.9093.
Dimension 0 has the shortest wavelength (2π); higher i give longer wavelengths.
questions.inputHint: Give each value to 4 decimal places.

questions.question: Explain the roles of the query, key and value vectors in self-attention, and why a Transformer uses three separate projections instead of one vector per token. (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Each token's embedding x is projected three ways: $q = W_Q x,\ k = W_K x,\ v = W_V x$.
• Query: what this token is looking for ('do you have this information?').
• Key: what each token offers, compared against the query to get the score ('I have this information, give me a large weight').
• Value: the information actually passed on: the output is the softmax-weighted sum of the values.
Why separate: in RNN attention one vector had to do everything at once (encode meaning, be easy to find, and supply the information). Decoupling 'where to look' ($Q \cdot K$) from 'what to take' ($V$) lets each be learned for its own job. The cost is more parameters, so more data is needed.

rubric.point: Query: the vector the current token uses to look for information
Key: compared with the query (dot product) to produce the attention scores
Value: the information combined by the attention weights into the output
Why separate: decouples matching from the information passed on (one vector no longer has to do both)

questions.question: Why does scaled dot-product attention divide $QK^T$ by $\sqrt{d_k}$? (2 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer: For vectors with $d_k$ roughly independent components, the variance of $q \cdot k$ grows with $d_k$, so large dimensions give very large scores. Large scores push the softmax into saturation (almost one-hot weights) where its gradients are tiny, which hurts training. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the variance of the scores around 1 whatever the dimension.

rubric.point: The dot product's magnitude/variance grows with $d_k$
Large scores saturate the softmax (near one-hot, vanishing gradients); scaling keeps the variance ~1

questions.question: Explain why the Transformer decoder uses masked self-attention and how the mask is applied. (3 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
At inference time the decoder generates left to right, so it can't see future tokens. During training the whole target sentence is processed in parallel, so without a mask each position could attend to the tokens it is supposed to predict (cheating), and training would not match inference.
The mask sets the scores for future positions ($j > i$) to $-\infty$ before the softmax, so their weights are exactly 0 and each position only attends to itself and earlier positions. The allowed weights form a lower-triangular matrix.

rubric.point: Future tokens are unknown at generation time
Training processes all target tokens in parallel, so without a mask the model could see the future (training/inference mismatch)
Future scores set to $-\infty$ before softmax, giving zero weight (lower-triangular)

questions.question: Explain the purpose of residual connections and layer normalisation in the Transformer. (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Residual connections: each sublayer's output is added to its input, x + F(x). The block only has to learn an update (and can learn to do nothing), gradients flow directly through the skip path, and the loss landscape becomes much smoother, which makes deep stacks trainable (the idea comes from ResNet).
Layer normalisation: after each residual addition, each token's vector is normalised over its features (mean 0, variance 1), then scaled and shifted by learned γ, β. This keeps activations at a stable scale as many blocks are stacked (stops values from exploding or drifting), which stabilises and speeds up training.

rubric.point: Residual: output = x + F(x); the block learns an update
Residual benefit: easier gradient flow / smoother loss landscape, so deep networks train
Layer norm: normalise each token's features to mean 0, variance 1, then learned γ, β
Layer norm benefit: keeps the scale stable across stacked layers

questions.question: Why does a Transformer need positional encodings, and how do the original sinusoidal encodings represent position? (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Self-attention has no recurrence or convolution and treats the input as a set: it is permutation equivariant, so without extra information 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would give the same token representations, just permuted. Word order matters, so position must be injected.
A position vector is added to each token embedding. In the original Transformer, dimension $2i$ is $\sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})$ and dimension $2i+1$ is $\cos(\ldots)$. Each pair of dimensions is a wave with its own frequency: early dimensions change quickly (fine position), later ones slowly (coarse position), so together they give every position a distinct pattern, and nearby positions get similar vectors. (Learned position embeddings are the common alternative.)

rubric.point: Self-attention is order-agnostic (permutation equivariant), so order must be added
A position vector is added to each token embedding
sin for even dimensions, cos for odd, with $pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}}$
Different frequencies per dimension give each position a distinguishable code

questions.question: Why does a Transformer use multiple attention heads, and how are the heads' outputs combined? (3 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
A single attention distribution can only focus on one kind of relationship at a time, but a token may need several kinds of information at once (e.g. its subject, its object, agreement, nearby words). Each head has its own $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$, so it can learn a different relation (positional, syntactic, rare-token heads…). Gradient descent decides what each head does.
The heads run in parallel; their outputs are concatenated and multiplied by an output matrix $W_O$, which projects back to $d_{model}$ so the result can be added to the residual and the layers stacked.

rubric.point: One head can only capture one attention pattern; several relations are needed at once
Each head has its own projections and learns a different relation
Outputs concatenated and projected by $W_O$ back to $d_{model}$

questions.question: Explain why Transformers can be trained much faster than RNNs, and state what is still sequential in a Transformer. (3 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
An RNN must process tokens one after another ($O(N)$ sequential steps), because $h_t$ depends on $h_{t-1}$; it can't be parallelised over the sequence and long-range information has to pass through many steps.
A Transformer computes self-attention for all tokens at once with matrix multiplications: a constant number of sequential steps per layer, fully parallel on a GPU, so it can be trained on far more data. Every token can also see every other token directly.
Still sequential: autoregressive generation at inference: the decoder produces one token at a time and feeds it back in.

rubric.point: RNN: $h_t$ depends on $h_{t-1}$, so $O(N)$ sequential steps, not parallelisable
Transformer: all positions processed in parallel with matrix operations (constant steps), so more data per unit time
Generation (decoding) is still one token at a time

questions.question: Label the parts of the Transformer architecture marked 1–9.

image.alt: The Transformer (encoder on the left, decoder on the right) with nine component labels hidden and numbered 1–9.

questions.explanation: Bottom up. Encoder (left): input embedding + positional encoding → [multi-head self-attention → add & norm → feed forward → add & norm] $\times N$. choices: True
False
questions.explanation: With teacher forcing and a causal mask, every target position is processed in one pass. At inference each new token depends on the previous ones.

choices: Every token can see every other token directly, instead of through a long chain of recurrent steps

They need no data to train

questions.question: An RNN processes a sentence of $N$ tokens. How many sequential steps does it need, compared with a Transformer encoder with $L$ layers?
choices: RNN: $N$ steps; Transformer: $L$ steps whatever the sentence length
RNN: $L$ steps; Transformer: $N$ steps
