questions.question: What makes self-attention "self"?
choices: Each state in a set looks at all other states in the same set
A token attends only to itself
The decoder state looks at the encoder states
The model attends to its own weights
questions.explanation: Decoder–encoder attention looks from one decoder state at all encoder states. Self-attention looks from each state at all states of the same sequence (Quiz 2 Q16: "only to itself" is false).

questions.question: True or False: If one attention weight in a row is 1 and the rest are 0, self-attention simply passes that one token's value forward, so attention generalises a normal layer.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: From the recording: the output is $\sum_j a_{ij} v_j$, so a one-hot weight row copies one value.

questions.question: Match each role to its description.

pairs.answer: The vector from which attention is looking ("do you have this information?")
The vector the query is compared with to compute weights ("I have this, give me a large weight")
Their weighted sum is the attention output ("here is the information I have")

options: The vector from which attention is looking ("do you have this information?")
The vector the query is compared with to compute weights ("I have this, give me a large weight")
Their weighted sum is the attention output ("here is the information I have")
The position of the token in the sentence
questions.explanation: The lecturer's analogy: the query is "I want to know about cats", the key "I know about cats, come talk to me", the weight is how much of your hour you spend with each person and the value is what they tell you.

questions.question: Which statements about $Q$, $K$ and $V$ are true?
choices: For each token, $q = W_Q x$, $k = W_K x$ and $v = W_V x$: three separate learned projections of the same input
Splitting the roles decouples where to look ($q \cdot k$) from what to take ($v$)
Having three matrices means more parameters, so more data is needed and overfitting is a risk
The value of a token is its query
questions.explanation: In RNN attention one vector had to encode meaning, be findable and provide the information. Option (d) is a misreading corrected in your notes.

questions.question: You are asked for the attention matrix of a self-attention layer. What do you give?
choices: $A = \text{softmax}(QK^\top / \sqrt{d_k})$, row-wise, after any mask
$\text{softmax}(QK^\top / \sqrt{d_k})\,V$
$QK^\top$
$QK^\top V / \sqrt{d_k}$
questions.explanation: The lecturer: "do not multiply by V… and I am going to ask you this." $AV$ is the attention output.

questions.question: True or False: To find a single attention weight $a_{12}$ you only need $q_1$ and $k_2$.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The softmax normalises over all keys, so $a_{12}$ needs every score in row 1: $q_1 \cdot k_j$ for all $j$.

questions.question:
Three tokens have embeddings (rows) $X = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$. Use the row convention $Q = XW_Q$, $K = XW_K$, $V = XW_V$ with
$W_Q = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $W_K = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, $W_V = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $d_k = 2$.
Give the unmasked attention matrix $A = \text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})$, row by row (rows = queries, columns = keys).
questions.solution:
$Q = XW_Q = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $K = XW_K = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $V = XW_V = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$.
$$QK^\top = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 4 \\ 1 & 4 & 3\end{bmatrix}$$
$$S = QK^\top/\sqrt{2} = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1.4142 & 0.7071 \\ 1.4142 & 2.8284 & 2.8284 \\ 0.7071 & 2.8284 & 2.1213\end{bmatrix}$$
Row-wise softmax:
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}0.14 & 0.576 & 0.284 \\ 0.1084 & 0.4458 & 0.4458 \\ 0.0743 & 0.62 & 0.3057\end{bmatrix}$$
Each row sums to 1. (The output would be $AV = \begin{bmatrix}0.424 & 1.86 \\ 0.5542 & 1.8916 \\ 0.38 & 1.9257\end{bmatrix}$, but the question asks for $A$: stop there.)

questions.question:
Same setup: $X = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $W_Q = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $W_K = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, $W_V = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $d_k = 2$, row convention.
Now apply a causal (decoder) mask.
(a)–(c) The masked attention weights in row 2 ($a_{21}$, $a_{22}$, $a_{23}$) and row 3 ($a_{31}$, $a_{32}$, $a_{33}$).
(d) The attention output for token 2 ($[AV]_2$, both components).
questions.solution:
Scores as before, $S = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1.4142 & 0.7071 \\ 1.4142 & 2.8284 & 2.8284 \\ 0.7071 & 2.8284 & 2.1213\end{bmatrix}$. Mask: set every score above the diagonal ($j > i$) to $-\infty$ before the softmax:
$$S_{\text{mask}} = \begin{bmatrix}0 & -\infty & -\infty \\ 1.4142 & 2.8284 & -\infty \\ 0.7071 & 2.8284 & 2.1213\end{bmatrix}$$
Softmax per row ($e^{-\infty} = 0$):
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.1956 & 0.8044 & 0 \\ 0.0743 & 0.62 & 0.3057\end{bmatrix}$$
Row 1 is always $(1, 0, 0)$; row 3 is unchanged by the mask.
Output for token 2: $a_{21} v_1 + a_{22} v_2 = 0.1956(1,1) + 0.8044(0,2) = (0.1956, 1.8044)$.
questions.explanation: Setting a score to 0 would not mask anything, because $e^0 = 1$. The allowed weights form a lower-triangular matrix (rows = queries, columns = keys).

questions.question:
As in the tutorial, each row of $X$ is a token and you left-multiply by the weights: $Q = W_Q X^\top$, $K = W_K X^\top$, $V = W_V X^\top$ (so each column is one token).
$X = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, $W_Q = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $W_K = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $W_V = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $d_k = 2$.
(a) The self-attention matrix $A$ (rows = query tokens).
(b) The attention output for token 1.
questions.solution:
Columns are tokens:
$Q = W_Q X^\top = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2.5 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, so $q_1 = (1,2.5)$, $q_2 = (2,1)$.
$K = W_K X^\top = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, $V = W_V X^\top = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}$.
Scores $S_{ij} = q_i \cdot k_j / \sqrt 2$, i.e. $S = Q^\top K/\sqrt 2 = \begin{bmatrix}5.6569 & 1.4142 \\ 5.6569 & 2.8284\end{bmatrix}$.
$A = \begin{bmatrix}0.9858 & 0.0142 \\ 0.9442 & 0.0558\end{bmatrix}$.
(b) $a_{11} v_1 + a_{12} v_2 = (2.0283, 2.9858)$ with $v_j$ the columns of $V$.
questions.explanation: Watch the orientation: with tokens as columns the score matrix is $Q^\top K$, not $QK^\top$. Either way, entry $(i, j)$ is query $i$ against key $j$.

questions.concept: Cross-attention and where each attention type lives
questions.question:
In encoder–decoder (cross) attention, two decoder positions have queries $Q = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ (rows), and three encoder tokens have keys $K = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ and values $V = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}$. $d_k = 2$.
(a) What shape is the attention matrix (rows × columns)? Give the rows then the columns.
(b) The attention weights of decoder position 2 over the three encoder tokens.
(c) The first component of decoder position 2's output.
questions.solution:
(a) One row per query (decoder position), one column per key (encoder token): $2 \times 3$. Cross-attention matrices need not be square.
(b) Scores row 2: $q_2 \cdot k_j / \sqrt 2 = (0.7071, 0.7071, 0)$; softmax $(0.4011, 0.4011, 0.1978)$.
(c) $\sum_j a_{2j} v_j = (0.7967, 0.7967)$.
questions.explanation: Q comes from the decoder; K and V come from the (final) encoder output. No causal mask is needed: the whole source is known.

questions.concept: Scaling by the square root of d_k
questions.question:
A query has dot products $(16, 8, 0)$ with three keys, and $d_k = 64$.
(a) The weight on the first key without scaling.
(b) The weight on the first key with the usual scaling by $\sqrt{d_k}$.
(c) The weight on the third key with scaling.
questions.solution:
(a) $\text{softmax}(16, 8, 0)$: $a_1 = 0.99966$: essentially one-hot.
(b) Divide by $\sqrt{64} = 8$: scores $(2, 1, 0)$, $a_1 = 0.6652$.
(c) $a_3 = 0.09$.
questions.explanation: The variance of $q \cdot k$ grows with $d_k$ (it is $d_k$ if the components have unit variance). Without scaling the softmax saturates, acting like a very low temperature: weights become nearly one-hot and gradients vanish.

questions.concept: Scaling by the square root of d_k
questions.question: True or False: Dividing the scores by $\sqrt{d_k}$ has the same effect on the attention weights as a softmax temperature of $\tau = \sqrt{d_k}$.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: $\text{softmax}(s/\sqrt{d_k})$ is exactly temperature sampling's formula with $\tau = \sqrt{d_k}$: a link between L5 and L7.

questions.question: Which statements about the causal mask are correct?
choices: Masked scores are set to $-\infty$ before the softmax, so their weights become 0
Without the mask, training would let position 3 see the word at position 4, which will not exist at inference
Setting the masked scores to 0 would be enough
The mask makes training and inference consistent
questions.explanation: The lecturer was unsure whether the mask goes on the score or after the softmax; the standard answer is $-\infty$ on the score, before the softmax. $e^0 = 1$, so 0 masks nothing.

questions.question: Which statements about multi-head attention are correct?
choices: Every head sees all the tokens; heads differ in their own (smaller) $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$
The head outputs are concatenated and multiplied by $W_O$ to return to $d_{model}$
Nothing tells a head what to specialise in; gradient descent decides
The sentence is split into $h$ chunks, one per head

questions.question: True or False: At a fixed $d_{model}$ with $d_k = d_{model}/h$, using 8 heads instead of 1 multiplies the attention projection parameters by 8.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Each head has $W_Q, W_K, W_V$ of size $d_{model} \times d_{model}/h$, so all heads together still have $3 d_{model}^2$, plus $W_O$. The lecturer suggested otherwise; the standard design costs the same.

questions.question:
A BERT-base encoder layer has $d_{model} = 768$, $h = 12$ heads and a feed-forward inner size $d_{ff} = 3072$.
(a) $d_k$ per head.
(b) Weights in $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$, $W_O$ (no biases).
(c) Parameters in the feed-forward block (both linear layers, with biases).
(d) Total parameters in the layer, counting attention biases ($4 \times d_{model}$) and the two LayerNorms ($\gamma$ and $\beta$ each).
questions.explanation: The feed-forward block holds about two thirds of a layer's parameters. Twelve such layers give about 85M of BERT-base's ~110M parameters; the rest is mostly the embeddings.

questions.question: A Transformer has $d_{model} = 256$. Count the weights in $W_Q, W_K, W_V$ (all heads together) plus $W_O$, no biases, when (a) $h = 1$ with $d_k = 256$ and (b) $h = 8$ with $d_k = 32$. (c) What is the size of one head's $W_Q$ in case (b)? Give the number of entries.
questions.solution:
(a) $3 \times 256^2 + 256^2$ = 262,144.
(b) Each head: three $256 \times 32$ matrices; 8 heads: $3 \times 8 \times 256 \times 32 = 3 \times 256^2$; plus $W_O$ ($256 \times 256$): the same 262,144.
(c) $256 \times 32 = 8192$ entries.

questions.concept: Cross-attention and where each attention type lives
questions.question: In encoder–decoder (cross) attention:
choices: Q comes from the decoder; K and V come from the encoder output
Q comes from the encoder; K and V come from the decoder
Q, K and V all come from the encoder
Q and K come from the decoder; V comes from the encoder
questions.explanation: The lecturer: "If you understand the key–query–value mechanism and how keys and queries can be paired differently, I'm happy."

questions.question: Which statements about where attention appears are correct?
choices: Encoder: unmasked self-attention (tokens look left and right)
Decoder: masked self-attention first, then cross-attention, then the feed-forward block
Every decoder layer cross-attends to the final encoder output
The encoder uses a causal mask
questions.explanation: Decoder order: masked self-attention → add & norm → cross-attention → add & norm → FFN → add & norm. The encoder sees the whole source, so it needs no causal mask.

questions.question: What is the Transformer's feed-forward block?
choices: $\text{FFN}(x) = \max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2$, applied to each token separately
A second attention layer over all tokens
A recurrent layer that carries information between tokens
A softmax over the vocabulary
questions.explanation: A two-layer ReLU MLP per token ("take a moment to think"). Tokens only exchange information in attention.

questions.question: True or False: A residual connection computes $x + F(x)$, so a block learns an update to its input and can easily "do nothing".
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Residuals come from ResNet; they smooth the loss landscape and "do a lot of heavy lifting". They have nothing to do with the value vectors (a correction to your notes).

questions.question: Why must the output of an attention block have the same dimension as its input?
choices: So that the residual connection $x + F(x)$ can be added
So that blocks can be stacked $N$ times
Because each layer moves a token within the same representation space
Because the softmax requires it
questions.explanation: That is why $W_O$ projects the concatenated heads back to $d_{model}$.

questions.question:
A token vector is $x = (2,4,4,6)$. Apply layer normalisation ignoring $\epsilon$: $\hat x = (x - \mu)/\sqrt{\sigma^2}$, output $\gamma \odot \hat x + \beta$, with $\gamma = (1,1,2,2)$ and $\beta = (0,0,0,1)$.
(a) $\mu$  (b) $\sigma^2$  (c) $\hat x_1$  (d) the fourth output component.
questions.explanation: LayerNorm normalises each token across its own $d_{model}$ features (not across the batch: that is BatchNorm). The learned $\gamma, \beta$ keep flexibility.

questions.question: Why do Transformers use layer normalisation, according to the lecturer?
choices: If every block scaled its vectors by 2, ten blocks would scale them by $2^{10}$; normalising keeps the scale stable
To make the attention weights sum to 1
To remove the need for positional encodings
To mask future tokens
questions.explanation: Stable scale across many stacked blocks; $\gamma$ and $\beta$ give back flexibility.

questions.question:
Use $PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})$ and $PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos(pos/10000^{2i/d_{model}})$ with $d_{model} = 4$ (radians).
(a)–(d) The four components of the positional encoding for $pos = 3$.
(e) The wavelength (in positions) of dimensions 2 and 3.
questions.explanation: Sin goes on even dimensions, cos on odd. High-frequency dimensions give fine resolution; low-frequency ones cover long ranges, so the combination does not repeat over realistic lengths (though a single wave does).

questions.question: Which statements about positional encoding are correct?
choices: Without it, self-attention is permutation equivariant: shuffle the tokens and the outputs shuffle the same way
The position vector is added to the token embedding
Learned position embeddings are a valid alternative to sinusoids
Sinusoidal encodings never repeat for arbitrarily long sentences
questions.explanation: Quiz 2 Q18: they can repeat. Strictly the term is equivariant (the lecturer ended up saying "invariant").

questions.question: True or False: In the original Transformer the encoder and decoder both have $N = 6$ layers, but they do not strictly have to match, because every decoder layer attends to the final encoder output.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The lecturer said they must match; the watch-out in your notes corrects this.

questions.question: Which roles did the analysis of NMT Transformer heads find for the important heads?
choices: Positional heads that attend to neighbouring tokens
Syntactic heads that track dependencies such as verb → subject and object → verb
Heads that attend to rare tokens
Heads that always attend uniformly to every token
questions.explanation: Voita et al.: the important heads play interpretable roles, and many of the rest can be pruned with little loss.

questions.question: True or False: Many heads can be pruned from a trained Transformer with little loss of quality.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Only a few heads are "important". The lecturer added that many heads end up doing nothing for African languages because they are tuned to English syntax.

questions.question: What is "probing" a representation?
choices: Training a simple classifier on the (frozen) representations and using its accuracy to see whether a property is encoded
Masking random input tokens and predicting them
Visualising one attention head
Fine-tuning the whole model on a new task
questions.explanation: A high probe accuracy shows the information is decodable; it does not prove the model uses it.

questions.question: Which analysis methods are model-agnostic (they do not depend on the architecture)?
choices: Probing representations with a classifier
Contrastive evaluation with minimal pairs
Looking at attention heads
Inspecting individual neurons of a specific model
questions.explanation: Model-specific methods look inside (heads, neurons); model-agnostic methods only need representations or output probabilities.

questions.question: What did probing NMT encoders for morphology find (as shown in Lecture 7)?
choices: Layer 0 (the embeddings) is worst at predicting morphology
Layer 1 is better than layer 2
Surprisingly, translating into a target language with weaker morphology gives a better encoder for source morphology
The decoder learns morphology better than the encoder in every setting

choices: True
False

questions.question:
Two tokens have embeddings (rows) $X = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}$. Use $Q = XW_Q$, $K = XW_K$, $V = XW_V$ with $W_Q = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$, $W_K = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$, $W_V = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ and $d_k = 2$.
(a) Compute $Q$, $K$ and $V$. (2)
(b) Compute the attention matrix (unmasked). (3)
(c) Compute the attention output for both tokens. (1)
(d) Give the masked attention matrix for a decoder, and explain exactly how and why the mask is applied. (2)
(e) Explain why the scores are divided by $\sqrt{d_k}$ and what would happen at $d_k = 512$ without it. (2)
(f) Using the lecturer's analogy, explain intuitively what $q$, $k$ and $v$ do. (2) (12 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $Q = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, $K = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}$, $V = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$.

(b) $QK^\top = \begin{bmatrix}5 & 6 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}$, $S = QK^\top/\sqrt 2 = \begin{bmatrix}3.5355 & 4.2426 \\ 1.4142 & 2.8284\end{bmatrix}$, row-wise softmax: $A = \begin{bmatrix}0.3302 & 0.6698 \\ 0.1956 & 0.8044\end{bmatrix}$. This is the attention matrix: stop here (no $V$).

(c) $AV = \begin{bmatrix}0.3302 & 1.6698 \\ 0.1956 & 1.8044\end{bmatrix}$.

(d) Set scores above the diagonal to $-\infty$ before the softmax: $A_{\text{mask}} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0.1956 & 0.8044\end{bmatrix}$. Token 1 may only attend to itself; token 2 to tokens 1 and 2. In training the decoder sees the whole target at once, so without the mask it would cheat by looking at future words that do not exist at inference. Setting a score to 0 would not mask anything, since $e^0 = 1$.

(e) If $q$ and $k$ have components with unit variance, $q \cdot k$ has variance $d_k$. At $d_k = 512$ the scores would be around $\pm 22$, the softmax would saturate (nearly one-hot, like a very low temperature) and its gradients would vanish. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ brings the variance back to about 1.

(f) The query says "I want to know about X"; each key says "I know about Y, come talk to me"; $q \cdot k$ (after the softmax) decides how much of your time you spend with each token; the value is what that token actually tells you. Splitting the roles lets where-to-look ($Q$, $K$) be learned separately from what-to-take ($V$).

questions.question: Compare RNNs, CNNs and Transformers as sequence encoders. For each, explain how information travels between distant tokens, how parallelisable the computation is, and one weakness. Then explain what Transformers need that the other two do not, and why. (8 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
RNN: information travels step by step through the hidden state, so distant tokens interact through $O(N)$ sequential steps; this suffers from vanishing/exploding gradients and recency bias. Computation is sequential over positions (not parallelisable within a sequence). Weakness: slow, hard credit assignment, fixed-size state.

CNN: each filter sees a local window; distant tokens interact only after stacking layers (receptive field grows with depth/kernel size). Fully parallel over positions. Weakness: long-range dependencies need many layers; for generation it reprocesses the whole input per token.

Transformer: self-attention connects every pair of tokens in one layer (constant path length), and all positions are processed in parallel, so a sentence takes a constant number of sequential layer steps. Weaknesses: attention cost grows with $N^2$, it is data hungry (three projection matrices per layer), and generation is still sequential.

What it needs: positional encodings. Self-attention is permutation equivariant, so without them "cat" as subject and as object look the same; RNNs (time) and CNNs (spatial windows) get order for free.

rubric.point: RNN: path length, sequential, weakness
CNN: local windows, receptive field, parallel, weakness
Transformer: direct pairs, parallel, weakness (N², data)
Needs positional encodings because of permutation equivariance

questions.question: Describe one encoder layer and one decoder layer of the original Transformer in order, naming every sub-layer. For each attention sub-layer state where Q, K and V come from and whether a mask is used. Then explain the purpose of the residual connections, layer normalisation and the feed-forward block, and why the output dimension of every sub-layer equals its input dimension. (8 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Encoder layer: (1) multi-head self-attention (Q, K, V all from the encoder's previous layer; no mask: tokens look left and right) → add & norm; (2) position-wise feed-forward → add & norm.

Decoder layer: (1) masked multi-head self-attention (Q, K, V from the decoder's previous layer; causal mask: look left only and at yourself) → add & norm; (2) cross-attention (Q from the decoder, K and V from the final encoder output; no causal mask) → add & norm; (3) feed-forward → add & norm. A final linear layer and softmax give the next-token distribution.

Residuals: each sub-layer computes $x + F(x)$, learning an update; easier optimisation and smoother loss landscape, and a block can do nothing. LayerNorm: normalises each token across its features so the scale does not explode over many layers ($\gamma, \beta$ learned). FFN: $\max(0, xW_1 + b_1)W_2 + b_2$ per token, the per-token processing step (most of the parameters).

Same dimension: so the residual addition works and layers can be stacked $N$ times; each layer moves the token within the same space (multi-head outputs are concatenated and projected back with $W_O$).

Decoder sub-layers in order

Purpose of residuals
Purpose of LayerNorm (per token)
Purpose of FFN
Why output dim = input dim

questions.question: Explain why Transformers need positional encodings and how sinusoidal encodings work. Compute $PE_{(pos=2, 0)}$ and $PE_{(pos=2, 1)}$ for any $d_{model}$. Explain why many dimensions with different wavelengths are used, and name the alternative mentioned in the lecture. (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Self-attention is permutation equivariant: it treats the input as a set, so shuffling the tokens just shuffles the outputs, and word order (subject vs object) is lost. A position vector is therefore added to each token embedding.

$PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin(pos/10000^{2i/d})$, $PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos(pos/10000^{2i/d})$: sin on even dimensions, cos on odd. For $i = 0$ the denominator is 1, so $PE_{(2,0)} = \sin 2 = 0.9093$ and $PE_{(2,1)} = \cos 2 = -0.4161$.

A single wave repeats, so two positions a wavelength apart would look the same. Using many dimensions whose wavelengths grow geometrically (from $2\pi$ to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$) gives fine resolution from the fast dimensions and long range from the slow ones, so the combination identifies positions. Alternative: learned position embeddings trained by gradient descent.

rubric.point: Permutation equivariance explained
Added to embeddings; sin/cos formula on even/odd dims
Correct values
Why many wavelengths
Learned embeddings as the alternative

questions.question: Explain multi-head attention: how the heads are formed and combined, what they buy you, and how many projection parameters they cost compared with a single head at the same $d_{model}$. Comment on the lecturer's remark that many heads end up doing nothing for African languages. (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Each head $i$ has its own $W_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^V$ of size $d_{model} \times d_{model}/h$, computes scaled dot-product attention over all tokens in its own subspace, and the $h$ outputs are concatenated and multiplied by $W_O$ back to $d_{model}$. Every head sees every token; the split is across representation subspaces.

Benefit: one softmax can focus on only one or two things; several heads can track different relations at once (agreement, who is the subject, properties, prepositions). Nothing tells a head what to specialise in; gradient descent decides.

Cost: $h \times 3 \times d_{model} \times d_{model}/h = 3d_{model}^2$, the same as one full-width head, plus $d_{model}^2$ for $W_O$. (The lecturer suggested they multiply; in the standard design they do not.)

African languages: heads specialise in whatever the training data rewards, which is mostly English syntax; for agglutinative, under-represented languages these heads do not match the structure (and tokenization is poor), so many contribute nothing, which links to the fairness concerns of Lecture 9.

rubric.point: How heads are formed and combined (subspaces, concat, W_O)
What they buy (different relations; no assigned roles)
Correct parameter comparison

questions.question: Describe how you would find out what a trained Transformer encoder knows about syntax. Cover looking at attention heads and probing, what each found in the lecture, and the limits of each. (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Attention heads (model-specific): visualise head weights and measure which heads attend in consistent patterns; find which heads matter by pruning. Lecture finding: the important heads are positional (neighbours), syntactic (verb → subject, object → verb, subject → verb) and rare-token heads; many others can be pruned. Limit: attention weights are not a full explanation of what the model uses, and only some heads are interpretable.

Probing (model-agnostic): freeze the representations at each layer, train a simple classifier to predict a property (e.g. part of speech, morphology, dependency labels) and compare accuracy across layers. Lecture finding (NMT): layer 0 is worst for morphology, layer 1 better than layer 2; a target language with weaker morphology gives a better encoder. Limit: high probe accuracy shows the information can be decoded, not that the model uses it; a powerful probe may learn the task itself.

A limit of probing

questions.question: Contrast ELMo representations with Word2Vec embeddings. Give four differences. (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
• Context: Word2Vec gives one static vector per word type; ELMo gives a contextual vector that depends on the whole sentence ('bank' differs by context).
• Input: Word2Vec looks up word vectors (no vector for unseen words); ELMo builds words from characters with a char-CNN + highway layers, so it is open-vocabulary.
• Model: Word2Vec is a shallow predictor of context words; ELMo uses deep forward and backward 2-layer LSTM language models.

Shallow model vs deep bidirectional LSTM language models

questions.question: What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do adapters and LoRA help to avoid it? (3 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Catastrophic forgetting: when all of a pre-trained model's weights are fine-tuned on a new task, the updates can overwrite the general knowledge learned during pre-training, so the model loses abilities it had.
Adapters and LoRA freeze the pre-trained weights and train only a small number of new parameters (adapters: small bottleneck layers inserted into each block; LoRA: a low-rank update BA added to the weights). The original knowledge stays intact, the per-task additions are small to store, and the frozen base can be shared across tasks.

rubric.point: Definition: fine-tuning overwrites/loses pre-trained knowledge
Pre-trained weights are frozen
Only small new parameters are trained (adapter bottlenecks / low-rank BA), so the base knowledge is preserved and shareable

questions.question: How would you modify GPT-2 for a task that takes in an MCQ question, the correct answer and four other options, and must choose the correct answer? Describe the input format, any new parameters, how each option is scored, the training loss, and inference. Mention at least two practical pitfalls. (10 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
GPT-2 is a decoder-only (causal) language model, so it cannot look at all five options bidirectionally in one encoder pass; follow the GPT multiple-choice recipe (slide 56): build one sequence per option.

Input: for each option $a_i$ ($i = 1..5$), the sequence "[start] Question: … [delim] Answer: $a_i$ [extract]". Add the delimiter/extract tokens to the vocabulary (new embeddings) and define a padding token with an attention mask for batching.

Scoring (two options):
(1) LM scoring, no new head: the score is the conditional log-likelihood of the answer tokens given the question, $\sum_t \log p(a_{i,t} \mid \text{question}, a_{i,<t})$, length-normalised (divide by the number of tokens) so long options are not penalised.
(2) Classification head (as in the figure): take the final hidden state at the [extract] token (the last position, the only one that has seen the whole sequence under the causal mask) and apply a new linear layer $w^\top h \to$ a scalar logit $s_i$.
Either way, apply a softmax across the five scores: $p(i) = e^{s_i} / \sum_j e^{s_j}$.

Training: cross-entropy over the five options with the index of the correct option as the label (multiclass, not BCE per option); fine-tune the whole model, or freeze it and train adapters or LoRA. Optionally add the LM loss as an auxiliary objective (as in GPT).

Inference: score all five options and pick the argmax; no generation is needed.

Pitfalls: the correct answer is a training label and must not be given as privileged input at test time; shuffle option order so the model cannot learn a position shortcut; total log-probabilities favour short options unless length-normalised; GPT-2 has no pad token by default; sequences must fit the context window.

rubric.point: Recognises GPT-2 is causal: one sequence per option (question + option) with delimiters
Uses the last-token state (or answer log-likelihood) to score each option
New parameters: linear head and/or special-token embeddings
Softmax across the five scores and cross-entropy with the correct index
Inference: argmax over options, no generation
Two practical pitfalls (leakage, position bias, length bias, padding)

questions.question:
You must build an extractive question-answering system: given a question and a passage, return the span of the passage that answers it.
(a) Explain why feeding static Word2Vec embeddings into a classifier would struggle here, using "bank" in "she sat on the bank" vs "the bank raised rates". How do ELMo and BERT fix this? (3)
(b) Describe in detail how you would fine-tune BERT for this task: input format, segment embeddings, new parameters, how start and end are predicted, the loss, and decoding at inference with a valid-span constraint. (5)
(c) Why is BERT a better starting point than GPT-2 for this task? (2) (10 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Word2Vec gives one vector per word type, so "bank" has the same vector in both sentences: the classifier cannot tell the senses apart, and it gets no transferred knowledge of how to combine words or relate the question to the passage. ELMo: a biLSTM LM produces representations of words in context (task-weighted sum of layers), so "bank" differs by sentence; the task model on top stays the same. BERT: a deep bidirectional Transformer encoder whose every token representation attends to the whole input, fine-tuned end to end.

(b) Input: "[CLS] question tokens [SEP] passage tokens [SEP]", with segment embedding A for the question and B for the passage, plus position embeddings. New parameters: a start vector $S$ and an end vector $E$ (each of size $d$). For each passage token $i$ with final hidden state $T_i$: $P_{\text{start}}(i) = \text{softmax}_i(S \cdot T_i)$ and $P_{\text{end}}(j) = \text{softmax}_j(E \cdot T_j)$. Loss: cross-entropy on the gold start plus cross-entropy on the gold end (averaged). Inference: score every span $(i, j)$ with $S \cdot T_i + E \cdot T_j$, keep only $i \le j$, both inside the passage, length at most some maximum, and return the best; if the passage is longer than the limit, use overlapping windows. (A no-answer option can use [CLS].)

(c) BERT is bidirectional: each passage token sees the question and the text on both sides, which is what span prediction needs, and SQuAD-style fine-tuning is exactly its design (slide 51). GPT-2's causal mask means a token cannot see what follows it, and it is designed for generation.

rubric.point: (a) Static vectors cannot separate senses
(a) ELMo and BERT give contextual representations
(b) Input format with [CLS]/[SEP] and segments
(b) Start and end vectors with softmax over tokens
(b) Loss: CE on start + CE on end
(b) Decoding with i ≤ j, max length, in-passage constraint
(c) Bidirectionality and design fit

questions.question: Describe how you would fine-tune BERT for (a) natural language inference (premise, hypothesis → entailment / contradiction / neutral) and (b) named entity recognition with BIO tags. For each give the input format, the output layer, the loss and how predictions are made. (c) Explain one problem that WordPiece subword tokenisation causes for NER and how you would handle it. (d) Explain how BERT's pre-training (MLM and NSP) helps each task. (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) NLI: "[CLS] premise [SEP] hypothesis [SEP]" with segment A/B. Output: a linear layer + softmax on the final [CLS] vector, 3 classes. Loss: cross-entropy with the gold label. Predict the argmax class.

(b) NER: "[CLS] sentence [SEP]" (single segment). Output: a linear layer + softmax applied to every token's final vector (K tags: B-PER, I-PER, …, O). Loss: token-level cross-entropy averaged over tokens. Predict the argmax tag per token (optionally enforce valid BIO sequences, e.g. I- cannot follow O).

(c) A word like "Ngubane" may split into several WordPieces, so labels and words do not line up: label only the first subword of each word (ignore the rest in the loss) and read the prediction from the first subword; or give all pieces the word's tag.

(d) NSP trains [CLS] to relate two sentences, which is what NLI needs (and why the pair format is natural). MLM trains every token's output to encode its identity from both-side context, which is what token-level tagging needs. Both start from bidirectional contextual representations instead of from scratch.

rubric.point: (a) NLI input, [CLS] head, 3-way CE, prediction
(b) NER per-token head, CE over tokens, prediction
(c) Subword/label alignment problem and a fix
(d) How MLM and NSP help

questions.concept: Using ELMo in a task model
questions.question: Compare three ways of transferring knowledge into a sentiment classifier: (1) frozen Word2Vec embeddings, (2) ELMo features, (3) fine-tuning BERT. For each, explain what is transferred, what is trained for the task, and one weakness. Then explain why ELMo is open-vocabulary while Word2Vec is not. (8 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(1) Word2Vec: transfers one static vector per word type learned from co-occurrence; the whole task model (e.g. CNN/RNN) is trained from scratch on top. Weakness: no context (polysemy: "bank"), unknown words get UNK, nothing about how to process a sentence is transferred.

(2) ELMo: transfers representations of words in context from a pretrained biLSTM LM (char-CNN + highway → 2-layer forward and backward LSTM-LMs), combined with task-specific weights $\gamma \sum_j \lambda_j h_j$; the task model on top is (almost) the same and is trained, ELMo usually frozen. Weakness: still needs a task-specific architecture; LSTMs are sequential and slower; left and right LMs are trained separately (shallow bidirectionality).

(3) BERT: transfers the whole deep bidirectional Transformer encoder (MLM + NSP pre-training); for the task only a small head on [CLS] is added and everything is fine-tuned. Weakness: expensive to fine-tune and store a full copy per task (motivating adapters/LoRA); catastrophic forgetting; [MASK] mismatch between pre-training and fine-tuning.

Open vocabulary: ELMo builds each word's vector from its characters with a CNN, so any string (unseen words, typos, rich morphology) gets a representation and similar spellings get similar vectors; Word2Vec only has vectors for words in its fixed vocabulary.

rubric.point: Word2Vec: what transfers, trained part, weakness
ELMo: what transfers (contextual, layer weighting), trained part, weakness
BERT: whole encoder fine-tuned with a small head, weakness
Open vocabulary via character CNN

questions.question:
A team wants to fine-tune a pretrained model for news summarisation.
(a) Explain why BERT on its own is a poor fit and which kinds of model are suitable. (2)
(b) Describe how to fine-tune GPT-2 for summarisation: the input format, which tokens the loss is computed on, and how you would decode at inference (discuss greedy, beam search and sampling, as covered in Lectures 5–6). (4)
(c) The team has one GPU. Explain how LoRA would make fine-tuning feasible and what is stored per task. (2) (8 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Summarisation is generation: the output is a new sequence. BERT is an encoder trained with MLM; it gives contextual representations but has no left-to-right generation mechanism. Suitable: an encoder–decoder (seq2seq) Transformer, where the decoder cross-attends to the article, or a decoder-only LM such as GPT-2 conditioned on the article.

(b) Input: "article [SEP/TL;DR:] summary <eos>" as one sequence. Training: teacher forcing with the causal LM cross-entropy, computed only on the summary tokens (mask the article positions out of the loss); the model learns $P(\text{summary} \mid \text{article})$, a conditional LM. Truncate long articles to fit the context window. Inference: feed the article and separator and generate token by token. Greedy is short and repetitive; beam search (e.g. $k = 4$) finds higher-probability, more faithful summaries for this constrained, short-output task, but costs memory; sampling with temperature/top-p gives more diversity but risks hallucination, so beam search or low-temperature decoding is the usual choice here.

(c) LoRA freezes $W_0$ and trains a low-rank update $BA$ on (some of) the projection matrices: far fewer trainable parameters and optimiser states, so it fits in memory; the update can be merged into the weights, so no extra latency. Per task only $A$ and $B$ (megabytes) are stored, not a new copy of the model.

rubric.point: (a) BERT cannot generate; seq2seq or decoder-only is suitable
(b) Input format and loss on summary tokens (conditional LM)
(b) Decoding choice justified (greedy vs beam vs sampling)
(c) LoRA: frozen W₀, low-rank BA, small storage per task

questions.question:
Compare adapters and LoRA as parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods.
(a) Describe how each modifies the network, with a diagram-level description. (3)
(b) For a 4096 × 4096 weight in fp16 with rank $r = 8$, compute the trainable parameters and the memory for full fine-tuning vs LoRA, and the LoRA fraction. (3)
(c) Give two advantages of LoRA over adapters and explain how LoRA achieves each. (2)
(d) Explain catastrophic forgetting and why both methods reduce it. (2) (10 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Adapters: small bottleneck modules inserted inside every Transformer layer (after attention and after the FFN): down-project $d \to m$, nonlinearity, up-project $m \to d$, plus a skip connection; the pretrained model is frozen and only adapters (and layer norms) are trained, about 1% of parameters. LoRA: no new layers; for chosen weight matrices the update is reparameterised as $W = W_0 + BA$ with $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$, running in parallel with $W_0$; $W_0$ is frozen.

(b) Full: 4096 × 4096 = 16,777,216 parameters, 33,554,432 bytes (32 MiB). LoRA: $r(d + k)$ = 65,536 parameters, 131,072 bytes (128 KiB). Fraction 0.39%.

(c) No inference latency: after training $BA$ can be added into $W_0$, so the network has exactly its original shape; adapters add sequential layers to every forward pass. Fewer parameters / smaller checkpoints: low rank (intrinsic rank hypothesis) means tiny $A$, $B$ per task (GPT-3: 1 TB → ~25 MB). Also: LoRA keeps the full sequence length (unlike prefix tuning) and the rank can be raised if it underperforms.

(d) Catastrophic forgetting: fine-tuning all weights on a narrow task overwrites knowledge from pre-training, so the model loses general abilities. Both methods freeze the pretrained weights and learn a small separate set of parameters, so the original knowledge is preserved (remove the adapter/LoRA to get the original model back) and the small capacity limits how far the model can drift.

rubric.point: (a) Adapter structure and placement
(a) LoRA reparameterisation
(b) Correct parameter counts
(b) Correct memory and fraction
(c) Two advantages with mechanism
(d) Forgetting explained and why both reduce it

questions.question: Trace the move from static to contextual embeddings: Word2Vec → ELMo → BERT. For each, state how a token's representation is computed and whether it depends on context, and comment on Word2Vec's place in modern transfer learning. Use one ambiguous word as an example throughout. (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Word2Vec: a lookup table learned by predicting context words from a centre word (skip-gram) or vice versa (CBOW), with negative sampling; one vector per word type, the same in every sentence: "bank" mixes the river and finance senses (the vector is a frequency-weighted blend). It transfers only word-level knowledge; the task model learns processing from scratch.

ELMo: characters → char-CNN + highway → 2-layer forward and backward LSTM LMs; the representation is a task-weighted sum of the layers, computed from the whole sentence, so "bank" near "river" differs from "bank" near "rates". Transfers how to process text, not just words.

BERT: WordPiece + segment + position embeddings → deep bidirectional Transformer encoder trained with MLM/NSP; every layer re-represents the token by attending to all others; fine-tuned end to end.

Word2Vec today: still a cheap, strong baseline/feature extractor and the conceptual root (distributional hypothesis, embedding layers = first layer of every model), but superseded where context matters; BERT's input embedding layer plays the role Word2Vec did, before context is added.

rubric.point: Word2Vec: static, training objective, ambiguity example
ELMo: contextual via biLSTM + char-CNN
BERT: deep bidirectional attention, fine-tuned
Comment on Word2Vec's role today

questions.question: Using Ruder's taxonomy, explain the difference between transductive and inductive transfer learning, and give an example of domain adaptation, cross-lingual learning, multi-task learning and sequential transfer learning. Which is the most popular today and why? (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Transductive: the task stays the same and labels exist for the source task; what changes is the domain or language. Domain adaptation: sentiment on product reviews → sentiment on tweets. Cross-lingual learning: English NER → isiZulu NER.

Inductive: the tasks differ and labels exist for the target task. Multi-task learning: train one model on NER and POS tagging at the same time with a shared encoder. Sequential transfer learning: pretrain a language model (e.g. BERT with MLM/NSP) on huge unlabelled text, then fine-tune on sentiment classification.

Sequential transfer is the most popular: pre-training needs no labels and uses huge, diverse text once; the same pretrained model can then be fine-tuned cheaply for many small labelled tasks.

Four correct examples
Most popular is sequential, with a reason

questions.question: Explain the "poverty of the stimulus" argument and the Universal Grammar view, then the alternative offered by iterated learning. Describe the iterated-learning procedure for neural networks and explain how it relates to expressivity, regularity and compositionality, and to model collapse (Lecture 9). (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Poverty of the stimulus (Chomsky): children learn language quickly from limited data, so the capacity for language may be innate; Universal Grammar: only a limited set of languages is learnable, and the brain is tuned to structures such as compositional generalisation.

Iterated learning (Kirby) flips this: language is tuned to our brains. Each generation learns from the previous one; the parts easiest to learn survive (the learning/communication bottleneck), refining the language over generations.

Neural procedure: train a network but stop early, relabel the data with its outputs (logits), train a new network on those labels, repeat for $k$ generations.

The bottleneck favours regularity (systematic, compressible structure); the need to communicate favours expressivity (many distinct meanings). Together they produce compositionality: reusable parts combined by rules. Model collapse is the dark side of the same loop: when models train on previous models' outputs without a pressure to stay expressive (and without real data), the distribution narrows, tails vanish and outputs degenerate.

rubric.point: Poverty of the stimulus and UG
Iterated learning idea and bottleneck
Neural procedure
Link to expressivity, regularity and compositionality
Link to model collapse

questions.question: Describe three ways Lecture 8 analyses what BERT has learned (model components, probing, looking at predictions), with one finding for each and one limitation of each. (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Model components (model-specific): look at self-attention heads. Finding: most heads follow a few typical patterns (attend to [CLS]/[SEP], to the previous/next token, broadly), and some encode semantic links. Limitation: attention weights are only part of the computation and many heads are redundant, so patterns don't prove use.

Probing (model-agnostic): train simple classifiers on frozen representations, with learned layer weights like ELMo's. Finding: BERT rediscovers the classical NLP pipeline: POS and syntax lower, then entities, semantic roles and coreference higher. Limitation: decodable ≠ used; probe capacity matters.

Looking at predictions: query the model with cloze facts ("Dante was born in [MASK]", LAMA). Finding: BERT recalls many relational facts without fine-tuning, so LMs can act as knowledge bases. Limitation: sensitive to phrasing, single-token answers, and it can be confidently wrong.

rubric.point: Heads: finding and limitation
Probing: finding and limitation
Predictions/LAMA: finding and limitation

questions.question: Explain the problems with traditional full fine-tuning listed in Lecture 8, the prior solutions and their drawbacks, and how LoRA and QLoRA address them. Explain the intrinsic rank hypothesis in your answer. (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Problems: time (training all parameters is slow), computational resources and memory (gradients and optimiser state for every parameter), and catastrophic forgetting (the model loses abilities from pre-training).

Prior solutions: adapter layers (few parameters, but extra layers add inference latency) and prefix tuning (learned prefix vectors; hard to optimise and eats into the sequence length).

LoRA: freeze $W_0$ and learn $\Delta W = BA$ of rank $r \ll d$. The intrinsic rank hypothesis says the important changes needed to adapt a model lie in a low-dimensional subspace, so a low-rank update captures them. Trainable parameters drop from $dk$ to $r(d + k)$ (10,000× fewer for GPT-3, 3× less GPU memory); no latency once merged; tiny checkpoints. QLoRA additionally quantises the frozen weights to lower precision (e.g. 32-bit → 8- or 4-bit), cutting memory further so large models fit on limited hardware.

rubric.point: Three problems of full fine-tuning
Prior solutions and their drawbacks
LoRA mechanism and intrinsic rank hypothesis
QLoRA adds quantisation
