It makes the sentence ungrammatical for a language model
questions.explanation: Extra context in a writer responsible language can lead a model, which learns from co-occurrence (the distributional hypothesis), to pick up false correlations such as gender ↔ occupation.

questions.question: True or False: Because modern NLP rests on the distributional hypothesis, context that is added to text without being needed can teach models implicit biases.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Words that share contexts get similar representations. If "nurse" keeps appearing with "she", that association is learned whether or not it is relevant (Lecture 9, linking back to the Tej example of Lecture 1).

questions.question: Which statements connect Lecture 9's linguistics points to NLP, as the slides do?
choices: Useful context is needed to impart meaning
Implicit bias can stem from the nature of some languages themselves
Removing all context from training data removes all bias
The distributional hypothesis is foundational to modern NLP
questions.explanation: The "Connections to NLP" slide: the need for useful context to impart meaning, and implicit bias stemming from the nature of some languages. Removing context would also remove meaning.

questions.question: Which points about multilingualism appear in Lecture 9?
choices: In some cultures it is rude to ask a person their name directly
People often have a home language and a separate professional language
English is typical of scientific papers, and many languages lack vocabulary for every domain
Every language has an equal amount of text on the internet
questions.explanation: All three are on the multilingualism slides. The Wikipedia table later in the lecture shows the opposite of (d).

questions.question: Lecture 9 asks: "Is it fair to translate Zulu books into English if it means there are less Zulu speakers but more awareness of Zulu culture?" Which tension does this question capture?
choices: Preserving cultural identity vs providing access to information
Coherence vs diversity in generated text
Writer responsible vs reader responsible grammar
Training cost vs inference cost
questions.explanation: The slide asks how we preserve cultural identity while also providing access to information, i.e. what happens when language, as a piece of culture, does not help convey that culture.

questions.question: What is "code-switching"?
choices: Switching between languages, often within one conversation or sentence
Rewriting a prompt so that it bypasses a model's safeguards
Converting text into sub-word tokens
Switching a model from training to inference mode
questions.explanation: Lecture 9: having to switch between languages can be tiring, and code-switching is a big problem for LLMs as well.

questions.question: True or False: Lecture 9 describes code-switching as a big problem for LLMs as well as being tiring for people.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Mixed-language text is rare in (mostly monolingual, English-heavy) training data, and the tokenizer and many heads are tuned to one language, so models handle it badly.

questions.question: A user writes a request that mixes isiZulu and English in one sentence. Which outcomes are plausible for an English-centric LLM, given Lecture 9?
choices: The isiZulu parts are split into many more tokens than the English parts
The model may answer only in English, nudging the user away from their home language
The model is guaranteed to perform better because it sees two languages at once
The model's quality for this user may be lower than for an English-only user
questions.explanation: Tokenization is poor for African languages (more tokens per word), code-switching is a known LLM problem, and unequal quality between subgroups is one of the "bias from the model" concerns. Nothing guarantees better performance.

questions.question: In the "stochastic parrots" paper (Bender et al., 2021), a language model is described as:
choices: A system for haphazardly stitching together sequences of linguistic forms it has observed, according to probabilistic information about how they combine, but without any reference to meaning
A model that memorises its training data exactly and repeats it word for word
A model trained with stochastic gradient descent on parrot speech
A grounded agent that shares context and intent with the listener
questions.explanation: This is the quotation on the slide. Fluency and coherence are consistent, but opinions or semantic content are sampled.

questions.question: True or False: According to Lecture 9, in a stochastic parrot the fluency and coherence of the text are consistent, while opinions or semantic content are sampled.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: That is the slide's summary of the problem. We don't even know how to measure "correct language".

questions.question: Why does Lecture 9 say LMs (as of the stochastic parrots paper) are "ungrounded"?
choices: Coherence in human language revolves around a shared context between speaker and listener with intent
LMs require the speaker to describe their own intent and context
LMs have no training data
LMs cannot produce fluent text
questions.explanation: Human coherence relies on shared context and intent. An LM has neither, so the user has to supply both. LMs are fluent and have plenty of data.

questions.question: Lecture 9 says LMs have come a long way since 2021. Which developments does it list as addressing the stochastic-parrot criticism?
choices: Incorporating multiple modalities can fix the grounding problem
Context windows are becoming bigger and persistent, allowing more detailed comprehension
Removing the softmax so that outputs are deterministic
Training only on English to avoid ambiguity
questions.explanation: The slides cite multi-modal grounding (video grounding) and bigger, persistent context windows (SelfExtend).

questions.question: True or False: Lecture 9 claims that notions of intent, agency and context in LMs are shifting as models gain more modalities and longer contexts.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The slide: "LMs have come a long way since 2021 and have shifting notions of intent, agency and context."

questions.question: Why do LMs "enforce a hegemonic view", according to Lecture 9?
choices: They need a lot of data, mostly from the internet, where the dominant voices are over-represented
They are trained only on government documents
Their tokenizers delete minority-language words
They are fine-tuned by a single annotator
questions.explanation: LMs require a lot of data, mainly from the internet, and the dominant voices there are over-represented. The hegemonic view is also context specific: common or important contexts may trigger a specific viewpoint.

questions.question: True or False: Lecture 9 argues that a bigger training set automatically makes a model more diverse.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The slide is titled "Size does not equal diversity": the chart shows English at about 49% of the data, far ahead of every other language.

questions.question: True or False: According to Lecture 9, all views can be represented in an LM, but common or important contexts may trigger one specific viewpoint.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The hegemonic viewpoint is context specific. The model can represent many views; which one it produces depends on the context.

questions.question: Which concerns about the widespread adoption of Gen AI tools does Lecture 9 list under "bias from the model"?
choices: Unequal quality between subgroups in society
Vulnerabilities in the tool which can cause harm
Language now serving a third role: as an interface to tools used across cultures
Models becoming too cheap to run
questions.explanation: These three are on the slides. Cost appears later, but as a concern about expense, not cheapness.

questions.question: Lecture 9 says language now serves a "third role". What is it?
choices: An interface to tools used across cultures
A way of storing knowledge in model weights
A replacement for programming languages
A training signal for image models
questions.explanation: Language describes culture, is a piece of culture, and is now also the interface to tools used across cultures.

questions.question: What is an adversarial trigger, as described in Lecture 9?
choices: A prompt that produces inappropriate behaviour indirectly through the context
A training example with a wrong label
A token that ends generation
A hardware fault that stops a model
questions.explanation: Adversarial examples or triggers are certain prompts which produce inappropriate behaviour indirectly through the context. Jailbreaking is the extreme case.

questions.question: True or False: Lecture 9 states that jailbreaking prompts can over-ride the manual safeguards placed on LLMs.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The slide: "Jailbreaking: These can over-ride manual safeguards!" (citing the "Do Anything Now" study).

questions.question: Which statements about adversarial triggers are consistent with Lecture 9 (and the L5 point about continuous representation spaces)?
choices: They work through the context of the prompt rather than by changing the model's weights
Universal triggers can be designed that work across many inputs
They can only be found by having access to the training data
Gaps in a model's continuous representation space are one reason such inputs exist
questions.explanation: The cited work finds "universal and context-independent triggers". In L5 the lecturer linked jailbreaks to gaps in the continuous space neural LMs interpolate over. Training data access is not required.

questions.question: On the tokenizer slide, "I love the cat" is 4 tokens and the isiZulu "Ngiyalithanda ikati" is 7 tokens. What is the main point?
choices: Tokenizers trained mostly on English split African-language text into more, less meaningful pieces
isiZulu sentences carry more meaning per token
English needs more tokens than isiZulu
Token counts do not affect cost or quality
questions.explanation: Tokenization "is a big problem for African languages": the same meaning costs more tokens, the pieces do not match morphemes, and the slide shows translation failing ("ikati" → "cat" works only with the right split).

questions.question: True or False: Lecture 9 argues that even if AI is used carefully, models remain limited for under-represented languages, and tokenization is a big problem for African languages in particular.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Both points are on the "Tokenization & Prompting" slides.

questions.question: Why is a BPE tokenizer learned mostly on English text a problem for an agglutinative language such as isiZulu? (Lectures 1, 4 and 10)
choices: Its merges reflect English character pairs, so isiZulu words break into many short pieces that ignore morpheme boundaries
More tokens per sentence means higher cost and less text fitting in the context window
Agglutinative words pack many morphemes (subject, tense, object, verb root…) into one word, so whitespace splitting is already hard
BPE cannot represent unseen words at all
questions.explanation: BPE falls back to characters, so it can represent any word ((d) is false), but badly: the merges were learned on English frequencies. L1's "Abashana bayazithengiselana" example shows how much one agglutinative word contains.

questions.question:
The slide shows "I love the cat" as 4 tokens / 14 characters and "Ngiyalithanda ikati" (the same meaning in isiZulu) as 7 tokens / 19 characters.
(a) How many times more tokens does the isiZulu sentence use?
(b) Characters per token for English.
(c) Characters per token for isiZulu.
(d) How many complete copies of each sentence fit in a 4096-token context window? Give the English number then the isiZulu number.
questions.solution:
(a) $7/4 = 1.75$: the same meaning costs 1.75× as many tokens (and so 1.75× the price on a per-token API).
(b) $14/4 = 3.5$ characters per token.
(c) $19/7 \approx 2.7143$ characters per token: shorter, less meaningful pieces.
(d) $\lfloor 4096/4 \rfloor = 1024$ and $\lfloor 4096/7 \rfloor = 585$. An isiZulu user gets about 43% less text into the same context, which also means less room for helpful context.
questions.explanation: This is the fairness-and-efficiency argument in numbers: more tokens for the same meaning means higher cost, slower generation and a smaller effective context window for speakers of under-represented languages.

questions.question: Lecture 9 names two problems with "prompting". Which are they?
choices: Prompting is not a universal skill and is an emerging technology which favours affluence
It leans into the speaker-responsible view, so not everyone will be equally comfortable depending on their background
Prompts cannot contain context
Prompting only works in English
questions.explanation: Problem 1: not a universal skill, favours affluence. Problem 2: it leans into the speaker (writer) responsible view, which is uncomfortable for people from reader-responsible backgrounds.

questions.question: According to Lecture 9, what does good prompting do?
choices: Makes sure the most useful context is provided to the model
Changes the model's weights for the task
Removes the need for a tokenizer
Guarantees the model is grounded
questions.explanation: "Prompting" is the skill of designing questions so that the most useful context is provided to the model. Weights are unchanged.

questions.question: True or False: In the chain-of-thought example on the slides, showing a worked reasoning step in the example answer leads the model to reason step by step and get the cafeteria apples question right (9) where standard prompting got it wrong (27).
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Wei et al. (2022): standard prompting gave "27"; chain-of-thought prompting gave 23 − 20 = 3, 3 + 6 = 9.

questions.question: What is the "dead internet theory"?
choices: The theory that the internet is slowly being dominated by AI-generated content
The theory that internet traffic is falling every year
The theory that old websites are deleted to train new models
The theory that LLMs cannot access the internet
questions.explanation: The slides add that this creates mistrust in information and hides authentic communication.

questions.question: Which consequences of AI-generated content does Lecture 9 list under the dead internet theory?
choices: Bias propagation: generated content is fed back into the training data of future models
It crowds out real content creators with interesting perspectives
It can lead to feelings of isolation among under-represented groups
It makes the internet more democratic
questions.explanation: It undermines efforts to democratise the internet and highlight broader perspectives, because AI is more efficient at content generation.

questions.question: What is model collapse?
choices: The degradation of models over generations when each generation is trained on data produced by the previous generation
A model crashing because it runs out of GPU memory
A model forgetting old tasks after fine-tuning on a new one
Attention weights becoming one-hot
questions.explanation: The diagram on the slides: Data⁰ → fit Model 0 → sample Data¹ → fit Model 1 → … Each model is trained on the previous model's samples, and the data drifts away from the real distribution. (Catastrophic forgetting, option c, is an L8 concept.)

questions.question: Which observations on the Lecture 9 slides are signs of model collapse?
choices: Generated MNIST digits become blurry and then all look alike by generation 20
OPT-125m outputs drift from architecture to lists of "jackrabbits" by generation 9
The perplexity of generated data narrows towards low values over generations
Face images keep their diversity no matter how much generated data is mixed in
questions.explanation: The face experiment shows the opposite of (d): with more "poisoned" (generated) data the faces degrade within a few iterations. In the perplexity histograms the distribution of generated data sharpens around low perplexity, i.e. the model reproduces its own most probable outputs and loses the tails.

questions.question: True or False: Keeping some of the original real data in each generation's training set reduces model collapse.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The Shumailov et al. figure compares "no data preserved" with "10% data preserved": with real data kept, the generations stay much closer to the original distribution.

questions.question: The final model-collapse slide plots log perplexity for several languages (English, Danish, French, Polish, Indonesian, Albanian, Swedish). The distributions are clearly shifted from one another. What concern does this raise?
choices: Models already score different languages very differently, so collapse and generated-data effects will not hit all languages equally
All languages have the same perplexity, so collapse is language-independent
Perplexity cannot be measured for non-English languages
Lower-resource languages are immune to collapse
questions.explanation: Under-represented languages start from a worse position (more surprise per token) and have less real data to anchor them, so the double edge of resource use applies to model collapse too. Devon said it outright in the L9 recording: "lower resource languages collapse faster than English and French" (Swedish and Danish fragment, while English and French shift left more slowly). Model collapse is a mechanism for injustice.

questions.question:
Strubell et al.'s table on the slides estimates CO₂e (lbs): training a big Transformer 192; the same with neural architecture search 626,155; a car over its lifetime (incl. fuel) 126,000; one passenger flying NY↔SF 1,984; an average human life for one year 11,023.
(a) How many car lifetimes is the architecture-search run?
(b) How many NY↔SF passenger flights is it?
(c) How many times more than the plain big-Transformer training run is it?
questions.solution:
(a) $626155/126000 \approx 4.97$ car lifetimes.
(b) $626155/1984 \approx 315.6$ flights.
(c) $626155/192 \approx 3261$: the tuning and search around a model can cost thousands of times more than one training run.
questions.explanation: Lecture 9's point: consider the bias and harm from training models, not only from using them. Training is extremely expensive, with impacts on the economy and environment.

questions.question: Which statements about resource use are made in Lecture 9?
choices: Training LLMs is extremely expensive and has impacts on the economy and the environment
LLM power usage tends to scale with parameter count, now in the billions
Training a model can cause large power transients on electricity grids
Inference is free once a model has been trained
questions.explanation: The GPU power trace (Li et al., "LLM-induced transients") shows training power swinging sharply. Using the model also costs energy.

questions.question: Lecture 9 says lower-resource communities feel the impact of high-resource models "twice" (and more). Which points are on that slide?
choices: Through exclusion and inability to compete
The effects of climate change tend to hit the world's most marginalised first and they bounce back slower
The technology will scale more poorly for these communities
They pay lower prices for the same API calls
questions.explanation: The three numbered points on the slide. Point 3 links back to tokenization: the same request costs more tokens.

questions.question: Which are listed in Lecture 9 as forms of exploitation in data collection involving marginalised communities?
choices: Institutions use the data for research without inclusion beyond the collection (asymmetric power balance)
Communities cannot control the use of their data (lack of trust, conflicts of interest)
Data is taken out of context or misinterpreted
The data will be eroded more quickly by generative AI
questions.explanation: All four are on the slide. The last links to model collapse and the dead internet.

questions.question:
The participation slide lists Wikipedia articles and speakers: English 6,087,118 articles / 1,268,100,000 speakers; Zulu 2,219 / 27,800,000; Yoruba 32,572 / 39,800,000.
(a) Articles per million speakers for English.
(b) Articles per million speakers for Zulu.
(c) How many times more articles per speaker does English have than Zulu?
questions.explanation: Even after accounting for the number of speakers, Zulu has roughly 60 times less Wikipedia text per speaker than English. Web-scraped training data inherits this imbalance, which is why the slides call for participatory data creation.

questions.question: Which are listed in Lecture 9 as pros of data curation?
choices: Removes social biases
Preserves privacy through anonymisation
Removes potentially exploitable patterns and balances the data
The curator cannot introduce any bias
questions.explanation: The curator plays a role and can be biased: that is one of the cons.

questions.question: Which are listed in Lecture 9 as cons of data curation?
choices: The curator plays a role and can be biased
It throws away data, which can be expensive
There is no clear best approach
It is a step away from studying the world "organically"
questions.explanation: All four cons are on the slide (Rogers, "Changing the world by changing the data").

questions.question: Lecture 9 defines data curation as:
choices: The organisation, selection and integration of data collected from various sources
Generating extra training data with an LLM
Translating a dataset into every target language
Deleting all rare words from a corpus
questions.explanation: The slide's definition. Generating data with an LLM is closer to what causes model collapse.

questions.question: True or False: Lecture 9 argues that all aspects of the development pipeline (e.g. for machine translation) must be diverse and inclusive.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: The "increase participation" slide (Nekoto et al., participatory research for low-resourced MT in African languages).

questions.question: Which of these is one of Lecture 9's conclusions?
choices: Even if the skills gap is addressed, data quality and quantity issues are likely to create lingering inequality
Bigger models will remove inequality between languages on their own
Prompting is a universal skill that everyone has equal access to
AI should be treated as a neutral tool that does not shape culture
questions.explanation: The conclusions: AI is an entity shaping culture in its own right; disproportionate access to skills and tools is a risk for low-resource communities; and data issues are likely to create lingering inequality.

questions.question: Match each term from the iterated-learning discussion to its meaning.

pairs.answer: The language can convey many distinct meanings
The language follows systematic, consistent patterns, so it is easy to learn
The meaning of the whole is built from the meanings of reusable parts
Each generation learns from limited data, so easy-to-learn structure survives

options: The language can convey many distinct meanings
The language follows systematic, consistent patterns, so it is easy to learn
The meaning of the whole is built from the meanings of reusable parts
Each generation learns from limited data, so easy-to-learn structure survives
The model forgets previous tasks after fine-tuning
questions.explanation: Pressure to communicate pushes towards expressivity; the learning bottleneck pushes towards regularity. A language under both pressures becomes compositional. (Tutorial 7.3; Kirby's iterated learning in Lecture 8.)

questions.question: True or False: In iterated learning, each generation learns the language from the one before, and the parts that are easiest to learn are remembered and come to dominate.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Lecture 8 (iterated learning, Kirby): the "communication bottleneck" refines the language. The ML version trains a network, stops early, relabels the data with its outputs and trains a new network on them, for k generations.

questions.question: What is the "poverty of the stimulus" argument (Chomsky) that iterated learning offers an alternative to?
choices: Children learn language quickly from relatively little data, so the capacity for language may be built into the brain
Languages with fewer speakers have simpler grammar
Models need less data than children to learn language
Language cannot be learned from examples at all
questions.explanation: Chomsky's conclusion is a Universal Grammar. Iterated learning flips it: maybe language is well tuned to our brains, because it was shaped by generations of learners.

questions.question:
A clinic in KwaZulu-Natal wants an LLM chatbot that answers patients in isiZulu. The team plans to (1) fine-tune an English-centric LLM that keeps its original BPE tokenizer, (2) machine-translate an English medical-chat dataset into isiZulu for training, and (3) deploy it with a short English system prompt.
(a) Using the slide example ("I love the cat" = 4 tokens, "Ngiyalithanda ikati" = 7 tokens), explain two concrete costs of step (1) for isiZulu users. (3)
(b) Patients often code-switch between isiZulu and English. Explain why this is hard for the model and one bias it could induce. (3)
(c) Give one risk of step (2) in terms of responsible language use, and one data-curation step you would add, with a con of that step. (3)
(d) Explain why relying on users to write good prompts is not a neutral design choice. (2) (11 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The same meaning takes 7/4 = 1.75× as many tokens. Costs: (i) higher price and slower generation per message for isiZulu speakers (per-token billing and decoding time); (ii) less text fits in the context window, so less conversation history and supporting context. Also, the pieces ignore morpheme boundaries (agglutinative words such as "Ngi-ya-li-thanda" are cut into frequency-based English-like fragments), so the representations are poorer and quality is lower: unequal quality between subgroups.

(b) Mixed-language text is rare in training data, the tokenizer and many attention heads are tuned to English, and the two languages are encoded very differently, so the model handles switches poorly. Bias: the model may drift into English or answer better in English, nudging users away from their home language and giving lower-quality help to people who code-switch (often the most multilingual and marginalised users).

(c) Risk: translated English text carries English (writer-responsible) conventions and cultural assumptions (e.g. how directly to ask a name or discuss illness), and translation errors, so the model learns translationese rather than how isiZulu speakers actually communicate; it also adds the English hegemonic view. Curation step: have native-speaker clinicians review and filter samples, remove unsafe or culturally inappropriate dialogues, balance topics and anonymise patient data. Con: the curator can be biased, it throws data away and is expensive, and there is no clear best approach.

(d) Prompting is not a universal skill and favours the affluent; it leans into the speaker (writer) responsible view, so users from reader-responsible backgrounds, or with less experience of these tools, get worse answers. The system should supply useful context itself (e.g. a good isiZulu system prompt, examples) instead of shifting the burden to patients.

rubric.point: (a) Quantifies the 1.75× token cost
(a) Names two concrete costs (price/latency, context window, poorer morpheme-blind representations)
(b) Explains why code-switching is hard (rare in data, English-tuned tokenizer/heads)
(b) Names a resulting bias (drift to English, lower quality for code-switchers)
(c) Risk of machine-translated data (cultural conventions, errors, hegemonic view)
(c) A sensible curation step
(c) A con of curation (curator bias, cost, discarding data)
(d) Prompting is not universal / favours affluence
(d) Leans into the writer-responsible view, disadvantaging some users

questions.explanation: Calibrated to the written section: a scenario that mixes calculation with explanation and pulls in L1 (agglutinative tokenization) and L4 (BPE).

questions.question:
A company trains a new language model every year on a fresh web crawl. More and more of the web is now generated by earlier models.
(a) Describe the model-collapse loop shown in Lecture 9 and explain why the tails of the distribution disappear first. (4)
(b) Describe one way model collapse can be identified and why it corresponds to collapse. (2)
(c) Link this to the dead internet theory and say why the harm is not evenly spread across communities. (2)
(d) Propose one mitigation and say what it costs. (2) (10 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Real data Data⁰ is used to fit Model 0; samples from Model 0 become (part of) Data¹, which trains Model 1, and so on, so Dataⁿ drifts from Data⁰. Each step loses information through finite sampling (rare events may simply not be sampled) and approximate fitting (the model smooths and over-weights what it has seen). Probable events are over-estimated and improbable events under-estimated, so each generation is more concentrated than the last: the tails shrink and eventually vanish, and errors compound ("probable events poison reality").

(b) Evaluate each generation's outputs with a model trained on real data (or look at the outputs): in the slides the perplexity histogram of generated text narrows towards low values over generations, and the OPT-125m outputs degrade into repetitive nonsense ("jackrabbits"). Lower perplexity on its own outputs with less spread means the model is reproducing its own most likely text and has lost the diversity of real data: that loss of the tails is collapse. (Other valid signs: falling diversity, MNIST digits converging to one blurry shape.)

(c) The dead internet theory says the web is increasingly AI-generated, so web crawls feed generated data back in (bias propagation). Under-represented languages and groups have little real data to anchor them (e.g. ~80 Zulu Wikipedia articles per million speakers vs ~4,800 for English), so their real data is eroded fastest, their content creators are crowded out, and the hegemonic view is amplified.

(d) Preserve a share of verified real (human) data in every generation (the slides' 10% preserved setting keeps the model much closer to the original), or detect and filter generated content, or curate. Cost: real data is expensive to collect and verify, filtering throws data away, curation can introduce curator bias, and detectors are imperfect.

rubric.point: (a) Describes the loop: fit → sample → train the next model on samples
(a) Explains tails vanishing (finite sampling / approximation; probable over-, improbable under-estimated)
(b) A valid identification method (perplexity distribution, diversity, degraded outputs)
(b) Explains why it indicates collapse (concentration, lost tails)
(c) Links generated web content to future training data (dead internet / bias propagation)
(c) Explains uneven harm for low-resource languages or groups
(d) A mitigation (keep real data, filter, curate)
(d) Its cost or downside

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the term "stochastic parrots" in relation to neural language models. Then discuss how (i) grounding through other modalities and longer contexts and (ii) the hegemonic make-up of web training data relate to this criticism. Use what you know about how an LM is trained (Lecture 5) in your answer. (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Stochastic parrots (Bender et al., 2021): an LM "haphazardly stitches together sequences of linguistic forms it has observed in its vast training data, according to probabilistic information about how they combine, but without any reference to meaning". Fluency and coherence are consistent, but opinions or semantic content are sampled.

Why this follows from training: an LM is trained with cross-entropy to predict the next token from the previous ones. It only ever sees text (form), never the world or the speaker's intent, so it learns which forms co-occur (the distributional hypothesis) rather than grounded meaning. Human coherence relies on a shared context between speaker and listener with intent; the LM has neither, so the user must describe their intent and context.

(i) Grounding: adding modalities (images, video) ties words to perception, and bigger, persistent context windows let the model use more of the speaker's context, so notions of intent and context are shifting since 2021. This weakens, but does not remove, the criticism: the model still optimises likelihood of forms.

(ii) Hegemony: LMs need huge data, mainly from the internet, where dominant voices are over-represented (≈49% English on the slide; "size does not equal diversity"). A parrot repeats what it heard most, so common contexts trigger the dominant viewpoint and minority views and languages are under-served.

rubric.point: Defines stochastic parrots (stitching forms by probability, no reference to meaning)
Links to next-token training on form only / no shared context or intent (ungrounded)
(i) Explains how modalities and longer contexts address grounding, and the limit of this
(ii) Explains the hegemonic view: web data over-represents dominant voices; size ≠ diversity

questions.question:
Lecture 9 contrasts "They want to be a nurse when they grow up" with "He wants to be a nurse when he grows up".
(a) Explain how the second sentence can lead a model to learn an implicit bias, referring to the distributional hypothesis. (2)
(b) Word2Vec is trained on a large English corpus. Explain why you might find that the vector for "nurse" is closer to "she" than to "he", and how this would show up in an analogy test. (2)
(c) Explain why this kind of bias is linked to writer-responsible languages in particular. (2) (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The distributional hypothesis says words that share contexts get similar meanings/representations. The second sentence adds the gender as implicit context where it is not necessary. Across a corpus, "nurse" co-occurs with gendered words, so the model learns a correlation between gender and occupation that is not part of the meaning of "nurse": a false correlation.

(b) Word2Vec learns vectors by predicting context words in a sliding window. If "nurse" appears near "she/her" more often than "he/him", the training updates pull v(nurse) towards the context vectors of female words, so cosine similarity to "she" is higher. In an analogy test, v(doctor) − v(man) + v(woman) may land nearest "nurse": the linear structure that gives king − man + woman ≈ queen also encodes social stereotypes.

(c) In writer-responsible languages the writer supplies the context with the message (more explicit context per sentence). English, for instance, forces gendered pronouns, so gender is stated even when irrelevant. That extra, unnecessary context is exactly what a co-occurrence-based model learns from.

rubric.point: (a) Distributional hypothesis + unnecessary gender context → false correlation
(b) Explains the training mechanism pulling vectors together
(b) Shows it in an analogy test
(c) Writer-responsible languages state more context explicitly (e.g. gendered pronouns)

questions.question: A large lab argues that its new multilingual LLM "benefits everyone equally". Using Lecture 9, critique this claim. Cover resource use, the "double edge" for lower-resource communities, exploitation in data collection, and what can be done. (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Resource use: training is extremely expensive (power scales with billions of parameters; architecture search ≈ 626k lbs CO₂e, about 5 car lifetimes), which has economic and environmental impacts.

Double edge: lower-resource communities (1) are excluded and cannot compete, (2) feel climate-change effects first and recover slower, and (3) get technology that scales poorly for them (more tokens per word, lower quality, higher cost).

Data collection: institutions may use community data for research without inclusion beyond collection (asymmetric power), communities can't control how their data is used (lack of trust, conflicts of interest), data is taken out of context or misinterpreted, and generative AI erodes their data faster.

What can be done: careful curation (removes biases, anonymises, balances, but the curator can be biased and it is expensive), increased participation so every part of the pipeline is diverse and inclusive (participatory MT research), and gathering perspectives from low- and middle-income countries whose notion of impact goes beyond short-term technical concerns. So the benefits are not equal unless these are addressed.

rubric.point: Resource use and its environmental/economic cost
At least two "double edge" points
At least two exploitation risks in data collection
Concrete remedies (participation, curation, broader perspectives)

questions.question: Explain what adversarial triggers and jailbreaking prompts are, why manual safeguards can fail against them, and why this is a responsibility issue rather than only a security issue. Relate your answer to how prompting provides context to a model. (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Adversarial triggers are inputs (prompts) that cause inappropriate behaviour indirectly through the context, rather than by asking directly; universal triggers work across many inputs and contexts. Jailbreaking prompts (e.g. "Do Anything Now" role-play) wrap a harmful request in context that over-rides the manual safeguards.

Why safeguards fail: safety behaviour is learned from a limited set of examples, while the model responds to the whole context; a neural LM interpolates in a continuous space, and inputs far from the safety training data (gaps in that space) fall outside what was taught. Because prompting works by supplying context, the same mechanism that lets a good prompt help also lets a crafted prompt steer the model.

Responsibility: vulnerabilities in a widely used tool can cause harm to people who never wrote the prompt, and the burden of safe use falls unequally; language is now an interface to tools used across cultures, so these failures have social impact, not just technical impact.

rubric.point: Defines adversarial triggers (indirect, through context) and jailbreaking (over-rides safeguards)
Explains why safeguards fail (context-driven behaviour, gaps beyond safety training)
Explains why this is a responsibility issue (harm, tool used across cultures)

questions.question: Lecture 9 says language both describes culture and is a piece of culture. Explain this distinction, and use it to discuss the question "Is it fair to translate Zulu books into English if it means there are less Zulu speakers but more awareness of Zulu culture?" Refer to multilingualism (home vs professional language). (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Communication directs others' attention and thoughts, so it carries responsibility. What is conveyed describes culture (the information); how it is conveyed appropriately is itself a piece of culture (norms such as not asking a name directly, how much context to give).

Translating Zulu books into English makes the information about Zulu culture accessible to more people (describing culture), but the English version loses the piece of culture that lives in the language itself: its conventions, idioms and reader/writer responsibility. If English becomes the default for reading, and people already use English as their professional language (science, many domains lack vocabulary), fewer people use Zulu, which erodes the culture being described. A fair approach preserves cultural identity while giving access: translate both ways, build tools and vocabulary in Zulu, and involve speakers.

rubric.point: Explains describes-culture vs is-a-piece-of-culture
Applies it to the translation dilemma (access vs loss of identity)
Uses home vs professional language / domain vocabulary

questions.question: Describe the difference between reader-responsible and writer-responsible languages. Then explain why prompting an LLM "leans into the speaker-responsible view", and who this disadvantages. (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Writer responsible (e.g. English): the person conveying the message must make it understandable; the context needed is presented with the message, so less situational awareness is needed. Reader responsible (e.g. Mandarin): the receiver must make sense of it; context can be omitted for brevity and lots of situational awareness is needed. (A coarse grouping, open to stereotypes.)

An LLM is ungrounded and shares no situation with the user, so it only knows what is written: the user must spell out intent and context in the prompt. That is the writer/speaker-responsible style. People from reader-responsible linguistic backgrounds, or who are less practised with these tools, will be less comfortable doing this and get worse answers, and prompting as a skill already favours the affluent.

rubric.point: Defines writer responsible with an example
Defines reader responsible with an example
Explains why prompting is speaker-responsible (no shared context, must state intent)
Names who is disadvantaged

questions.question: What is the value-lock problem in Lecture 9?

A security lock that stops jailbreaks

In-context learning, retrieval and diffusion LMs

questions.question: What does a language model's training loss measure, in Lecture 10's words?
choices: How surprised the model is by the true next token: the average of $-\log p(\text{true next token})$
The number of grammar rules the model has learned
The fraction of tokens the model copies from its context
The distance between the input and output embeddings
questions.explanation: Slide 4: a high probability for the true token means low surprise. Grammar, facts and some reasoning emerge because they all help predict the next token.

questions.question: Which statements about neural scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020) are true?
choices: Language-model loss improves smoothly and predictably as compute, data and parameters grow
Each factor has a power-law relationship with the loss when not bottlenecked by the others
On log–log axes the loss curve is close to a straight line, so cheap small runs can forecast a much larger run
Scaling up the parameters removes the need for more data
questions.explanation: Slide 5: loss falls as a power law ($\mathcal{L} \propto N^{-0.076}$ for size), which is a straight line on log–log axes. The three must grow in proportion: scaling only one makes another the bottleneck.

questions.question: With $\mathcal{L} \propto N^{-0.076}$ (and data and compute not the bottleneck), by what factor is the loss multiplied when the number of parameters $N$ (a) doubles, (b) grows 10×?
questions.solution: (a) $2^{-0.076} = 0.9487$: about 5% lower loss per doubling. (b) $10^{-0.076} = 0.8395$: about 16% lower.
questions.explanation: Each doubling gives the same small fractional improvement, which is why the curve is a straight line on log–log axes (slide 5).

questions.question:
Use the Chinchilla rule of about 20 training tokens per parameter and $C \approx 6ND$.
(a) How many tokens (in trillions) should a 70B-parameter model see?
(b) Its training compute in units of $10^{23}$ FLOPs.
(c) Gopher (280B parameters, 300B tokens): its compute in units of $10^{23}$ FLOPs.
questions.solution: (a) $20 \times 70\text{B} = 1.4\text{T}$ tokens. (b) $6 \times 7\times10^{10} \times 1.4\times10^{12} = 5.88\times10^{23}$. (c) $6 \times 2.8\times10^{11} \times 3\times10^{11} = 5.04\times10^{23}$.
questions.explanation: Roughly the same compute, but Chinchilla (4× smaller, ~5× more data) performed better (slide 7): grow the model and the data together.

choices: True
False
questions.question: True or False: The scaling-law line means you can keep increasing the number of parameters alone and the loss will keep falling along the same straight line.
questions.explanation: False. The line traces the compute-optimal points with data and compute kept in proportion; scale parameters alone and data or compute becomes the bottleneck (slides 5–6).

questions.question: Explain neural scaling laws and the Chinchilla result. Why do modern models such as Llama 3 train far beyond the Chinchilla optimum? (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Loss falls predictably as a power law in model size $N$, data $D$ and compute $C \approx 6ND$ (Kaplan et al.), a straight line on log–log axes, so small runs forecast big ones; the three must grow in proportion or one becomes the bottleneck.

Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al.): at fixed compute a model can be too big (undertrained, reads too little) or too small (underpowered); the optimum is about 20 tokens per parameter. Chinchilla (70B, 1.4T tokens) beat Gopher (280B, 300B tokens) at about the same compute.

Beyond the optimum: training is paid once but inference on every request, so a smaller model trained longer (Llama 3 8B: ~1,900 tokens/param) is cheaper to deploy and leaves room for test-time compute.

rubric.point: Power law in N, D and C; straight line on log–log axes / predictable
Must scale in proportion, otherwise one resource bottlenecks
Fixed compute: too big = undertrained, too small = underpowered; one optimum
~20 tokens per parameter; Chinchilla beats Gopher at equal compute
Over-training small models: training paid once, inference every request; test-time compute

questions.explanation: Lecture 10 Part 1 (slides 4–8).

questions.question: With a fixed compute budget, what goes wrong if the model is too large?
choices: It is undertrained: it can't read enough tokens in the budget
It is underpowered: it lacks the capacity to learn the data
It overfits because it sees every token many times
Nothing: bigger is always better at fixed compute
questions.explanation: Slide 6 (Hoffmann et al., 2022): too big means it reads too little (undertrained); too small means underpowered. Each budget has one compute-optimal size.

questions.question: Llama 3 8B was trained on roughly 1,900 tokens per parameter, far past the Chinchilla optimum. Which reasons does Lecture 10 give for training a small model this long?
choices: Training is paid once, but inference is paid on every request, so a smaller model is cheaper to deploy
A cheaper forward pass leaves room for test-time compute (letting the model 'think' longer)
Chinchilla's rule says more tokens per parameter always lowers loss for free
Small models can't be undertrained
questions.explanation: Slide 7: going beyond compute-optimal costs extra training compute, but makes serving cheaper, and the saved inference cost can be spent on test-time compute.

questions.question: In Lecture 10's hospital analogy, a dense model is like:
choices: Showing every patient to every doctor: every token passes through every parameter
Sending each patient to the right specialist
A hospital with one doctor
Turning patients away when the hospital is full
questions.explanation: Slide 9: dense models use every weight for every token, so 2× size ≈ 2× work per token. MoE is conditional computation: send the token to the relevant specialists.

questions.question: Explain how a mixture-of-experts layer works, why it is more efficient than a dense model, and the problem of expert collapse with one way to fix it. (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
A dense model runs every parameter for every token, so cost grows with size. MoE replaces one big feed-forward block with many small experts; a small router scores them, picks the top $k$ per token and combines their outputs with the router weights (conditional computation).

Capacity and memory follow the total parameters, but compute per token follows only the active ones (Mixtral: 47B total, 13B active; DeepSeek-V3: 671B / 37B).

Expert collapse: experts that start slightly better are chosen more, train more and get better, so the rest go unused. Fix: load balancing, e.g. an auxiliary loss (Switch) or DeepSeek-V3's per-expert router bias, raised for under-used and lowered for over-used experts, which changes selection but not the mixing weights.

rubric.point: Router picks top-k small expert FFNs; output = router-weighted sum
Dense uses every weight per token; MoE = conditional computation
Total vs active parameters (capacity/memory vs compute), with an example
Expert collapse as a rich-get-richer loop
A load-balancing fix (bias on router scores or auxiliary loss)

questions.explanation: Lecture 10 Part 2 (slides 9–14).

questions.question: A router picks experts E2 and E6 for a token, with router weights 0.7 and 0.3. Their outputs are $E_2 = (1, 2)$ and $E_6 = (3, -1)$. What is the MoE layer's output? Give (a) the first and (b) the second component.
questions.explanation: The output is the router-weighted sum of the chosen experts only; the other six experts don't run (slide 10).

questions.question: In a mixture-of-experts layer:
choices: A small router scores the experts and picks the top $k$ for each token, so only part of the parameters is used per token
Every expert processes every token and the outputs are averaged
Experts are separate models trained on different languages
The gate is fixed by hand
questions.explanation: Slide 10: one big feed-forward network is replaced by many small experts; the router picks the top $k$ (two of eight in the diagram, weights 0.7 and 0.3) and their outputs are combined with the router weights.

questions.question: What fraction of its parameters is active for one token in (a) Mixtral 8×7B (47B total, 13B active) and (b) DeepSeek-V3 (671B total, 37B active)?
questions.explanation: Memory follows the total; compute per token follows the active parameters. 8×7B isn't 56B because the experts share attention and the other common weights (slide 11).

choices: True
False
questions.question: True or False: Mixtral "8×7B" has 56B parameters, all of which are used for every token.
questions.explanation: False on both counts: it has about 47B (experts share attention and other common weights), and only about 13B are active per token (2 of 8 experts).

questions.question: An MoE layer has 64 experts, each with 4.2M parameters, and the gate selects the top 2 experts per token. (a) What fraction of the expert parameters is used for one token? (b) How many expert parameters are stored? (c) How many are used per token?
questions.explanation: Capacity and memory follow the total (stored) parameters; the compute per token follows the active ones (slide 11). This is how MoE separates capacity from cost.

questions.question: What is expert collapse in a mixture-of-experts model?
choices: A rich-get-richer loop: experts that start slightly better get picked more, train more and get even better, so the rest go unused
The model's own generated data floods its training set
All experts learn identical weights because they share a router
The router stops working after training
questions.explanation: Slide 12. Don't confuse it with model collapse (Lecture 9), which comes from training on synthetic data.

questions.question: How does DeepSeek-V3's routing-bias load balancing work? Select all that apply.
choices: Each expert has a small bias added to its router score
An under-used expert's bias goes up and an over-used expert's bias goes down
The bias changes which experts are selected, not the weights used to combine their outputs
It adds an auxiliary load-balancing loss to the main training loss
It removes the router entirely
questions.explanation: Slide 13: the bias only affects selection, so it balances usage without an extra loss term (the Switch Transformer used an auxiliary penalty instead).

questions.question: What do mixture-of-experts experts usually specialise in?
choices: Token types such as punctuation, numbers, code or syntax
Broad topics such as biology or history
Different human languages, one per expert
Different layers of the network
questions.explanation: Slide 14: specialisation is by token type, not topic, and many small experts specialise more sharply. Dense models are also naturally sparse: most neurons are near-silent for any one token.

choices: True
False
questions.question: True or False: In in-context learning, the model's weights are updated from the examples in the prompt.
questions.explanation: False. No weights change: the worked examples constrain the continuation so much that following the pattern is the only coherent thing to do (slide 16). It's prompting, not fine-tuning.

questions.question: Explain in-context learning, how an induction head implements part of it, and why some "emergent" abilities may be a measurement effect. (4 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
In-context learning: a frozen model infers a task from examples in the prompt (English → French pairs, then "cheese →" gives "fromage") with no weight updates; the examples constrain the continuation so the pattern is the only coherent option.

Induction head: if token $A$ was followed by $B$ earlier, after $A$ again predict $B$. Two layers: a previous-token head marks each token with its predecessor, and the induction head finds the earlier $A$ and copies its successor. It works on made-up tokens, so it is an algorithm (match and copy), not word knowledge.

Emergence: with per-token accuracy $p$, an exact $L$-token answer is right with probability $p^L$, so smooth per-token gains look like a sudden jump in exact match; some thresholds are metric artefacts.

rubric.point: ICL: task from prompt examples, no weight change
Induction rule A…B…A → B
Two-head circuit; works on invented tokens (algorithmic)
p^L exact-match argument for apparent emergence

questions.explanation: Lecture 10 Part 3 (slides 16–18).

questions.question: Context: "… Mr Dursley saw Harry Potter. Later, Harry". An induction head predicts which next word?
questions.explanation: If $A$ was followed by $B$ earlier, then after $A$ again predict $B$ (slide 17): match the earlier "Harry" and copy what followed it.

questions.question: Which statements about induction heads are true?
choices: They work even on made-up tokens never seen in training
They are a match-and-copy algorithm rather than memorised word knowledge
They are a single attention head in the first layer
They only work for English words
questions.explanation: Slide 17: it is a two-layer circuit (a previous-token head plus the induction head), so it is an algorithm that doesn't care what the tokens are.

questions.question: True or False: An induction head needs two attention layers working together: a previous-token head and a head that uses it to copy what followed an earlier occurrence of the current token.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Slide 17: one head marks each token with its predecessor, a later head finds the earlier copy of the current token and copies what followed it. That's why it needs two layers, and why it works even on made-up tokens.

questions.question: If each token of an answer is correct with probability $p$ independently, an exact $L$-token answer is correct with probability $p^L$. For $L = 20$, give the exact-match accuracy when (a) $p = 0.9$, (b) $p = 0.95$, (c) $p = 0.99$.
questions.explanation: Smooth per-token gains look like a sudden jump in exact match on long answers, so some "emergent" abilities are a metric effect (slide 18).

questions.question: Why can a capability appear to "emerge" suddenly with scale even if the model improves smoothly?
choices: Exact-match scoring on long answers ($p^L$) turns smooth per-token gains into an apparent jump
Large models switch to a different architecture
Emergence is always a sign of a new circuit
The loss stops being a power law at large scale
questions.explanation: Slide 18: some emergence is real (circuits like induction heads appear during training), but some thresholds are measurement artefacts. Always ask what metric was used.

questions.question: Compare a plain model's parametric memory with RAG's non-parametric documents (slide 20).

pairs.prompt: How to update knowledge in the weights
How to update knowledge in RAG
Which one can cite its source

questions.explanation: A plain model is a closed-book exam; RAG is open-book: capacity grows with the corpus and answers can be cited, at the cost of a search step.

questions.question: Describe retrieval-augmented generation: why it is used, its pipeline, two ways to retrieve passages, and two ways it can fail. (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Why: a plain LM is a closed-book exam: knowledge is frozen in its weights, rare facts are weak and missing ones get hallucinated. RAG is open-book: knowledge is updated by editing an index, grows with the corpus and can be cited.

Pipeline: offline, split documents into passages, embed and index them; online, embed the query, retrieve the $k$ nearest passages, place them in the prompt and generate.

Retrieval: BM25 (shared words, rare terms weighted higher, like TF-IDF; misses synonyms) and dense embeddings (semantic, handles synonyms); often combined and reranked.

Failures: missing the right passage, lost in the middle of long contexts, irrelevant passages distracting, retrieved text contradicting memorised knowledge. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately.

rubric.point: Motivation: frozen/stale parametric memory, hallucination; updatable and citable
Pipeline: chunk → embed → index; query → nearest neighbours → prompt → generate
BM25 vs dense retrieval and the synonym problem
Failure mode 1
Failure mode 2 (or evaluating retrieval and generation separately)

questions.explanation: Lecture 10 Part 4 (slides 20–23).

questions.question: Which is the correct order of the RAG pipeline?
choices: Split documents into passages → embed and index them → embed the query → retrieve the $k$ nearest passages → put them in the prompt → generate
Embed the query → fine-tune the model on it → generate
Generate an answer → search for documents that agree → cite them
Retrieve every document → concatenate them all into the prompt → generate
questions.explanation: Slide 21: indexing is done once offline; per query you embed, find nearest neighbours, and generate from the prompt plus passages.

questions.question: A user asks about a "specialist" but the right passage only says "expert". Which retriever is more likely to find it, and why?
choices: Dense retrieval, because it compares meaning embeddings and handles synonyms
BM25, because it gives rare words more weight
BM25, because it counts shared words
Neither: retrieval only matches exact strings
questions.explanation: BM25 (like TF-IDF) matches shared words and weights rare ones, so it misses synonyms; dense embeddings handle them. Real systems often combine both and rerank (slide 22).

questions.question: Which are failure modes of RAG named in Lecture 10?
choices: Facts in the middle of a long context are used less well ("lost in the middle")
Irrelevant retrieved passages distract the model
A retrieved passage can contradict what the model memorised
Retrieval permanently changes the model's weights
questions.explanation: Slide 23: evaluate retrieval and generation separately: was the evidence found, and was the answer faithful to it? Agentic systems let the model decide when and what to search.

questions.question:
(a) How many sequential forward passes does an autoregressive model need for a 1,000-token answer?
(b) A masked diffusion LM fills 3 tokens per pass. How many passes for a 12-token sentence?
(c) Block diffusion with 16-token blocks fills 4 tokens per pass inside a block. How many passes for 1,024 tokens?
questions.solution: (a) One pass per token: 1,000. (b) $12/3 = 4$. (c) $1024/16 = 64$ blocks, each $16/4 = 4$ passes: $64 \times 4 = 256$.
questions.explanation: Slide 28's example: 12 autoregressive passes vs 4 diffusion passes. Too many tokens per pass lowers quality.

questions.question: Compare autoregressive generation with masked diffusion language models, including how a masked diffusion LM is trained, and explain what block diffusion adds. (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Autoregression writes one token at a time, left to right: 1,000 tokens need 1,000 sequential passes and tokens can't be revised, but output length is flexible and a KV cache makes it efficient.

Masked diffusion: training picks a masking level $t \in [0,1]$, hides each token with probability $t$ and predicts all hidden tokens (average surprise on them), over all levels, so generation can start fully masked and fill several tokens per round. It sees both sides, can revise guesses and fills middle gaps naturally, but the length is fixed in advance, there is no direct KV cache, and too many tokens per pass hurts quality.

Block diffusion generates blocks left to right and denoises tokens within a block in parallel; finished blocks are cached and any length is possible. Block size one is autoregression.

rubric.point: Autoregression: sequential, can't revise, flexible length, KV cache
Masked diffusion training: random masking level t, predict masked tokens
Diffusion pros: parallel, both sides, can revise / fill gaps
Diffusion cons: fixed length, no direct caching, quality drops with too many tokens per pass
Block diffusion: blocks left to right, parallel within, cacheable; block size 1 = AR

questions.explanation: Lecture 10 Part 5 (slides 25–31).

questions.question: Text can't be blurred like an image. What plays the role of "noise" in a masked diffusion language model?
choices: Replacing tokens with a mask token, with each token hidden independently with probability $t$
Adding Gaussian noise to the token ids
Shuffling the word order
Lowering the softmax temperature
questions.explanation: Slides 26–27: masking is the discrete analogue of noise. Training covers every masking level $t \in [0,1]$, so generation can start from a fully masked sequence.

questions.question: Match each property to the model it describes (slide 29).

pairs.prompt: Can use a KV cache directly
Filling a gap in the middle is natural
Can't revise a token once written

questions.explanation: Diffusion is parallel, sees both sides and can revise, but needs the length up front and can't cache directly.

choices: True
False
questions.question: True or False: Block diffusion with a block size of one is ordinary autoregression.
questions.explanation: True (slide 30). Blocks are generated left to right and denoised in parallel inside, so block size sets a continuum between fully sequential and fully parallel. Finished blocks are cacheable.

questions.question: What does Transfusion do?
choices: Trains one transformer on mixed text and image sequences: next-token prediction for text, diffusion for image patches
Fuses two language models into one by averaging weights
Uses diffusion for text and next-token prediction for images
Translates images into text before training
questions.explanation: Slide 31: a shared architecture doesn't need a shared loss. Text benefits from order; images from global denoising (a sun and its shadow are produced together).

questions.question: What is the order of the three RLHF stages?
choices: Supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations → reward model from pairwise preferences → RL (e.g. PPO) against the reward with a KL leash
Reward model → pre-training → supervised fine-tuning
RL from scratch → supervised fine-tuning → preference ranking
Pairwise preferences → pre-training → distillation
questions.explanation: Slide 33. People compare two answers because that is easier than writing a perfect one. InstructGPT showed a well post-trained small model can be preferred over a much larger base model.

questions.question: Explain how RLHF post-trains a language model, the role of the KL term, what reward hacking is, and how RLVR with GRPO differs. (6 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
A base model imitates text rather than following instructions, and goals like helpful/honest/harmless are hard to write as a loss.

RLHF: (1) SFT on demonstrations; (2) people compare pairs of answers (easier than writing a perfect one) and a reward model learns $r(A) > r(B)$; (3) RL (e.g. PPO) maximises reward $-\ \beta D_{KL}(\pi \| \pi_{SFT})$.

The KL leash keeps the policy near the SFT model: the reward model is only a proxy, so with small $\beta$ the policy exploits its errors (reward hacking: e.g. flattery, verbosity, sycophancy), while large $\beta$ changes little. DPO skips the reward model and RL loop but still optimises a proxy.

RLVR uses rewards a program can check (maths answers, code tests); GRPO samples a group of answers and reinforces those above the group average. It is grounded and harder to game, but only works where correctness is checkable.

rubric.point: Why post-train: base model imitates, goals hard to write as a loss
SFT → pairwise preferences → reward model
RL against reward with KL term to the SFT model
Reward hacking explained, and the effect of β
RLVR: verifiable reward (maths/code), grounded but limited to checkable tasks
GRPO: group of answers, compare to group average

questions.explanation: Lecture 10 Part 6 (slides 33–37).

questions.question:
The policy maximises $\text{reward} - \beta\, D_{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi_{SFT})$. Answer A has reward 3.0 and KL 2.0; answer B has reward 2.5 and KL 0.5.
(a) A's objective with $\beta = 0.1$. (b) B's with $\beta = 0.1$.
(c) A's with $\beta = 1$. (d) B's with $\beta = 1$.
questions.explanation: With a weak leash the high-reward answer that drifts far from the SFT model (e.g. flattery the reward model overrates) wins; a strong leash prefers the answer that stays close (slide 35).

questions.question: What is reward hacking?
choices: Maximising the learned reward (a proxy) without achieving the real human goal, e.g. sycophancy or verbosity
Humans giving deliberately wrong preference labels
Stealing another model's reward model
Training with too high a learning rate
questions.explanation: The reward model is only an approximation; a small $\beta$ lets the policy exploit its errors. Over-optimising any proxy can raise its score while lowering true quality (slides 35–36).

choices: True
False
questions.question: True or False: DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation) needs a separately trained reward model and an RL loop.
questions.explanation: False. DPO skips both and directly makes preferred answers more likely than rejected ones relative to a reference model. It still relies on preference data, an imperfect proxy (slide 36).

questions.question:
GRPO samples a group of 4 answers to a maths problem; a checker gives rewards $(1, 0, 0, 0)$. Each answer's advantage is its reward minus the group mean.
(a) The group mean. (b) The correct answer's advantage. (c) A wrong answer's advantage.
questions.explanation: Slide 37: above-average answers become more likely, below-average ones less. (Real GRPO also divides by the group's standard deviation; the slide keeps it to "compare with the group average".)

questions.question: Which statements about RLVR (reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards) are true?
choices: The reward is a program's check, such as a maths answer checker or code tests
It is harder to game than a learned preference model because it is grounded in an external check
It only applies where correctness can be checked automatically
It needs humans to compare pairs of answers
questions.explanation: Slide 37: used for reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1 (with GRPO). The grounding links back to Lecture 9: verified, grounded synthetic data avoids collapse.

questions.question: Why can a toy network pack five features into a two-dimensional hidden layer?
choices: The features are sparse (usually zero), so they rarely clash and can share almost-orthogonal directions
Each feature gets its own neuron
The network stores only the two most frequent features
Superposition works best when the features always occur together
questions.explanation: Slide 40: if features co-occur often, interference is costly and only two survive; if they are sparse, all five fit as a pentagon. Real concepts ("king" and "chainsaw") are rarely active together.

choices: True
False
questions.question: True or False: In a large language model each concept is stored in its own dedicated neuron.
questions.explanation: False. Models know more concepts than neurons, so a feature is a direction across neurons; concepts share neurons through almost-orthogonal directions ($h = \sum_i a_i w_i$, most $a_i = 0$).

questions.question: Explain superposition and why sparsity makes it possible, then describe two tools used to read what a model represents (sparse autoencoders, the logit lens or the J-lens). (5 Marks)
questions.modelAnswer:
Concepts are directions in activation space (king − man + woman ≈ queen). Models know more concepts than they have neurons, so features share neurons as almost-orthogonal directions: superposition, $h = \sum_i a_i w_i$ with most $a_i = 0$.

Sparsity: in the toy model, five features squeezed through 2D clash if they co-occur (only two survive), but if they are usually zero, interference is rare and all five fit as a pentagon. So individual neurons are hard to interpret.

Tools: a sparse autoencoder expands activations into many features with only a few active (reconstruction + sparsity loss), giving fairly monosemantic, steerable features (Golden Gate Bridge), though imperfectly. The logit lens applies $W_U$ to a middle layer; the J-lens first applies an averaged Jacobian of the later layers, $W_U(J_l h_l)$, revealing a small "J-space" of word-like concepts that can be steered (Spanish ↔ French). J-space is very recent and not widely replicated.

rubric.point: Concepts as directions; more concepts than neurons
Superposition: features share neurons as near-orthogonal directions
Sparsity makes it work (toy model: co-occurring vs sparse features)
Tool 1 explained
Tool 2 explained (with a limitation)

questions.explanation: Lecture 10 Part 7 (slides 39–43).

questions.question: Five features are packed in 2D as the corners of a regular pentagon (72° apart). What is the cosine between neighbouring feature directions (the interference when both are active)?
questions.solution: $\cos 72^\circ = 0.309$ (and $\cos 144^\circ = -0.809$ for non-neighbours).
questions.explanation: Not orthogonal, so two active features interfere; that's acceptable only because they are rarely active together.

questions.question: Which statements about sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are true?
choices: They expand an activation into many possible features, keep only a few active and reconstruct the activation
Their loss combines reconstruction error with a sparsity penalty
Their features can be fairly monosemantic (e.g. French text, the Golden Gate Bridge), and boosting one can steer the output
They reconstruct the activations perfectly, so they explain all of the computation
questions.explanation: Slide 41: SAEs try to untangle superposed features, but the reconstruction is imperfect.

questions.question: How does the J-lens differ from the logit lens?
choices: It first applies an averaged Jacobian $J_l$ of the remaining layers before the unembedding: $W_U(J_l h_l)$
It trains a new classifier on each layer
It applies $W_U$ directly to a middle layer
It reads the attention weights instead of the activations
questions.explanation: Slide 42: the logit lens applies $W_U$ straight to a middle layer (works better late than early); the J-lens translates the direction through the rest of the network first, so it shows concepts that influence later output.

questions.question: Which statements about J-space match Lecture 10?
choices: The J-lens finds a small set (roughly 25 or fewer) of word-like concepts active together in middle layers
Swapping a Spanish direction for a French one changes the output language
It is compared functionally to global workspace theory, as an analogy
It proves the model is conscious
questions.explanation: Slide 43: very recent (July 2026) and not widely replicated. The safety interest is that it may reveal internal goals or awareness of being tested; it is not evidence of consciousness.

questions.question: What is the high-level goal of mechanistic interpretability (Tutorial 8.1)?
choices: To reverse-engineer the computations inside a trained network into human-understandable mechanisms (circuits), such as induction heads
To make models smaller by pruning
To measure a model's accuracy on benchmarks
To write programs that generate neural networks
questions.explanation: Not on the slides: this follows the standard definition used in the tutorial. Induction heads are a classic example of a circuit found this way. Lecture 10's Part 7 (superposition, sparse autoencoders, the logit lens and J-lens) is mechanistic interpretability in practice.

questions.question: True or False: Probing a representation with a classifier shows that information is present, while mechanistic interpretability tries to show how the network actually uses it.
choices: True
False
questions.explanation: Probing is correlational ("decodable"); mechanistic work traces the causal circuit (e.g. which heads compose into an induction head). Tutorial 8.1 topic; standard definitions. Lecture 10's Part 7 (superposition, sparse autoencoders, the logit lens and J-lens) is mechanistic interpretability in practice.
